Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 26, verse 1–9:

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. It is Meccan according to the majority of scholars. Muqatil said: "Among it is a Medinan part: the verse in which the poets are mentioned, and His saying: 'Does it not suffice them that the scholars of the Children of Israel know it?'" Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: "It is Meccan except for four verses of it, which were revealed in Medina, from His saying: 'And the poets, the erring follow them' to the end of it." It has two hundred and twenty-seven verses. In another narration, two hundred and twenty-six.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I was given the surah in which the Cow is mentioned from the first Reminder, and I was given Ta-Ha and Ta-Sin-Mim from the tablets of Musa, and I was given the openings of the Qur'an and the closings of Surat al-Baqarah from beneath the Throne, and I was given the Mufassal as an extra gift."

It is narrated from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah gave me the seven long surahs in place of the Torah, and He gave me al-Mubin in place of the Gospel, and He gave me the Ta-Sin surahs in place of the Psalms, and He favoured me with the Hawamim and the Mufassal, which no prophet before me recited."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Ta-Sin-Mim (1). These are the verses of the Clear Book (2). Perhaps you will be killing yourself with grief that they do not become believers (3). If We willed, We would send down upon them from the sky a sign, and their necks would remain humbled before it (4).

And no fresh reminder comes to them from the Most Gracious except that they turn away from it (5). So they have denied, and there will come to them the news of what they used to mock (6). Have they not looked at the earth, how many noble pairs of every kind We have caused to grow in it? (7) Indeed in that is a sign, yet most of them are not believers (8). And indeed your Lord, He is the Almighty, the Most Merciful (9).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Ta-Sin-Mim﴾. Al-A'mash, Yahya, Abu Bakr, al-Mufaddal, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read the ta with imalah (inclination) and lengthening (ishba') in this surah and in its two sisters. Nafi', Abu Ja'far, Shaybah and al-Zuhri read it between the two pronunciations, and this was chosen by Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim. The rest read it with fath (open vowel) and lengthening. Al-Tha'labi said: "All of them are eloquent dialects." The statement of al-Nahhas on this has already passed in "Ta-Ha" [[See vol. 11, p. 168, first or second edition.]]. Al-Nahhas said: The Madinans, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and al-Kisa'i read "Ta-Sin-Mim" with idgham (assimilation) of the nun into the mim, while al-Farra' says with ikhfa' (concealment) of the nun. Al-A'mash and Hamzah read "Ta-Sin Mim" with izhar (clear pronunciation) of the nun. Al-Nahhas said: The sakinah nun and tanwin have four categories according to Sibawayh: they are made clear before the throat letters, they are assimilated before ra, lam, mim, waw and ya, they are changed to mim before ba, and they are nasalised, meaning they are not made clear. According to these four categories which Sibawayh stated, this reading is not permissible, because there is no throat letter here for the nun to be made clear before. However, there is a justification for it: the letters of the alphabet are to be pronounced in pause, and when they are pronounced in pause, the nun becomes clear. Al-Tha'labi said: Idgham is the choice of Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim by analogy with the whole Qur'an, and those who made it clear did so for clarity and distinctness, while those who assimilated it did so because it is adjacent to the letters of the mouth. Al-Nahhas said: Abu Ishaq related in his book "What is Declined and What is Not Declined" that it is permissible to say "Ta-sina mimu" with fath on the nun and damm on the mim, just as one says "hadha Ma'di Karib". Abu Hatim said: Khalid read "Ta-sina mimu". Ibn 'Abbas said: "Ta-Sin-Mim" is an oath, and it is one of the names of Allah the Exalted, and the thing sworn to is "If We willed, We would send down upon them from the sky a sign." Qatadah said: It is a name of the Qur'an which Allah swore by. Mujahid said: It is the name of the surah, and it beautifies the opening of the surah. Al-Rabi' said: It is the reckoning of the duration of a people. It was also said: it is a calamity that strikes a people. "Ta-Sin-Mim" and "Ta-Sin" are the same. The poet said [[This is al-Mutanabbi, the verse being the opening of a qasidah he composed praising Abu al-Hasan 'Ali ibn 'Abd Allah al-'Adawi. Ashjahu: saddened him. Al-Tasim: the effaced. Al-Sajim: the one shedding tears. The meaning: he asked of them fulfilment of their pledge by aiding weeping and agreement, and therefore said: "and the tear, its shedding has tormented him." The meaning: weep with me with tears in profuse flow, for it is more healing to the longing, since the abandoned encampment is in a state of total effacement, and it is more saddening to the lover. He meant by fulfilment here weeping, because they had pledged him to assist. Sharh al-Tibyan vol. 2 by al-'Ukbari.]]:

Your fulfilment is like the abandoned encampment, which its effacement has saddened, that you two should help, and the tear, its flow has tormented him.

Al-Qurazi said: Allah swore by His greatness, His bounty and His dominion. 'Abd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn 'Aqil said: The ta is Mount Sinai, the sin is Alexandria, and the mim is Mecca. Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn 'Ali said: The ta is the tree of Tuba, the sin is the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary, and the mim is Muhammad (ﷺ). It was said: the ta is from "al-Tahir" (the Pure), the sin is from "al-Quddus" (the Holy) — it was also said: from "al-Sami'" (the All-Hearing), and it was also said: from "al-Salam" (the Source of Peace) — and the mim is from "al-Majid" (the All-Glorious). It was also said: from "al-Rahim" (the Most Merciful). It was also said: from "al-Malik" (the King). This meaning has already passed at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, p. 154.]]. The "Tawasim" and "Tawasin" are surahs in the Qur'an, pluralised without analogy. Abu 'Ubaydah recited:

And by the Tawasim, which were made threefold, and by the Hawamim, which were made sevenfold.

Al-Jawhari said: The correct form is to pluralise with dhawat and attach it to a singular noun, so one says: dhawat Ta-Sin-Mim and dhawat Ha-Mim.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿These are the verses of the Clear Book﴾ is in the nominative by presupposing a subject, meaning: these are "the verses of the Clear Book" which you were promised, for they had been promised in the Torah and the Gospel the sending down of the Qur'an. It was also said: "Tilka" means "hadhihi" (these).

(Perhaps you will be killing yourself) meaning destroying yourself and causing its ruin. Its explanation has passed in "al-Kahf" [[See vol. 10, p. 348.]].

(That they do not become believers) meaning because of their abandoning faith. Al-Farra' said: "an" is in the accusative position because it is a conditional. Al-Nahhas said: It is commonly said "bi-in" with a kasra because it is a conditional, as is commonly known. The position on this is what Abu Ishaq said in his book on the Qur'an: "an" is in the accusative position as an object of purpose, and the meaning is: perhaps you are killing yourself because of their abandoning faith.

(If We willed, We would send down upon them from the sky a sign) meaning a manifest miracle and a dazzling power, so that their knowledge would become necessary; but the decree had already preceded that their knowledge would be by reflection. Abu Hamzah al-Thumali said regarding this verse: a sound heard from the sky in the middle of the month of Ramadan, by which the unmarried women come out of their houses and the earth cries out. This is far-fetched, because what is meant is Quraysh and no one else.

(Then their necks would remain) meaning then their necks would remain (humbled before it). Mujahid said: "their necks" means their chiefs. Al-Nahhas said: This is well known in the language; it is said: "a neck of people came to me," meaning chiefs among them. Abu Zayd and al-Akhfash said: "a'naquhum" means their groups; it is said: "a neck of people came to me," meaning a group. It was also said: he meant the owners of the necks, so the governed noun was omitted and the governing noun was placed in its position. Qatadah said: The meaning is that if He willed, He would send down a sign by which they would be humbled, so none of them would turn his neck to disobedience. Ibn 'Abbas said: It was revealed concerning us and the Banu Umayyah: "Dominion will be ours over them, and their necks will be humbled to us after Mu'awiyah," narrated by al-Tha'labi and al-Ghaznawi. "Khadi'in" and "khadi'ah" are the same here, said 'Isa ibn 'Umar, and al-Mubarrad chose it. The meaning: when their necks are humbled, they are humbled; so the report about the necks is a report about their owners. It is permissible in Arabic speech to leave out the report about the first and report about the second. The rajiz said:

The lengthening of the nights hastened my wearing away; they stretched out my length and my breadth.

He reported about the nights and left out "length". Jarir said [[The verse was cited in vol. 7, p. 264.]]:

I see the passing of years has taken from me as the crescent takes from the moon.

This is permissible because if "passing" and "length" were dropped from the speech, its meaning would not be corrupted; likewise the verb is returned to the pronoun in His saying: "their necks remained", because if the necks were dropped the speech would not be corrupted, and what remained of the speech would convey the meaning, so that it would say: "they remained humbled before it." On this al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubaydah relied. Al-Kisa'i holds that the meaning is "its humblers are they," and this is an error according to the Basrans and al-Farra'. Such omission does not occur in any speech, said al-Nahhas.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Yet no fresh reminder comes to them from the Most Gracious except that they turn away from it﴾ has passed in "al-Anbiya'" [[See vol. 11, p. 268.]].

(So they have denied) meaning they turned away, and whoever turns away from something and does not accept it has denied it.

(So there will come to them the news of what they used to mock) is a threat to them, meaning: the consequence of what they denied and what they mocked will surely come to them.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Have they not looked at the earth, how many noble pairs of every kind We have caused to grow in it?﴾ alerts to His greatness and His power, and that if they had seen with their hearts and looked with their insight, they would have known that He is the One deserving to be worshipped, since He is capable of everything. "Zawj" (pair) is a kind, said al-Farra'. "Karim" means good and noble; the root meaning of generosity in the language is nobility and excellence, so a "karimah" palm is an excellent palm abundant in fruit [[In another copy: abundant in fruiting.]], and a "karim" man is noble, excellent and forgiving. "Nabatat al-ard" and "anbatat" have the same meaning. It has been mentioned in the surahs of al-Baqarah, and Allah the Glorified is the One who brings forth and causes to grow. It is narrated from al-Sha'bi that he said: People are from the plants of the earth; whoever among them goes to Paradise is noble, and whoever goes to the Fire is base.

(Indeed in that is a sign) meaning in what was mentioned of the growing in the earth, for it indicates that Allah is capable, and nothing can overcome Him.

(Yet most of them are not believers) meaning not affirming what has preceded from My knowledge concerning them. "Kana" here is superfluous according to Sibawayh's view, its estimated form being: "and how many of them are believers." (And indeed your Lord, He is the Almighty, the Most Merciful) means the Impregnable, the Avenger against His enemies, the Most Merciful to His friends.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Have they not looked at the earth, how many noble pairs of every kind We have caused to grow in it? (7) Indeed in that is a sign, yet most of them are not believers (8). In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Have they not looked at the earth, how many noble pairs of every kind We have caused to grow in it? (7) Indeed in that is a sign, yet most of them are not believers (8). And indeed your Lord, He is the Almighty, the Most Merciful (9).

Abu Hatim said: Khalid read "Ta-sina mimu". Ibn 'Abbas said: "Ta-Sin-Mim" is an oath, and it is one of the names of Allah the Exalted, and the thing sworn to is "If We willed, We would send down upon them from the sky a sign." Qatadah said: It is a name of the Qur'an which Allah swore by. Mujahid said: It is the name of the surah, and it beautifies the opening of the surah. Al-Rabi' said: It is the reckoning of the duration of a people. It was also said: it is a calamity that strikes a people. "Ta-Sin-Mim" and "Ta-Sin" are the same. The poet said [[This is al-Mutanabbi, the verse being the opening of a qasidah he composed praising Abu al-Hasan 'Ali ibn 'Abd Allah al-'Adawi. Ashjahu: saddened him. Al-Tasim: the effaced. Al-Sajim: the one shedding tears. The meaning: he asked of them fulfilment of their pledge by aiding weeping and agreement, and therefore said: "and the tear, its shedding has tormented him." Your fulfilment is like the abandoned encampment, which its effacement has saddened, that you two should help, and the tear, its flow has tormented him.

Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn 'Ali said: The ta is the tree of Tuba, the sin is the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary, and the mim is Muhammad (ﷺ). Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 26, verses 10–15:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when your Lord called out to Musa﴾. "Idh" (when) is in the accusative position; the meaning is: "And recite to them, when your Lord called out to Musa." This is supported by what follows: "And recite to them the news of Ibrahim." This is mentioned by al-Nahhas. It is also said that the meaning is: "Remember when he called out," as made explicit in His saying: "And remember the brother of 'Ad," and His saying: "And remember Our servants Ibrahim," and His saying: "And remember in the Book Maryam." It is also said that the meaning is: "When your Lord called out to Musa, it was such and such." The "nida'" (calling) is supplication with "ya" plus a name, meaning: your Lord said, "O Musa: (Go to the wrongdoing people)," then He informed who they were, saying: (the people of Pharaoh; will they not fear God?). So "qawma" (the people of) is an apposition (badal), and the meaning of "alla yattaqun" is: will they not fear the punishment of God? It is also said that this is an allusion to the matter, because He commanded him to go to the wrongdoing people, and His saying "yattaqun" indicates that they do not fear God, and that He commanded them to be God-conscious. It is also said that the meaning is: say to them, "Will you not fear God?" and it came with the "ya" (yattaqun) because they were absent at the time of address; had it come with the "ta" (tattaqun) it would have been permissible. A similar case is: "Say to those who disbelieve, you will be overcome," read with both "ta" and "ya." Ubayd ibn 'Umayr and Abu Hazim read "alla tattaqun" with two "ta"s, meaning: say to them, "Will you not fear God?"

(He said, "My Lord") i.e., Musa said, (My Lord, I fear that they will deny me) i.e., regarding the message and the prophethood.

(And my breast will be constrained) by their denying me. The common reading is "wa yadiqu" and "wa la yantaliqu" in the nominative, as a new sentence (isti'naf). Ya'qub, 'Isa ibn 'Umar and Abu Haywa read "wa yadiqa" and "wa la yantaliqa" in the accusative in both, as a response to His saying: "that they will deny me." Al-Kisa'i said: the reading is with the nominative, meaning in "my breast is constrained and my tongue does not speak," being a separate clause following "inni akhafu." Al-Farra' said: it is also read in the accusative; this is related from al-A'raj, Talha and 'Isa ibn 'Umar, and both have a valid basis. Allah's words: ﴿That you send with us the Children of Israel.﴾ That is, release them and let them go, so that they may travel with us to Palestine, and do not enslave them. Pharaoh had enslaved them for four hundred years, and at that time they numbered six hundred thousand and thirty thousand.

They went to Pharaoh, but they were not permitted to enter upon him for a year. Then the gatekeeper entered upon Pharaoh and said: "Here is a man who claims he is a messenger of the Lord of the worlds." Pharaoh said: "Permit him, perhaps we may laugh at him." So they entered upon him and delivered the message.

Wahb and others narrated: When they entered upon Pharaoh, they found him having brought out wild beasts, lions, leopards and panthers, which he was viewing for amusement. His keepers feared that they would attack Moses and Aaron, so they hurried toward them, and the beasts hurried toward Moses and Aaron. They came licking their feet, wagging their tails at them, and pressing their cheeks against their thighs. Pharaoh was amazed at this and said: "What are you two?" They said: "We are a messenger of the Lord of the worlds."

Moses recognized him, because he had grown up in his house. So he said, ﴿Did we not raise you among us as a child?﴾ in a manner of reminding him of a favour and of contempt, meaning: we raised you as a child and did not kill you among those whom we killed. ﴿And you stayed among us for years of your life.﴾ So when was this that you claim? Then he established against him the killing of the Copt by his saying: ﴿And you did your deed which you did.﴾ "Fa'latun" with a fatha on the fa' means a single occurrence of the action. Al-Sha'bi recited "fi'latak" with a kasra on the fa', but the fatha is preferable, because it denotes a single occurrence, whereas the kasra denotes a form and a state, meaning: "your deed which you know, so how do you claim, while we know your condition, that Allah has sent you?" The poet said:

*As if her walk from the house of her neighbour*
*was the passing of a cloud, neither slow nor hasty.*

It is also said: that was during the days of apostasy (riddah) and of the deed. ﴿And you were among the disbelievers.﴾ Al-Dahhak said: that is, in your killing of the Copt, since he was a soul whose killing was not permitted. It was also said: that is, by My favour which was ours upon you, of rearing and kindness to you. Ibn Zayd said this. Al-Hasan said: "among the disbelievers" in that I am your god. Al-Suddi said: "among the disbelievers" in Allah, because you were with us upon this religion of ours which you find fault with.

Between Moses' departure, when he killed the Copt, and his return as a prophet, there were eleven years, apart from some months.

﴿He said: I did it, then, when I was﴾ that is, you did that deed, meaning the killing of the Copt, ﴿and I was then among the astray﴾ that is, among the ignorant. So he denied disbelief for himself and informed that he had done that out of ignorance. Mujahid also said likewise: "among the astray" means "among the ignorant." Ibn Zayd said: "among the ignorant of the fact that a blow could reach the point of killing." In the codex of Abdullah [[Ibn Mas'ud]] it reads "among the ignorant," and it is said of one who is ignorant of something that he has gone astray from it. It was also said: "and I am among the astray" means "among the forgetful," as Abu Ubayda said. It was also said: "and I am among the astray" means "astray concerning prophethood, and no command from Allah had come to me about it, so there is no reproach upon me for what I did in that state." By this it is made clear that rearing them does not contradict prophethood, nor does forbearance toward people, and that the killing was a mistake or occurred at a time when there was no law, which does not contradict prophethood.

Allah's words: ﴿So I fled from you when I feared you.﴾ That is, I went out from among you to Madyan, as in surah al-Qasas: ﴿So he went out from it, fearful, watching.﴾ This was at the time of the killing.

﴿Then my Lord granted me wisdom﴾ meaning prophethood, according to al-Suddi and others. Al-Zajjaj said: the teaching of the Torah, in which is the judgment of Allah. It was also said: knowledge and understanding.

﴿And made me one of the messengers.﴾

Allah's words: ﴿And is this a favour you reckon upon me, that you enslaved the Children of Israel?﴾ People differed about the meaning of this statement. Al-Suddi, al-Tabari and al-Farra' said: this statement from Moses, peace be upon him, is in the manner of acknowledging the favour, as if he were saying: "Yes! And your rearing of me is a favour upon me, inasmuch as you enslaved others and left me, but that does not remove my mission." It was also said: it is from Moses, peace be upon him, in the manner of denial, meaning: "Do you reckon upon me a favour, that you raised me as a child, while you had enslaved the Children of Israel and killed them?" That is, it is not a favour, because what was obligatory was that you should not kill them or enslave them, for they are my people, so how do you mention your kindness to me in particular? Qatada and others said this in meaning. It was also said: there is an implied interrogative in it, meaning: "Or is this a favour?" This was said by al-Akhfash and also al-Farra'. Al-Nahhas denied it and others did too. Al-Nahhas said: "This is not permissible, because the interrogative alif produces a meaning, and omitting it is impossible unless there is an 'am' in the statement, as the poet said:

*Does she depart from the tribe, or does she set out early?*

I know of no disagreement among the grammarians on this except for something said by al-Farra', who said: the interrogative alif is permitted with verbs of doubt, and it is related: "Do you see Zayd as departing?" meaning "Do you see...?" Ali ibn Sulayman used to say about this: "He only took it from the vulgar speech." Al-Tha'labi said: al-Farra' said, and whoever said that it is a denial, said its meaning is "or is that a favour?" in the manner of interrogation, as in His saying: ﴿This is my Lord﴾ and ﴿Then are they the immortals?﴾ The poet said [[he is Abu Khirash al-Hudhali; the explanation of this verse has been given earlier in vol. 11, p. 287 of this edition, first or second printing]]:

*They pushed me back and said: "O Khuwaylid, do not be alarmed,"*
*so I said, while denying the faces: "They are they!"*

Al-Ghaznawi cited as evidence for the omission of the alif the saying:

*I have not forgotten the day of departure, her standing,*
*and her eyelid was wet with her tears,*

and her saying, while the riding-camels were standing:
*"You leave me like this, and you depart?"*

I say: in this, the interrogative alif is omitted without "am," contrary to the saying of al-Nahhas. Al-Dahhak said: the statement came out in the manner of rebuke, and rebuke may occur with an interrogative or without one. The meaning is: "Had you not killed the Children of Israel, my parents would have reared me, so what favour is there for you upon me? You reckon upon me a favour for what you ought not to reckon it for." It was also said: the meaning is: "How do you reckon the rearing a favour, when you have humiliated my people? And whoever has his people humiliated is himself humbled."

"An 'abbadta" is in the nominative position as a substitute (badal) for "ni'matun." It may also be in the accusative position, with the meaning: "because you enslaved the Children of Israel," that is, "because you took them as slaves." It is said: "abbadtuhu" and "a'badtuhu" have the same meaning. Al-Farra' said, and recited:

*Why does my people enslave me, when they have multiplied*
*among them camels, which they hold as they wish, and slaves?*

**Allah's words: ﴿Pharaoh said: "And what is the Lord of the worlds?"﴾** When Musa (Moses) defeated Pharaoh with proof, and the accursed one could find no argument left after Musa's demonstration of his upbringing and other matters, he turned to opposing Musa's words, "a messenger of the Lord of the worlds." So he asked him a question about an unknown thing. Makki (Abu Muhammad Makki ibn Abi Talib) and others said: he asked as one asks about kinds (ajnas) of things, which is why he used "ma" (what). Makki said: he also used "man" (who) in another place, and it seems these are different occasions. So Musa answered with attributes that indicate Allah through His creatures, which no creature shares with Him. Pharaoh asked about the genus, but Allah has no genus, because genera are created things. Musa knew his ignorance, so he turned away from his question and informed him of the great power of Allah, which makes clear to the listener that Pharaoh has no share in it.

Pharaoh said, **(Do you not listen?)**, meaning to incite and to express astonishment at the foolishness of the statement, since the people's belief was that Pharaoh was their lord and their deity, and the pharaohs before him were likewise. Musa elaborated the explanation with his words, **(Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers of old)**, bringing evidence they could understand, because they know that they had fathers, that those fathers have perished, that there must be one who changes things, and that they came into existence after they were not, so they must have a Creator.

Then Pharaoh said, in contempt, **(Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is surely mad)**, meaning: he does not answer what I ask. Musa, peace be upon him, answered this by saying: **(Lord of the east and the west)**, meaning: His dominion is not like your dominion, for you only rule one land, your command does not extend beyond it, and those whom you do not wish to die die anyway, whereas the One who sent me possesses the east and the west **(and what is between them, if you were to understand)**.

It was also said: Musa, peace be upon him, knew that Pharaoh's intent in the question was to know who it was he was asking about, so he answered with what is the way to know the Lord today.

Then, when Pharaoh, may Allah curse him, was silenced in the matter of argument, he returned to domination and force, and threatened Musa with imprisonment. He did not say, "What is your proof that this God sent you?", because that would imply acknowledging that there is another god besides himself. His threat of imprisonment shows weakness. It is related that he (Musa) caused him great terror, to the point that the accursed one could not hold back his urine. It is also related that his prison was worse than execution: whenever he imprisoned someone, he did not release him until he died, so he was feared.

Then, since Musa, peace be upon him, had from Allah what would not make him fear, when Pharaoh threatened him, he said to him, out of gentleness toward him and hope for his faith: **(Even if I bring you something clear?)**, by which your truthfulness will become evident to you. When Pharaoh heard that, he hoped to find an opening for opposition in it, so he said: **(Then bring it, if you are among the truthful)**. According to Sibawayh, the conditional clause does not need an answer, because what preceded it suffices.

**(So Musa cast his staff)** from his hand, and it was what Allah has told of his story. Its explanation and details have already been given in *al-A'raf* (see vol. 7, p. 256 and following, in the first or second edition), up to the end of the story.

When Pharaoh threatened the magicians with cutting off their hands and feet, they said: **(No harm)**, meaning: there is no harm to us in what befalls us of the punishment of this world. That is, your punishment is only for a moment, so we will endure it, and we have met Allah as believers. This indicates the intensity of their insight and the strength of their faith. Malik said: Musa, peace be upon him, called Pharaoh to Islam for forty years, and the magicians believed in him in a single day.

It is said: *la ḍayra*, *wa-la ḍawra*, *wa-la ḍarra*, *wa-la ḍarar*, and *wa-la ḍarūra* all have the same meaning, related by al-Harawi. Abu 'Ubayda recited (the verse of Khidash ibn Zuhayr, which Sibawayh cited as an example of making the subject of *kāna* indefinite and its predicate definite out of necessity; its meaning is: you need not mind, once you stand on your own and no longer depend on your parents, whether the one you are ascribed to is noble or base, and it uses the examples of the gazelle or the donkey):

*"Indeed, after a year, it will not harm you whether your mother was a gazelle or a donkey."*

Al-Jawhari said: *darrahu yadurruhu wa-yadirruhu, ḍayran wa-ḍawran*, meaning, he harmed him. Al-Kisa'i said: I heard some of them say, "That does not benefit me, nor does it harm me (*ḥa yaḍūrunī*)." *Al-Tadawwur* is shouting and writhing under beating or hunger. *Al-Ḍūra* (with a damma) is a lowly, insignificant man.

**(Indeed, to our Lord we shall return)**, meaning: we shall return to a generous, merciful Lord. **(We hope that our Lord will forgive us our sins, because we were the first of the believers)**. The *an* here is in the accusative position, meaning *li-an kunnā* (because we were). Al-Farra' permitted its being read with a kasra, as a conditional. The meaning of "the first of the believers" is: at the appearance of the sign, among those who were on Pharaoh's side. Al-Farra' said: "the first believers of our time." Al-Zajjaj rejected this and said: it has been related that six hundred and seventy thousand people believed with him, and they are the small band of whom Pharaoh said, **"Indeed, these are a small band"**. This was related from Ibn Mas'ud and others.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 26, verses 52–68 (part 1 of 2):**

God's words: ﴿And We revealed to Moses: "Travel by night with My servants, for you will be pursued."﴾ Since it is among God's ways with His servants to save the believing, faithful men among His allies, who acknowledge the messengers and prophets He sent, and to destroy the disbelieving enemies who denied them, He commanded Moses to leave with the Children of Israel by night. He called them "His servants" because they had believed in Moses. The meaning of "for you will be pursued" is that Pharaoh and his people would follow you in order to turn you back. Implicit in this statement is the information that God would deliver them from Pharaoh. So Moses, peace be upon him, set out with the Children of Israel at dawn. He left the road to Syria on his left and headed toward the sea. A man from the Children of Israel would say to him, regarding leaving the road, "Why?" and he would reply, "I have been commanded thus." When Pharaoh rose in the morning and learned of Moses' night departure with the Children of Israel, he set out in their pursuit and sent to the cities of Egypt so that the armies would join him. It is reported that he caught up with them with a hundred thousand dark-coloured (adham) horses, besides the other colours. It is also reported that the Children of Israel numbered six hundred and seventy thousand. God knows best whether this is authentic. What is necessary from the verse, and what can be asserted with certainty, is that Moses, peace be upon him, left with a large host of the Children of Israel, and that Pharaoh pursued them with many times that number.

Ibn Abbas said: "There were with Pharaoh a thousand tyrants, each of whom wore a crown and each of whom was a commander of cavalry."

The shirdhimah (شِرْذِمَةٌ) is a small, despised group. Its plural is shara<u>dh</u>im (شَرَاذِم). Al-Jawhari said: "The shirdhimah is a group of people and a piece of something. A garment that is shara<u>dh</u>im means pieces (qita')." Al-Tha'labi recited the verse of the rajaz poet:

*The winter has come, and my garments are worn out,*
*Tattered; the naww<u>a</u>q laughs at them.*

The naww<u>a</u>q (النَّوَّاق) is a man who tames affairs and sets them right. This is what al-Jawhari said in the Sihah. [It is said that naww<u>a</u>q is the name of his son. It is also narrated as al-tawwaq (التَّوَّاق) with a ta'.]

The lam in God's words ﴿Indeed, these are a small group﴾ (لَشِرْذِمَةٌ) is the lam of emphasis (lam al-tawkid). It frequently enters the predicate of inna, except that the Kufans do not permit "inna Zayd la-sawfa yaqumu" (indeed Zayd will surely stand). The evidence that it is permissible is God's words ﴿So you will surely know﴾ (فَلَسَوْفَ تَعْلَمُونَ), where this same lam of emphasis has entered upon sawfa. This is what al-Nahhas said.

﴿And indeed they are enraging us﴾ (وَإِنَّهُمْ لَنا لَغائِظُونَ), meaning: they are enemies to us because they oppose our religion and take away our wealth, which they had borrowed, as mentioned earlier. Their virgin daughters (al-abkar) died that night. This has been fully discussed in al-A'raf and Ta-Ha. It is said: ghaza-ni kadha wa-aghaza-ni (this enraged me and made me enraged). Al-ghayz is anger, and from it come al-taghayyuz and al-ightiyaz. The meaning is that they enraged us by leaving without permission.

﴿And indeed we are a wary multitude (jami'un hadhirun)﴾ (وَإِنَّا لَجَمِيعٌ حاذِرُونَ), meaning: a gathered host taking precautions with our weapons. It is read as "hadhirun" (حَذِرُونَ), whose meaning is the same as "hadhirun" (حاذِرُونَ), i.e., fearful. Al-Jawhari said: it is read "hadhirun", "hadhirun" and "hadhirun" with a damma on the dhal (ḥadhirūna), reported by al-Akhfash. The meaning of "hadhirun" is "prepared (mutaahhibun)", and the meaning of "hadhirun" is "fearful (khaifun)." Al-Nahhas said: "hadhirun" is the reading of the people of Madina and Abu Amr. The reading of the people of Kufa is "hadhirun" (حَاذِرُونَ), and it is well known from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas. "Hadirun" with an undotted dal (حَادِرُونَ) is the reading of Abu Ubayd, and al-Mahdawi transmitted it from Ibn Abi Ammar, as did al-Mawardi and al-Tha'labi from Sumayt ibn Ajlan. Al-Nahhas said: Abu Ubayda holds that the meanings of "hadhirun" and "hadhirun" are one, and this is the view of Sibawayh, who permitted: "huwa hadhirun Zaydan," just as one says "hadhir Zaydan" (be wary of Zayd). He recited:

*Wary of matters that do no harm, and secure*
*From what cannot ward off the decrees.*

Abu Umar al-Jarmi claimed that it is permissible to say "huwa hadhirun Zaydan" by omitting min (from). However, most grammarians distinguish between hadhar and hadhir. Among them are al-Kisa'i, al-Farra', and Muhammad ibn Yazid, who hold that hadhar in its form means being alert and watchful, and so it is intransitive. Hadhir means "prepared," and this explanation was transmitted from the earlier authorities. Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, regarding God's words ﴿And indeed we are a wary multitude﴾, said: "Equipped with weapons and horses, well-prepared." This is the same meaning. His words "equipped (mu'dun)" mean that they have equipment (adah). It has also been said that the meaning is: we have weapons, and they have no weapons, which incites them to fight. As for "hadirun" with an undotted dal, it derives from the expression "a'yun hadratun," meaning full (eyes). That is, we are full of rage against them. From this is the verse of the poet, Imru' al-Qays:

*And an eye full and bright, its lids split from the corners.*

The lexicographers have said: "A man is hadirun" when he is full-fleshed. So it is possible that the meaning is "full of weapons." Al-Mahdawi said: "al-hadir" is strong and powerful.

God's words: ﴿So We expelled them from gardens and springs﴾, meaning from the land of Egypt. From Abdullah ibn Amr who said: "The gardens were on the two banks of the Nile, on both sides from Aswan to Rashid, and between the gardens were fields. The Nile has seven branches (khalij): the Alexandria branch, the Sakha branch, the Damietta branch, the Sardus branch, the Manf branch, the Fayyum branch, and the Manha branch [which is the Sea of Joseph, peace be upon him], all connected, none cut off from another, and the fields lay between all the branches. All of the land of Egypt was irrigated by sixteen cubits, through the dams, bridges and canals they had arranged and measured. For this reason, when the Nile rose to sixteen cubits it was called the Sultan's Nile. Ibn Abi al-Raddad was granted a robe of honour [He was Abdullah ibn al-Salam ibn Abdullah ibn Abi al-Raddad, the muezzin, who came to Egypt from Basra and narrated hadith there. He was appointed to measure the Nile during the governorship of Yazid ibn Abdullah al-Turki, when the Christians had been in charge of measuring it. He was given seven dinars every month, and his measuring remained in his descendants for a long time. Abu al-Raddad died in the year 266 AH. From al-Maqrizi's Khitat, vol. 1, p. 58.], and this state continues to the present. It is called the Sultan's Nile because at that point the kharaj (land tax) becomes due from the people. All of Egypt was irrigated by a finger's width from seventeen cubits. When the Nile rose to seventeen cubits and a finger was called out for it, the eighteen-cubit mark was reached and the kharaj increased by a million dinars. When it exceeded that and a finger was called out for it at nineteen cubits, the kharaj decreased by a million dinars. The reason for this was what was spent on public works, canals, bridges, and attention to their maintenance. As for now, most of it is not irrigated until a finger is called out at nineteen cubits by the Egyptian measure. As for the works of Upper Egypt, some of them are not fully irrigated until the water enters the twenty-second cubit in Upper Egypt."

I (al-Qurtubi) say: As for the land of Egypt, it is now not fully irrigated except from twenty cubits and fingers, because the land has risen and there is no attention to the maintenance of its dams. This is one of the wonders of the world: the Nile rises when the waters pour over all the land until it floods all of Egypt's land, and the regions remain like islands, not reachable except by boats and measuring instruments.

It is narrated from Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As that he said: "The Nile of Egypt is the lord of rivers. God subjected to it every river between East and West, and God made the rivers submissive to it. When God wills that the Nile of Egypt should flow, He commands every river to feed it, and the rivers supply it with their water. God causes springs to gush forth for it. When it reaches what God, the Mighty and Majestic, wills, God, blessed and exalted, reveals to every water to return to its origin."

Qays ibn al-Hajjaj said: "When Egypt was conquered, its people came to Amr ibn al-As when the month of Ba'una (one of the Coptic months) had arrived, and they said to him: 'O Amir, our Nile has a custom and it will not flow except by it.' He said to them: 'And what is that?' They said: 'When it is the twelfth night of this month, we go to a virgin girl between her parents, we satisfy her parents, we dress her in the finest jewelry and clothing, and then we throw her into this Nile.' Amr said to them: 'This cannot happen in Islam, for Islam obliterates what came before it.' So they remained in Abib and Misra, and neither little nor much of the Nile flowed, and they resolved to depart. When Amr ibn al-As saw this, he wrote to Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with them both, informing him of the matter. Umar ibn al-Khattab wrote back to him: 'You have done right in what you did, for Islam obliterates what came before it, and this should not happen.' He sent him a slip of paper inside his letter, and wrote to Amr: 'I have sent you a slip of paper inside my letter; throw it into the Nile when my letter reaches you.' When Umar's letter reached Amr ibn al-As, he took the slip and opened it, and in it was: 'From the servant of God, Umar, Commander of the Believers, to the Nile of Egypt. To proceed: if you flow by your own power, then do not flow; but if it is God, the One, the Subduer, who makes you flow, then we ask God, the One, the Subduer, to make you flow.' He said: 'So he threw the slip into the Nile the day before the Cross (al-Salib), when the people of Egypt had prepared to leave and depart from it, because their welfare there depended only on the Nile.' When he threw the slip into the Nile, they awoke on the day of the Cross and God had made it rise sixteen cubits in a single night, and God cut off that custom from the people of Egypt from that year onward."

Ka'b al-Ahbar said: "Four rivers from Paradise God placed in the world: Sayhan, Jayhan, the Nile, and the Euphrates. Sayhan is the river of water in Paradise, Jayhan is the river of milk in Paradise, the Nile is the river of honey in Paradise, and the Euphrates is the river of wine in Paradise." Ibn Lahi'a said: "The Tigris is the river of milk in Paradise."

I (al-Qurtubi) say: What is in the Sahih on this subject is the hadith of Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "Sayhan, Jayhan, the Nile and the Euphrates are each of them rivers of Paradise." This is the wording of Muslim. In the hadith of the Night Journey, from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik, from Malik ibn Sa'sa'a, a man of his people, he said: "The Prophet of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, related that he saw four rivers emerging from its root: two apparent and two hidden. I said: 'O Gabriel, what are these rivers?' He said: 'As for the two hidden ones, they are two rivers in Paradise; as for the two apparent ones, they are the Nile and the Euphrates.'" This is the wording of Muslim. Al-Bukhari said, through the chain of Shurayk from Anas: "Then he was in the lowest heaven, with two rivers flowing (yattaridan) [yattaridan: i.e., flowing, and they are of the form yaftaʿilan from al-tard]. He said: 'What are these two rivers, O Gabriel?' He said: 'These are the Nile and the Euphrates, their source.' Then he proceeded in the heaven and came upon another river, upon which was a palace of pearl and chrysolite. He struck it with his hand and it was pure musk, very fragrant. He said: 'What is this, O Gabriel?' He said: 'This is al-Kawthar, which your Lord has hidden for you.'" And he mentioned the hadith.

The majority hold that the word "springs" (ʿuyūn) refers to springs of water. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "What is meant is springs of gold." And in the Smoke (surah 44): ﴿How many gardens and springs and fields they left behind﴾. It has been said.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 26, verses 52–68 (part 2 of 2):

Indeed they used to cultivate what lay between the two mountains, from the beginning of Egypt to its end. In the verse of Surah al-Dukhan, "and treasures" (kunuz) is the plural of kanz, and this has already been discussed in Surah al-Tawbah [[See vol. 8, p. 123, first or second edition.]]. Here it means storehouses (al-khaza'in). It has also been said that it means buried treasures (al-dafa'in). Al-Dahhak said it means rivers, but this is open to question, because springs (al-'uyun) already include them.

(And a noble station). Ibn 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: the noble station means the pulpits (al-manabir). There were a thousand pulpits, one for each of a thousand tyrants, who would honour Pharaoh and his kingdom from them. It has also been said that it means the assemblies of the chiefs and rulers, related by Ibn 'Isa, and this is close to the first view. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the fine dwellings. Ibn Lahi'a said: I heard that the noble station is al-Fayyum. It has also been said that Yusuf, peace be upon him, had written on one of his assemblies: "There is no god but Allah; Ibrahim is the friend of Allah," and so Allah called it noble because of this. It has also been said that it means the places where horses were tethered, since the leaders alone kept horses tethered there as a sign of their readiness and adornment, so that its station became the most honoured dwelling because of this. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi. The most apparent view is that it means the fine dwellings in which they were honoured.

In the language, al-maqam (المقام) can mean a place and can also be a verbal noun. Al-Nahhas said: al-maqam in the language means the place, from your saying qama yaqumu. Likewise al-maqamat, whose singular is maqama, as the poet said [[It is Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma. Yantabuha means that what is fine is said in them and done in them.]]:

"Among them are noble assemblies whose faces are fair,
and gatherings in which speech and deed are exchanged."

Al-maqam is also the verbal noun from qama yaqumu. Al-muqam (with a dammah) means a place from aqama, and it is also the verbal noun from aqama yuqimu.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Thus, and We made the Children of Israel inherit them﴾. He means that all that Allah mentioned, the gardens, the springs, the treasures and the noble station, Allah made the Children of Israel inherit. Al-Hasan and others said: the Children of Israel returned to Egypt after the destruction of Pharaoh and his people. It has also been said that by inheritance here is meant what they borrowed of the ornaments of Pharaoh's family by the command of Allah, exalted is He. I say: both matters came to pass for them, and praise belongs to Allah.

(So they pursued them at sunrise). That is, Pharaoh and his people followed the Children of Israel. Al-Suddi said: when the sun rose with its rays. Qatada said: when the earth lit up with light. Al-Zajjaj said: it is said sharaqat al-shams when it rose, and ashraqat when it shone. There is disagreement about the delay of Pharaoh and his people behind Musa and the Children of Israel, on two views. The first: they were busy burying their firstborn during that night, because the plague struck them that night; so his saying "at sunrise" (mushriqin) is a circumstantial clause describing Pharaoh's people. The second: a cloud overshadowed them, and there was darkness, and they said: we are still in the night; and it did not clear from them until morning came. Abu 'Ubayda said: the meaning of "they pursued them at sunrise" is toward the direction of the east. Al-Hasan and 'Amr ibn Maymun read: "fa-attaba'uhum mushriqin" with the shaddah and an alif of connection, meaning toward the east, derived from their saying sharraqa and gharraba when one travels toward the east and the west. The meaning of the speech is: We had determined that the Children of Israel should inherit it, and so the people of Pharaoh pursued the Children of Israel at sunrise and perished, and the Children of Israel inherited their lands.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When the two groups saw each other﴾, that is, the two groups confronted one another in such a way that each party saw the other. It is a form of tafa'ul from ru'ya (seeing).

(The companions of Musa said: "We are surely overtaken"). That is, the enemy drew near to us and we have no power to face him. The reading of the majority is "lamudrakun" with light stress, from adraka. From this is His saying: ﴿until, when drowning overtook him﴾. 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, al-A'raj and al-Zuhri read "lamuddarakun" with stress on the dal [[And with the ra' kasrah, as in al-Bahr, Ruh al-Ma'ani and al-Kashshaf, on the pattern of mufta'alun, which is intransitive, meaning destruction and annihilation, from adraka al-shay' when it follows in succession until it is finished.]], from idda-raka. Al-Farra' said: hafara and ihtaqara have one meaning, and likewise "mudrakun" and "muddarakun" have one meaning. Al-Nahhas said: the skilled grammarians do not say this; rather they say: mudrakun means "overtaken," and muddarakun means "striving to overtake them," just as it is said kasabtu meaning I obtained and won, and iktasabtu meaning I strove and sought. This is the meaning of the words of Sibawayh.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said: "By no means! Indeed my Lord is with me; He will guide me."﴾ When Pharaoh overtook Musa's host with his army and drew near to them, and the Children of Israel saw the strong enemy and the sea before them, their suspicions grew, and they said to Musa, in a manner of reproach and rudeness: "We are surely overtaken." So he rejected their statement, rebuked them, and reminded them of Allah's promise to him of guidance and victory. ("By no means!") meaning: they will not overtake you. ("Indeed my Lord is with me") meaning: with victory over the enemy. ("He will guide me") meaning: He will show me the way to salvation. When the trial grew severe upon the Children of Israel, and they saw the armies, against which they had no power, Allah, exalted and mighty is He, commanded Musa to strike the sea with his staff. This was because He, mighty and majestic, willed that the sign should be connected to Musa and tied to an act he performs; otherwise striking the staff does not split the sea, nor does it in itself help with that, except through what was joined to it of the power and invention of Allah, exalted is He. The story of this sea has already passed in Surah al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, p. 389 and following, second or third edition.]]. When it split, there were twelve paths in it according to the number of the tribes of the Children of Israel, and the water stood between them like a great mountain (tawd 'azim), that is, a great mountain. Al-Tawd is a mountain, and from it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"While a man is among the living, a mountain,
the people cast him from close range, and he leaned over."

Al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur said:

"They alighted at Anqira, over them flows
the water of the Euphrates that comes from the mountains (atwad)."

Atwad is the plural of tawd, that is, mountain. Thus there became for Musa and his companions a dry path in the sea. When the companions of Musa had come out, and the last of Pharaoh's companions had entered, as has been mentioned in Surah Yunus [[See vol. 8, p. 378, first or second edition.]], it closed over them, and Pharaoh drowned. Then some of Musa's companions said: Pharaoh has not drowned, so he was cast onto the sea shore until they looked at him. Ibn al-Qasim related from Malik, who said: two merchants went out with Musa, peace be upon him, to the sea. When they came to it, they said to him: By what did Allah command you? He said: I was commanded to strike the sea with this staff of mine, and it will split. They said to him: Do what Allah has commanded you, for He will not fail you. Then they threw themselves into the sea, affirming him. The sea remained so until Pharaoh and those with him entered, and then it returned to how it had been. This meaning has already passed in Surah al-Baqarah.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We brought the others near there﴾, that is, We brought them near to the sea, meaning Pharaoh and his people. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and others. The poet said:

"Every day that passes, or night that has gone by,
in which souls draw nearer to their appointed terms."

Abu 'Ubayda said: "azlafna" means "We gathered," and from this the night of Muzdalifah is called the night of gathering (layla jam'). Abu 'Abd Allah ibn al-Harith, Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ibn 'Abbas read "wa-azlafna" with the qaf, meaning "We destroyed them," from the saying azlaqat al-naqah and azlaqat al-faras, so she is muzlik when she causes her offspring to slip (azlaqa waladaha).

(And We saved Musa and all those with him. Then We drowned the others.) That is, Pharaoh and his people.

(Indeed in that is a sign.) That is, a token of the power of Allah, exalted is He.

(And most of them were not believers.) Because none of Pharaoh's people believed except the believer from the family of Pharaoh, whose name was Hizqil, and the daughter of Pharaoh, Asiya, wife of Pharaoh, and Maryam daughter of Dhi Musa, the old woman who guided them to the grave of Yusuf the Truthful, peace be upon him. This is because when Musa, peace be upon him, went out with the Children of Israel from Egypt, the moon grew dark over them, and he said to his people: What is this? Their scholars said: when Yusuf, peace be upon him, was approaching death, he took a covenant from us in the name of Allah that we would not leave Egypt until we had carried his bones with us. Musa said: Which of you knows his grave? They said: No one knows it except an old woman of the Children of Israel. So he sent for her and said: Show me the grave of Yusuf. She said: By Allah, I will not do so until you give me my right. He said: And what is your right? She said: My right is that I be with you in Paradise. This was grievous to him, so it was said to him: Give her what she asks. So she showed them where it was, and they dug it up and took out his bones. When they lifted them, the way was like the light of day. In another narration: Allah revealed to him that he should give it to her, and he did so. She brought them to a pool, and said to them: Drain this water. They drained it and took out the bones of Yusuf, peace be upon him, and the way became clear to them like the light of day. This has already passed in Surah Yusuf [[See vol. 9, p. 270, second edition.]].

Abu Burda related from Abu Musa that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ stayed with a Bedouin and honoured him. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "What is your need?" He said: a she-camel that I may ride, and female goats whose milk I may milk. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Why did you fail to be like the old woman of the Children of Israel?" His companions said: What was the old woman of the Children of Israel? So he related to them the story of that old woman who made Musa judge that she should be with him in Paradise.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 26, verses 52–68 (part 1 of 2):**

God's words: ﴿And We revealed to Moses: "Travel by night with My servants, for you will be pursued."﴾ Since it is among God's ways with His servants to save the believing, faithful men among His allies, who acknowledge the messengers and prophets He sent, and to destroy the disbelieving enemies who denied them, He commanded Moses to leave with the Children of Israel by night. He called them "His servants" because they had believed in Moses. The meaning of "for you will be pursued" is that Pharaoh and his people would follow you in order to turn you back. Implicit in this statement is the information that God would deliver them from Pharaoh. So Moses, peace be upon him, set out with the Children of Israel at dawn. He left the road to Syria on his left and headed toward the sea. A man from the Children of Israel would say to him, regarding leaving the road, "Why?" and he would reply, "I have been commanded thus." When Pharaoh rose in the morning and learned of Moses' night departure with the Children of Israel, he set out in their pursuit and sent to the cities of Egypt so that the armies would join him. It is reported that he caught up with them with a hundred thousand dark-coloured (adham) horses, besides the other colours. It is also reported that the Children of Israel numbered six hundred and seventy thousand. God knows best whether this is authentic. What is necessary from the verse, and what can be asserted with certainty, is that Moses, peace be upon him, left with a large host of the Children of Israel, and that Pharaoh pursued them with many times that number.

Ibn Abbas said: "There were with Pharaoh a thousand tyrants, each of whom wore a crown and each of whom was a commander of cavalry."

The shirdhimah (شِرْذِمَةٌ) is a small, despised group. Its plural is shara<u>dh</u>im (شَرَاذِم). Al-Jawhari said: "The shirdhimah is a group of people and a piece of something. A garment that is shara<u>dh</u>im means pieces (qita')." Al-Tha'labi recited the verse of the rajaz poet:

*The winter has come, and my garments are worn out,*
*Tattered; the naww<u>a</u>q laughs at them.*

The naww<u>a</u>q (النَّوَّاق) is a man who tames affairs and sets them right. This is what al-Jawhari said in the Sihah. [It is said that naww<u>a</u>q is the name of his son. It is also narrated as al-tawwaq (التَّوَّاق) with a ta'.]

The lam in God's words ﴿Indeed, these are a small group﴾ (لَشِرْذِمَةٌ) is the lam of emphasis (lam al-tawkid). It frequently enters the predicate of inna, except that the Kufans do not permit "inna Zayd la-sawfa yaqumu" (indeed Zayd will surely stand). The evidence that it is permissible is God's words ﴿So you will surely know﴾ (فَلَسَوْفَ تَعْلَمُونَ), where this same lam of emphasis has entered upon sawfa. This is what al-Nahhas said.

﴿And indeed they are enraging us﴾ (وَإِنَّهُمْ لَنا لَغائِظُونَ), meaning: they are enemies to us because they oppose our religion and take away our wealth, which they had borrowed, as mentioned earlier. Their virgin daughters (al-abkar) died that night. This has been fully discussed in al-A'raf and Ta-Ha. It is said: ghaza-ni kadha wa-aghaza-ni (this enraged me and made me enraged). Al-ghayz is anger, and from it come al-taghayyuz and al-ightiyaz. The meaning is that they enraged us by leaving without permission.

﴿And indeed we are a wary multitude (jami'un hadhirun)﴾ (وَإِنَّا لَجَمِيعٌ حاذِرُونَ), meaning: a gathered host taking precautions with our weapons. It is read as "hadhirun" (حَذِرُونَ), whose meaning is the same as "hadhirun" (حاذِرُونَ), i.e., fearful. Al-Jawhari said: it is read "hadhirun", "hadhirun" and "hadhirun" with a damma on the dhal (ḥadhirūna), reported by al-Akhfash. The meaning of "hadhirun" is "prepared (mutaahhibun)", and the meaning of "hadhirun" is "fearful (khaifun)." Al-Nahhas said: "hadhirun" is the reading of the people of Madina and Abu Amr. The reading of the people of Kufa is "hadhirun" (حَاذِرُونَ), and it is well known from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas. "Hadirun" with an undotted dal (حَادِرُونَ) is the reading of Abu Ubayd, and al-Mahdawi transmitted it from Ibn Abi Ammar, as did al-Mawardi and al-Tha'labi from Sumayt ibn Ajlan. Al-Nahhas said: Abu Ubayda holds that the meanings of "hadhirun" and "hadhirun" are one, and this is the view of Sibawayh, who permitted: "huwa hadhirun Zaydan," just as one says "hadhir Zaydan" (be wary of Zayd). He recited:

*Wary of matters that do no harm, and secure*
*From what cannot ward off the decrees.*

Abu Umar al-Jarmi claimed that it is permissible to say "huwa hadhirun Zaydan" by omitting min (from). However, most grammarians distinguish between hadhar and hadhir. Among them are al-Kisa'i, al-Farra', and Muhammad ibn Yazid, who hold that hadhar in its form means being alert and watchful, and so it is intransitive. Hadhir means "prepared," and this explanation was transmitted from the earlier authorities. Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, regarding God's words ﴿And indeed we are a wary multitude﴾, said: "Equipped with weapons and horses, well-prepared." This is the same meaning. His words "equipped (mu'dun)" mean that they have equipment (adah). It has also been said that the meaning is: we have weapons, and they have no weapons, which incites them to fight. As for "hadirun" with an undotted dal, it derives from the expression "a'yun hadratun," meaning full (eyes). That is, we are full of rage against them. From this is the verse of the poet, Imru' al-Qays:

*And an eye full and bright, its lids split from the corners.*

The lexicographers have said: "A man is hadirun" when he is full-fleshed. So it is possible that the meaning is "full of weapons." Al-Mahdawi said: "al-hadir" is strong and powerful.

God's words: ﴿So We expelled them from gardens and springs﴾, meaning from the land of Egypt. From Abdullah ibn Amr who said: "The gardens were on the two banks of the Nile, on both sides from Aswan to Rashid, and between the gardens were fields. The Nile has seven branches (khalij): the Alexandria branch, the Sakha branch, the Damietta branch, the Sardus branch, the Manf branch, the Fayyum branch, and the Manha branch [which is the Sea of Joseph, peace be upon him], all connected, none cut off from another, and the fields lay between all the branches. All of the land of Egypt was irrigated by sixteen cubits, through the dams, bridges and canals they had arranged and measured. For this reason, when the Nile rose to sixteen cubits it was called the Sultan's Nile. Ibn Abi al-Raddad was granted a robe of honour [He was Abdullah ibn al-Salam ibn Abdullah ibn Abi al-Raddad, the muezzin, who came to Egypt from Basra and narrated hadith there. He was appointed to measure the Nile during the governorship of Yazid ibn Abdullah al-Turki, when the Christians had been in charge of measuring it. He was given seven dinars every month, and his measuring remained in his descendants for a long time. Abu al-Raddad died in the year 266 AH. From al-Maqrizi's Khitat, vol. 1, p. 58.], and this state continues to the present. It is called the Sultan's Nile because at that point the kharaj (land tax) becomes due from the people. All of Egypt was irrigated by a finger's width from seventeen cubits. When the Nile rose to seventeen cubits and a finger was called out for it, the eighteen-cubit mark was reached and the kharaj increased by a million dinars. When it exceeded that and a finger was called out for it at nineteen cubits, the kharaj decreased by a million dinars. The reason for this was what was spent on public works, canals, bridges, and attention to their maintenance. As for now, most of it is not irrigated until a finger is called out at nineteen cubits by the Egyptian measure. As for the works of Upper Egypt, some of them are not fully irrigated until the water enters the twenty-second cubit in Upper Egypt."

I (al-Qurtubi) say: As for the land of Egypt, it is now not fully irrigated except from twenty cubits and fingers, because the land has risen and there is no attention to the maintenance of its dams. This is one of the wonders of the world: the Nile rises when the waters pour over all the land until it floods all of Egypt's land, and the regions remain like islands, not reachable except by boats and measuring instruments.

It is narrated from Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As that he said: "The Nile of Egypt is the lord of rivers. God subjected to it every river between East and West, and God made the rivers submissive to it. When God wills that the Nile of Egypt should flow, He commands every river to feed it, and the rivers supply it with their water. God causes springs to gush forth for it. When it reaches what God, the Mighty and Majestic, wills, God, blessed and exalted, reveals to every water to return to its origin."

Qays ibn al-Hajjaj said: "When Egypt was conquered, its people came to Amr ibn al-As when the month of Ba'una (one of the Coptic months) had arrived, and they said to him: 'O Amir, our Nile has a custom and it will not flow except by it.' He said to them: 'And what is that?' They said: 'When it is the twelfth night of this month, we go to a virgin girl between her parents, we satisfy her parents, we dress her in the finest jewelry and clothing, and then we throw her into this Nile.' Amr said to them: 'This cannot happen in Islam, for Islam obliterates what came before it.' So they remained in Abib and Misra, and neither little nor much of the Nile flowed, and they resolved to depart. When Amr ibn al-As saw this, he wrote to Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with them both, informing him of the matter. Umar ibn al-Khattab wrote back to him: 'You have done right in what you did, for Islam obliterates what came before it, and this should not happen.' He sent him a slip of paper inside his letter, and wrote to Amr: 'I have sent you a slip of paper inside my letter; throw it into the Nile when my letter reaches you.' When Umar's letter reached Amr ibn al-As, he took the slip and opened it, and in it was: 'From the servant of God, Umar, Commander of the Believers, to the Nile of Egypt. To proceed: if you flow by your own power, then do not flow; but if it is God, the One, the Subduer, who makes you flow, then we ask God, the One, the Subduer, to make you flow.' He said: 'So he threw the slip into the Nile the day before the Cross (al-Salib), when the people of Egypt had prepared to leave and depart from it, because their welfare there depended only on the Nile.' When he threw the slip into the Nile, they awoke on the day of the Cross and God had made it rise sixteen cubits in a single night, and God cut off that custom from the people of Egypt from that year onward."

Ka'b al-Ahbar said: "Four rivers from Paradise God placed in the world: Sayhan, Jayhan, the Nile, and the Euphrates. Sayhan is the river of water in Paradise, Jayhan is the river of milk in Paradise, the Nile is the river of honey in Paradise, and the Euphrates is the river of wine in Paradise." Ibn Lahi'a said: "The Tigris is the river of milk in Paradise."

I (al-Qurtubi) say: What is in the Sahih on this subject is the hadith of Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "Sayhan, Jayhan, the Nile and the Euphrates are each of them rivers of Paradise." This is the wording of Muslim. In the hadith of the Night Journey, from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik, from Malik ibn Sa'sa'a, a man of his people, he said: "The Prophet of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, related that he saw four rivers emerging from its root: two apparent and two hidden. I said: 'O Gabriel, what are these rivers?' He said: 'As for the two hidden ones, they are two rivers in Paradise; as for the two apparent ones, they are the Nile and the Euphrates.'" This is the wording of Muslim. Al-Bukhari said, through the chain of Shurayk from Anas: "Then he was in the lowest heaven, with two rivers flowing (yattaridan) [yattaridan: i.e., flowing, and they are of the form yaftaʿilan from al-tard]. He said: 'What are these two rivers, O Gabriel?' He said: 'These are the Nile and the Euphrates, their source.' Then he proceeded in the heaven and came upon another river, upon which was a palace of pearl and chrysolite. He struck it with his hand and it was pure musk, very fragrant. He said: 'What is this, O Gabriel?' He said: 'This is al-Kawthar, which your Lord has hidden for you.'" And he mentioned the hadith.

The majority hold that the word "springs" (ʿuyūn) refers to springs of water. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "What is meant is springs of gold." And in the Smoke (surah 44): ﴿How many gardens and springs and fields they left behind﴾. It has been said.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 26, verses 52–68 (part 2 of 2):

Indeed they used to cultivate what lay between the two mountains, from the beginning of Egypt to its end. In the verse of Surah al-Dukhan, "and treasures" (kunuz) is the plural of kanz, and this has already been discussed in Surah al-Tawbah [[See vol. 8, p. 123, first or second edition.]]. Here it means storehouses (al-khaza'in). It has also been said that it means buried treasures (al-dafa'in). Al-Dahhak said it means rivers, but this is open to question, because springs (al-'uyun) already include them.

(And a noble station). Ibn 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: the noble station means the pulpits (al-manabir). There were a thousand pulpits, one for each of a thousand tyrants, who would honour Pharaoh and his kingdom from them. It has also been said that it means the assemblies of the chiefs and rulers, related by Ibn 'Isa, and this is close to the first view. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the fine dwellings. Ibn Lahi'a said: I heard that the noble station is al-Fayyum. It has also been said that Yusuf, peace be upon him, had written on one of his assemblies: "There is no god but Allah; Ibrahim is the friend of Allah," and so Allah called it noble because of this. It has also been said that it means the places where horses were tethered, since the leaders alone kept horses tethered there as a sign of their readiness and adornment, so that its station became the most honoured dwelling because of this. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi. The most apparent view is that it means the fine dwellings in which they were honoured.

In the language, al-maqam (المقام) can mean a place and can also be a verbal noun. Al-Nahhas said: al-maqam in the language means the place, from your saying qama yaqumu. Likewise al-maqamat, whose singular is maqama, as the poet said [[It is Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma. Yantabuha means that what is fine is said in them and done in them.]]:

"Among them are noble assemblies whose faces are fair,
and gatherings in which speech and deed are exchanged."

Al-maqam is also the verbal noun from qama yaqumu. Al-muqam (with a dammah) means a place from aqama, and it is also the verbal noun from aqama yuqimu.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Thus, and We made the Children of Israel inherit them﴾. He means that all that Allah mentioned, the gardens, the springs, the treasures and the noble station, Allah made the Children of Israel inherit. Al-Hasan and others said: the Children of Israel returned to Egypt after the destruction of Pharaoh and his people. It has also been said that by inheritance here is meant what they borrowed of the ornaments of Pharaoh's family by the command of Allah, exalted is He. I say: both matters came to pass for them, and praise belongs to Allah.

(So they pursued them at sunrise). That is, Pharaoh and his people followed the Children of Israel. Al-Suddi said: when the sun rose with its rays. Qatada said: when the earth lit up with light. Al-Zajjaj said: it is said sharaqat al-shams when it rose, and ashraqat when it shone. There is disagreement about the delay of Pharaoh and his people behind Musa and the Children of Israel, on two views. The first: they were busy burying their firstborn during that night, because the plague struck them that night; so his saying "at sunrise" (mushriqin) is a circumstantial clause describing Pharaoh's people. The second: a cloud overshadowed them, and there was darkness, and they said: we are still in the night; and it did not clear from them until morning came. Abu 'Ubayda said: the meaning of "they pursued them at sunrise" is toward the direction of the east. Al-Hasan and 'Amr ibn Maymun read: "fa-attaba'uhum mushriqin" with the shaddah and an alif of connection, meaning toward the east, derived from their saying sharraqa and gharraba when one travels toward the east and the west. The meaning of the speech is: We had determined that the Children of Israel should inherit it, and so the people of Pharaoh pursued the Children of Israel at sunrise and perished, and the Children of Israel inherited their lands.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When the two groups saw each other﴾, that is, the two groups confronted one another in such a way that each party saw the other. It is a form of tafa'ul from ru'ya (seeing).

(The companions of Musa said: "We are surely overtaken"). That is, the enemy drew near to us and we have no power to face him. The reading of the majority is "lamudrakun" with light stress, from adraka. From this is His saying: ﴿until, when drowning overtook him﴾. 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, al-A'raj and al-Zuhri read "lamuddarakun" with stress on the dal [[And with the ra' kasrah, as in al-Bahr, Ruh al-Ma'ani and al-Kashshaf, on the pattern of mufta'alun, which is intransitive, meaning destruction and annihilation, from adraka al-shay' when it follows in succession until it is finished.]], from idda-raka. Al-Farra' said: hafara and ihtaqara have one meaning, and likewise "mudrakun" and "muddarakun" have one meaning. Al-Nahhas said: the skilled grammarians do not say this; rather they say: mudrakun means "overtaken," and muddarakun means "striving to overtake them," just as it is said kasabtu meaning I obtained and won, and iktasabtu meaning I strove and sought. This is the meaning of the words of Sibawayh.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said: "By no means! Indeed my Lord is with me; He will guide me."﴾ When Pharaoh overtook Musa's host with his army and drew near to them, and the Children of Israel saw the strong enemy and the sea before them, their suspicions grew, and they said to Musa, in a manner of reproach and rudeness: "We are surely overtaken." So he rejected their statement, rebuked them, and reminded them of Allah's promise to him of guidance and victory. ("By no means!") meaning: they will not overtake you. ("Indeed my Lord is with me") meaning: with victory over the enemy. ("He will guide me") meaning: He will show me the way to salvation. When the trial grew severe upon the Children of Israel, and they saw the armies, against which they had no power, Allah, exalted and mighty is He, commanded Musa to strike the sea with his staff. This was because He, mighty and majestic, willed that the sign should be connected to Musa and tied to an act he performs; otherwise striking the staff does not split the sea, nor does it in itself help with that, except through what was joined to it of the power and invention of Allah, exalted is He. The story of this sea has already passed in Surah al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, p. 389 and following, second or third edition.]]. When it split, there were twelve paths in it according to the number of the tribes of the Children of Israel, and the water stood between them like a great mountain (tawd 'azim), that is, a great mountain. Al-Tawd is a mountain, and from it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"While a man is among the living, a mountain,
the people cast him from close range, and he leaned over."

Al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur said:

"They alighted at Anqira, over them flows
the water of the Euphrates that comes from the mountains (atwad)."

Atwad is the plural of tawd, that is, mountain. Thus there became for Musa and his companions a dry path in the sea. When the companions of Musa had come out, and the last of Pharaoh's companions had entered, as has been mentioned in Surah Yunus [[See vol. 8, p. 378, first or second edition.]], it closed over them, and Pharaoh drowned. Then some of Musa's companions said: Pharaoh has not drowned, so he was cast onto the sea shore until they looked at him. Ibn al-Qasim related from Malik, who said: two merchants went out with Musa, peace be upon him, to the sea. When they came to it, they said to him: By what did Allah command you? He said: I was commanded to strike the sea with this staff of mine, and it will split. They said to him: Do what Allah has commanded you, for He will not fail you. Then they threw themselves into the sea, affirming him. The sea remained so until Pharaoh and those with him entered, and then it returned to how it had been. This meaning has already passed in Surah al-Baqarah.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We brought the others near there﴾, that is, We brought them near to the sea, meaning Pharaoh and his people. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and others. The poet said:

"Every day that passes, or night that has gone by,
in which souls draw nearer to their appointed terms."

Abu 'Ubayda said: "azlafna" means "We gathered," and from this the night of Muzdalifah is called the night of gathering (layla jam'). Abu 'Abd Allah ibn al-Harith, Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ibn 'Abbas read "wa-azlafna" with the qaf, meaning "We destroyed them," from the saying azlaqat al-naqah and azlaqat al-faras, so she is muzlik when she causes her offspring to slip (azlaqa waladaha).

(And We saved Musa and all those with him. Then We drowned the others.) That is, Pharaoh and his people.

(Indeed in that is a sign.) That is, a token of the power of Allah, exalted is He.

(And most of them were not believers.) Because none of Pharaoh's people believed except the believer from the family of Pharaoh, whose name was Hizqil, and the daughter of Pharaoh, Asiya, wife of Pharaoh, and Maryam daughter of Dhi Musa, the old woman who guided them to the grave of Yusuf the Truthful, peace be upon him. This is because when Musa, peace be upon him, went out with the Children of Israel from Egypt, the moon grew dark over them, and he said to his people: What is this? Their scholars said: when Yusuf, peace be upon him, was approaching death, he took a covenant from us in the name of Allah that we would not leave Egypt until we had carried his bones with us. Musa said: Which of you knows his grave? They said: No one knows it except an old woman of the Children of Israel. So he sent for her and said: Show me the grave of Yusuf. She said: By Allah, I will not do so until you give me my right. He said: And what is your right? She said: My right is that I be with you in Paradise. This was grievous to him, so it was said to him: Give her what she asks. So she showed them where it was, and they dug it up and took out his bones. When they lifted them, the way was like the light of day. In another narration: Allah revealed to him that he should give it to her, and he did so. She brought them to a pool, and said to them: Drain this water. They drained it and took out the bones of Yusuf, peace be upon him, and the way became clear to them like the light of day. This has already passed in Surah Yusuf [[See vol. 9, p. 270, second edition.]].

Abu Burda related from Abu Musa that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ stayed with a Bedouin and honoured him. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "What is your need?" He said: a she-camel that I may ride, and female goats whose milk I may milk. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Why did you fail to be like the old woman of the Children of Israel?" His companions said: What was the old woman of the Children of Israel? So he related to them the story of that old woman who made Musa judge that she should be with him in Paradise.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 26, verses 52–68 (part 1 of 2):**

God's words: ﴿And We revealed to Moses: "Travel by night with My servants, for you will be pursued."﴾ Since it is among God's ways with His servants to save the believing, faithful men among His allies, who acknowledge the messengers and prophets He sent, and to destroy the disbelieving enemies who denied them, He commanded Moses to leave with the Children of Israel by night. He called them "His servants" because they had believed in Moses. The meaning of "for you will be pursued" is that Pharaoh and his people would follow you in order to turn you back. Implicit in this statement is the information that God would deliver them from Pharaoh. So Moses, peace be upon him, set out with the Children of Israel at dawn. He left the road to Syria on his left and headed toward the sea. A man from the Children of Israel would say to him, regarding leaving the road, "Why?" and he would reply, "I have been commanded thus." When Pharaoh rose in the morning and learned of Moses' night departure with the Children of Israel, he set out in their pursuit and sent to the cities of Egypt so that the armies would join him. It is reported that he caught up with them with a hundred thousand dark-coloured (adham) horses, besides the other colours. It is also reported that the Children of Israel numbered six hundred and seventy thousand. God knows best whether this is authentic. What is necessary from the verse, and what can be asserted with certainty, is that Moses, peace be upon him, left with a large host of the Children of Israel, and that Pharaoh pursued them with many times that number.

Ibn Abbas said: "There were with Pharaoh a thousand tyrants, each of whom wore a crown and each of whom was a commander of cavalry."

The shirdhimah (شِرْذِمَةٌ) is a small, despised group. Its plural is shara<u>dh</u>im (شَرَاذِم). Al-Jawhari said: "The shirdhimah is a group of people and a piece of something. A garment that is shara<u>dh</u>im means pieces (qita')." Al-Tha'labi recited the verse of the rajaz poet:
