*The winter has come, and my garments are worn out,*
*Tattered; the naww<u>a</u>q laughs at them.*

The naww<u>a</u>q (النَّوَّاق) is a man who tames affairs and sets them right. This is what al-Jawhari said in the Sihah. [It is said that naww<u>a</u>q is the name of his son. It is also narrated as al-tawwaq (التَّوَّاق) with a ta'.]

The lam in God's words ﴿Indeed, these are a small group﴾ (لَشِرْذِمَةٌ) is the lam of emphasis (lam al-tawkid). It frequently enters the predicate of inna, except that the Kufans do not permit "inna Zayd la-sawfa yaqumu" (indeed Zayd will surely stand). The evidence that it is permissible is God's words ﴿So you will surely know﴾ (فَلَسَوْفَ تَعْلَمُونَ), where this same lam of emphasis has entered upon sawfa. This is what al-Nahhas said.

﴿And indeed they are enraging us﴾ (وَإِنَّهُمْ لَنا لَغائِظُونَ), meaning: they are enemies to us because they oppose our religion and take away our wealth, which they had borrowed, as mentioned earlier. Their virgin daughters (al-abkar) died that night. This has been fully discussed in al-A'raf and Ta-Ha. It is said: ghaza-ni kadha wa-aghaza-ni (this enraged me and made me enraged). Al-ghayz is anger, and from it come al-taghayyuz and al-ightiyaz. The meaning is that they enraged us by leaving without permission.

﴿And indeed we are a wary multitude (jami'un hadhirun)﴾ (وَإِنَّا لَجَمِيعٌ حاذِرُونَ), meaning: a gathered host taking precautions with our weapons. It is read as "hadhirun" (حَذِرُونَ), whose meaning is the same as "hadhirun" (حاذِرُونَ), i.e., fearful. Al-Jawhari said: it is read "hadhirun", "hadhirun" and "hadhirun" with a damma on the dhal (ḥadhirūna), reported by al-Akhfash. The meaning of "hadhirun" is "prepared (mutaahhibun)", and the meaning of "hadhirun" is "fearful (khaifun)." Al-Nahhas said: "hadhirun" is the reading of the people of Madina and Abu Amr. The reading of the people of Kufa is "hadhirun" (حَاذِرُونَ), and it is well known from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas. "Hadirun" with an undotted dal (حَادِرُونَ) is the reading of Abu Ubayd, and al-Mahdawi transmitted it from Ibn Abi Ammar, as did al-Mawardi and al-Tha'labi from Sumayt ibn Ajlan. Al-Nahhas said: Abu Ubayda holds that the meanings of "hadhirun" and "hadhirun" are one, and this is the view of Sibawayh, who permitted: "huwa hadhirun Zaydan," just as one says "hadhir Zaydan" (be wary of Zayd). He recited:

*Wary of matters that do no harm, and secure*
*From what cannot ward off the decrees.*

Abu Umar al-Jarmi claimed that it is permissible to say "huwa hadhirun Zaydan" by omitting min (from). However, most grammarians distinguish between hadhar and hadhir. Among them are al-Kisa'i, al-Farra', and Muhammad ibn Yazid, who hold that hadhar in its form means being alert and watchful, and so it is intransitive. Hadhir means "prepared," and this explanation was transmitted from the earlier authorities. Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, regarding God's words ﴿And indeed we are a wary multitude﴾, said: "Equipped with weapons and horses, well-prepared." This is the same meaning. His words "equipped (mu'dun)" mean that they have equipment (adah). It has also been said that the meaning is: we have weapons, and they have no weapons, which incites them to fight. As for "hadirun" with an undotted dal, it derives from the expression "a'yun hadratun," meaning full (eyes). That is, we are full of rage against them. From this is the verse of the poet, Imru' al-Qays:

*And an eye full and bright, its lids split from the corners.*

The lexicographers have said: "A man is hadirun" when he is full-fleshed. So it is possible that the meaning is "full of weapons." Al-Mahdawi said: "al-hadir" is strong and powerful.

God's words: ﴿So We expelled them from gardens and springs﴾, meaning from the land of Egypt. From Abdullah ibn Amr who said: "The gardens were on the two banks of the Nile, on both sides from Aswan to Rashid, and between the gardens were fields. The Nile has seven branches (khalij): the Alexandria branch, the Sakha branch, the Damietta branch, the Sardus branch, the Manf branch, the Fayyum branch, and the Manha branch [which is the Sea of Joseph, peace be upon him], all connected, none cut off from another, and the fields lay between all the branches. All of the land of Egypt was irrigated by sixteen cubits, through the dams, bridges and canals they had arranged and measured. For this reason, when the Nile rose to sixteen cubits it was called the Sultan's Nile. Ibn Abi al-Raddad was granted a robe of honour [He was Abdullah ibn al-Salam ibn Abdullah ibn Abi al-Raddad, the muezzin, who came to Egypt from Basra and narrated hadith there. He was appointed to measure the Nile during the governorship of Yazid ibn Abdullah al-Turki, when the Christians had been in charge of measuring it. He was given seven dinars every month, and his measuring remained in his descendants for a long time. Abu al-Raddad died in the year 266 AH. From al-Maqrizi's Khitat, vol. 1, p. 58.], and this state continues to the present. It is called the Sultan's Nile because at that point the kharaj (land tax) becomes due from the people. All of Egypt was irrigated by a finger's width from seventeen cubits. When the Nile rose to seventeen cubits and a finger was called out for it, the eighteen-cubit mark was reached and the kharaj increased by a million dinars. When it exceeded that and a finger was called out for it at nineteen cubits, the kharaj decreased by a million dinars. The reason for this was what was spent on public works, canals, bridges, and attention to their maintenance. As for now, most of it is not irrigated until a finger is called out at nineteen cubits by the Egyptian measure. As for the works of Upper Egypt, some of them are not fully irrigated until the water enters the twenty-second cubit in Upper Egypt."

I (al-Qurtubi) say: As for the land of Egypt, it is now not fully irrigated except from twenty cubits and fingers, because the land has risen and there is no attention to the maintenance of its dams. This is one of the wonders of the world: the Nile rises when the waters pour over all the land until it floods all of Egypt's land, and the regions remain like islands, not reachable except by boats and measuring instruments.

It is narrated from Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As that he said: "The Nile of Egypt is the lord of rivers. God subjected to it every river between East and West, and God made the rivers submissive to it. When God wills that the Nile of Egypt should flow, He commands every river to feed it, and the rivers supply it with their water. God causes springs to gush forth for it. When it reaches what God, the Mighty and Majestic, wills, God, blessed and exalted, reveals to every water to return to its origin."

Qays ibn al-Hajjaj said: "When Egypt was conquered, its people came to Amr ibn al-As when the month of Ba'una (one of the Coptic months) had arrived, and they said to him: 'O Amir, our Nile has a custom and it will not flow except by it.' He said to them: 'And what is that?' They said: 'When it is the twelfth night of this month, we go to a virgin girl between her parents, we satisfy her parents, we dress her in the finest jewelry and clothing, and then we throw her into this Nile.' Amr said to them: 'This cannot happen in Islam, for Islam obliterates what came before it.' So they remained in Abib and Misra, and neither little nor much of the Nile flowed, and they resolved to depart. When Amr ibn al-As saw this, he wrote to Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with them both, informing him of the matter. Umar ibn al-Khattab wrote back to him: 'You have done right in what you did, for Islam obliterates what came before it, and this should not happen.' He sent him a slip of paper inside his letter, and wrote to Amr: 'I have sent you a slip of paper inside my letter; throw it into the Nile when my letter reaches you.' When Umar's letter reached Amr ibn al-As, he took the slip and opened it, and in it was: 'From the servant of God, Umar, Commander of the Believers, to the Nile of Egypt. To proceed: if you flow by your own power, then do not flow; but if it is God, the One, the Subduer, who makes you flow, then we ask God, the One, the Subduer, to make you flow.' He said: 'So he threw the slip into the Nile the day before the Cross (al-Salib), when the people of Egypt had prepared to leave and depart from it, because their welfare there depended only on the Nile.' When he threw the slip into the Nile, they awoke on the day of the Cross and God had made it rise sixteen cubits in a single night, and God cut off that custom from the people of Egypt from that year onward."

Ka'b al-Ahbar said: "Four rivers from Paradise God placed in the world: Sayhan, Jayhan, the Nile, and the Euphrates. Sayhan is the river of water in Paradise, Jayhan is the river of milk in Paradise, the Nile is the river of honey in Paradise, and the Euphrates is the river of wine in Paradise." Ibn Lahi'a said: "The Tigris is the river of milk in Paradise."

I (al-Qurtubi) say: What is in the Sahih on this subject is the hadith of Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "Sayhan, Jayhan, the Nile and the Euphrates are each of them rivers of Paradise." This is the wording of Muslim. In the hadith of the Night Journey, from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik, from Malik ibn Sa'sa'a, a man of his people, he said: "The Prophet of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, related that he saw four rivers emerging from its root: two apparent and two hidden. I said: 'O Gabriel, what are these rivers?' He said: 'As for the two hidden ones, they are two rivers in Paradise; as for the two apparent ones, they are the Nile and the Euphrates.'" This is the wording of Muslim. Al-Bukhari said, through the chain of Shurayk from Anas: "Then he was in the lowest heaven, with two rivers flowing (yattaridan) [yattaridan: i.e., flowing, and they are of the form yaftaʿilan from al-tard]. He said: 'What are these two rivers, O Gabriel?' He said: 'These are the Nile and the Euphrates, their source.' Then he proceeded in the heaven and came upon another river, upon which was a palace of pearl and chrysolite. He struck it with his hand and it was pure musk, very fragrant. He said: 'What is this, O Gabriel?' He said: 'This is al-Kawthar, which your Lord has hidden for you.'" And he mentioned the hadith.

The majority hold that the word "springs" (ʿuyūn) refers to springs of water. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "What is meant is springs of gold." And in the Smoke (surah 44): ﴿How many gardens and springs and fields they left behind﴾. It has been said.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 26, verses 52–68 (part 2 of 2):

Indeed they used to cultivate what lay between the two mountains, from the beginning of Egypt to its end. In the verse of Surah al-Dukhan, "and treasures" (kunuz) is the plural of kanz, and this has already been discussed in Surah al-Tawbah [[See vol. 8, p. 123, first or second edition.]]. Here it means storehouses (al-khaza'in). It has also been said that it means buried treasures (al-dafa'in). Al-Dahhak said it means rivers, but this is open to question, because springs (al-'uyun) already include them.

(And a noble station). Ibn 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: the noble station means the pulpits (al-manabir). There were a thousand pulpits, one for each of a thousand tyrants, who would honour Pharaoh and his kingdom from them. It has also been said that it means the assemblies of the chiefs and rulers, related by Ibn 'Isa, and this is close to the first view. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the fine dwellings. Ibn Lahi'a said: I heard that the noble station is al-Fayyum. It has also been said that Yusuf, peace be upon him, had written on one of his assemblies: "There is no god but Allah; Ibrahim is the friend of Allah," and so Allah called it noble because of this. It has also been said that it means the places where horses were tethered, since the leaders alone kept horses tethered there as a sign of their readiness and adornment, so that its station became the most honoured dwelling because of this. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi. The most apparent view is that it means the fine dwellings in which they were honoured.

In the language, al-maqam (المقام) can mean a place and can also be a verbal noun. Al-Nahhas said: al-maqam in the language means the place, from your saying qama yaqumu. Likewise al-maqamat, whose singular is maqama, as the poet said [[It is Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma. Yantabuha means that what is fine is said in them and done in them.]]:

"Among them are noble assemblies whose faces are fair,
and gatherings in which speech and deed are exchanged."

Al-maqam is also the verbal noun from qama yaqumu. Al-muqam (with a dammah) means a place from aqama, and it is also the verbal noun from aqama yuqimu.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Thus, and We made the Children of Israel inherit them﴾. He means that all that Allah mentioned, the gardens, the springs, the treasures and the noble station, Allah made the Children of Israel inherit. Al-Hasan and others said: the Children of Israel returned to Egypt after the destruction of Pharaoh and his people. It has also been said that by inheritance here is meant what they borrowed of the ornaments of Pharaoh's family by the command of Allah, exalted is He. I say: both matters came to pass for them, and praise belongs to Allah.

(So they pursued them at sunrise). That is, Pharaoh and his people followed the Children of Israel. Al-Suddi said: when the sun rose with its rays. Qatada said: when the earth lit up with light. Al-Zajjaj said: it is said sharaqat al-shams when it rose, and ashraqat when it shone. There is disagreement about the delay of Pharaoh and his people behind Musa and the Children of Israel, on two views. The first: they were busy burying their firstborn during that night, because the plague struck them that night; so his saying "at sunrise" (mushriqin) is a circumstantial clause describing Pharaoh's people. The second: a cloud overshadowed them, and there was darkness, and they said: we are still in the night; and it did not clear from them until morning came. Abu 'Ubayda said: the meaning of "they pursued them at sunrise" is toward the direction of the east. Al-Hasan and 'Amr ibn Maymun read: "fa-attaba'uhum mushriqin" with the shaddah and an alif of connection, meaning toward the east, derived from their saying sharraqa and gharraba when one travels toward the east and the west. The meaning of the speech is: We had determined that the Children of Israel should inherit it, and so the people of Pharaoh pursued the Children of Israel at sunrise and perished, and the Children of Israel inherited their lands.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When the two groups saw each other﴾, that is, the two groups confronted one another in such a way that each party saw the other. It is a form of tafa'ul from ru'ya (seeing).

(The companions of Musa said: "We are surely overtaken"). That is, the enemy drew near to us and we have no power to face him. The reading of the majority is "lamudrakun" with light stress, from adraka. From this is His saying: ﴿until, when drowning overtook him﴾. 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, al-A'raj and al-Zuhri read "lamuddarakun" with stress on the dal [[And with the ra' kasrah, as in al-Bahr, Ruh al-Ma'ani and al-Kashshaf, on the pattern of mufta'alun, which is intransitive, meaning destruction and annihilation, from adraka al-shay' when it follows in succession until it is finished.]], from idda-raka. Al-Farra' said: hafara and ihtaqara have one meaning, and likewise "mudrakun" and "muddarakun" have one meaning. Al-Nahhas said: the skilled grammarians do not say this; rather they say: mudrakun means "overtaken," and muddarakun means "striving to overtake them," just as it is said kasabtu meaning I obtained and won, and iktasabtu meaning I strove and sought. This is the meaning of the words of Sibawayh.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said: "By no means! Indeed my Lord is with me; He will guide me."﴾ When Pharaoh overtook Musa's host with his army and drew near to them, and the Children of Israel saw the strong enemy and the sea before them, their suspicions grew, and they said to Musa, in a manner of reproach and rudeness: "We are surely overtaken." So he rejected their statement, rebuked them, and reminded them of Allah's promise to him of guidance and victory. ("By no means!") meaning: they will not overtake you. ("Indeed my Lord is with me") meaning: with victory over the enemy. ("He will guide me") meaning: He will show me the way to salvation. When the trial grew severe upon the Children of Israel, and they saw the armies, against which they had no power, Allah, exalted and mighty is He, commanded Musa to strike the sea with his staff. This was because He, mighty and majestic, willed that the sign should be connected to Musa and tied to an act he performs; otherwise striking the staff does not split the sea, nor does it in itself help with that, except through what was joined to it of the power and invention of Allah, exalted is He. The story of this sea has already passed in Surah al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, p. 389 and following, second or third edition.]]. When it split, there were twelve paths in it according to the number of the tribes of the Children of Israel, and the water stood between them like a great mountain (tawd 'azim), that is, a great mountain. Al-Tawd is a mountain, and from it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"While a man is among the living, a mountain,
the people cast him from close range, and he leaned over."

Al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur said:

"They alighted at Anqira, over them flows
the water of the Euphrates that comes from the mountains (atwad)."

Atwad is the plural of tawd, that is, mountain. Thus there became for Musa and his companions a dry path in the sea. When the companions of Musa had come out, and the last of Pharaoh's companions had entered, as has been mentioned in Surah Yunus [[See vol. 8, p. 378, first or second edition.]], it closed over them, and Pharaoh drowned. Then some of Musa's companions said: Pharaoh has not drowned, so he was cast onto the sea shore until they looked at him. Ibn al-Qasim related from Malik, who said: two merchants went out with Musa, peace be upon him, to the sea. When they came to it, they said to him: By what did Allah command you? He said: I was commanded to strike the sea with this staff of mine, and it will split. They said to him: Do what Allah has commanded you, for He will not fail you. Then they threw themselves into the sea, affirming him. The sea remained so until Pharaoh and those with him entered, and then it returned to how it had been. This meaning has already passed in Surah al-Baqarah.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We brought the others near there﴾, that is, We brought them near to the sea, meaning Pharaoh and his people. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and others. The poet said:

"Every day that passes, or night that has gone by,
in which souls draw nearer to their appointed terms."

Abu 'Ubayda said: "azlafna" means "We gathered," and from this the night of Muzdalifah is called the night of gathering (layla jam'). Abu 'Abd Allah ibn al-Harith, Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ibn 'Abbas read "wa-azlafna" with the qaf, meaning "We destroyed them," from the saying azlaqat al-naqah and azlaqat al-faras, so she is muzlik when she causes her offspring to slip (azlaqa waladaha).

(And We saved Musa and all those with him. Then We drowned the others.) That is, Pharaoh and his people.

(Indeed in that is a sign.) That is, a token of the power of Allah, exalted is He.

(And most of them were not believers.) Because none of Pharaoh's people believed except the believer from the family of Pharaoh, whose name was Hizqil, and the daughter of Pharaoh, Asiya, wife of Pharaoh, and Maryam daughter of Dhi Musa, the old woman who guided them to the grave of Yusuf the Truthful, peace be upon him. This is because when Musa, peace be upon him, went out with the Children of Israel from Egypt, the moon grew dark over them, and he said to his people: What is this? Their scholars said: when Yusuf, peace be upon him, was approaching death, he took a covenant from us in the name of Allah that we would not leave Egypt until we had carried his bones with us. Musa said: Which of you knows his grave? They said: No one knows it except an old woman of the Children of Israel. So he sent for her and said: Show me the grave of Yusuf. She said: By Allah, I will not do so until you give me my right. He said: And what is your right? She said: My right is that I be with you in Paradise. This was grievous to him, so it was said to him: Give her what she asks. So she showed them where it was, and they dug it up and took out his bones. When they lifted them, the way was like the light of day. In another narration: Allah revealed to him that he should give it to her, and he did so. She brought them to a pool, and said to them: Drain this water. They drained it and took out the bones of Yusuf, peace be upon him, and the way became clear to them like the light of day. This has already passed in Surah Yusuf [[See vol. 9, p. 270, second edition.]].

Abu Burda related from Abu Musa that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ stayed with a Bedouin and honoured him. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "What is your need?" He said: a she-camel that I may ride, and female goats whose milk I may milk. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Why did you fail to be like the old woman of the Children of Israel?" His companions said: What was the old woman of the Children of Israel? So he related to them the story of that old woman who made Musa judge that she should be with him in Paradise.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 26, verses 52–68 (part 1 of 2):**

God's words: ﴿And We revealed to Moses: "Travel by night with My servants, for you will be pursued."﴾ Since it is among God's ways with His servants to save the believing, faithful men among His allies, who acknowledge the messengers and prophets He sent, and to destroy the disbelieving enemies who denied them, He commanded Moses to leave with the Children of Israel by night. He called them "His servants" because they had believed in Moses. The meaning of "for you will be pursued" is that Pharaoh and his people would follow you in order to turn you back. Implicit in this statement is the information that God would deliver them from Pharaoh. So Moses, peace be upon him, set out with the Children of Israel at dawn. He left the road to Syria on his left and headed toward the sea. A man from the Children of Israel would say to him, regarding leaving the road, "Why?" and he would reply, "I have been commanded thus." When Pharaoh rose in the morning and learned of Moses' night departure with the Children of Israel, he set out in their pursuit and sent to the cities of Egypt so that the armies would join him. It is reported that he caught up with them with a hundred thousand dark-coloured (adham) horses, besides the other colours. It is also reported that the Children of Israel numbered six hundred and seventy thousand. God knows best whether this is authentic. What is necessary from the verse, and what can be asserted with certainty, is that Moses, peace be upon him, left with a large host of the Children of Israel, and that Pharaoh pursued them with many times that number.

Ibn Abbas said: "There were with Pharaoh a thousand tyrants, each of whom wore a crown and each of whom was a commander of cavalry."

The shirdhimah (شِرْذِمَةٌ) is a small, despised group. Its plural is shara<u>dh</u>im (شَرَاذِم). Al-Jawhari said: "The shirdhimah is a group of people and a piece of something. A garment that is shara<u>dh</u>im means pieces (qita')." Al-Tha'labi recited the verse of the rajaz poet:

*The winter has come, and my garments are worn out,*
*Tattered; the naww<u>a</u>q laughs at them.*

The naww<u>a</u>q (النَّوَّاق) is a man who tames affairs and sets them right. This is what al-Jawhari said in the Sihah. [It is said that naww<u>a</u>q is the name of his son. It is also narrated as al-tawwaq (التَّوَّاق) with a ta'.]

The lam in God's words ﴿Indeed, these are a small group﴾ (لَشِرْذِمَةٌ) is the lam of emphasis (lam al-tawkid). It frequently enters the predicate of inna, except that the Kufans do not permit "inna Zayd la-sawfa yaqumu" (indeed Zayd will surely stand). The evidence that it is permissible is God's words ﴿So you will surely know﴾ (فَلَسَوْفَ تَعْلَمُونَ), where this same lam of emphasis has entered upon sawfa. This is what al-Nahhas said.

﴿And indeed they are enraging us﴾ (وَإِنَّهُمْ لَنا لَغائِظُونَ), meaning: they are enemies to us because they oppose our religion and take away our wealth, which they had borrowed, as mentioned earlier. Their virgin daughters (al-abkar) died that night. This has been fully discussed in al-A'raf and Ta-Ha. It is said: ghaza-ni kadha wa-aghaza-ni (this enraged me and made me enraged). Al-ghayz is anger, and from it come al-taghayyuz and al-ightiyaz. The meaning is that they enraged us by leaving without permission.

﴿And indeed we are a wary multitude (jami'un hadhirun)﴾ (وَإِنَّا لَجَمِيعٌ حاذِرُونَ), meaning: a gathered host taking precautions with our weapons. It is read as "hadhirun" (حَذِرُونَ), whose meaning is the same as "hadhirun" (حاذِرُونَ), i.e., fearful. Al-Jawhari said: it is read "hadhirun", "hadhirun" and "hadhirun" with a damma on the dhal (ḥadhirūna), reported by al-Akhfash. The meaning of "hadhirun" is "prepared (mutaahhibun)", and the meaning of "hadhirun" is "fearful (khaifun)." Al-Nahhas said: "hadhirun" is the reading of the people of Madina and Abu Amr. The reading of the people of Kufa is "hadhirun" (حَاذِرُونَ), and it is well known from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas. "Hadirun" with an undotted dal (حَادِرُونَ) is the reading of Abu Ubayd, and al-Mahdawi transmitted it from Ibn Abi Ammar, as did al-Mawardi and al-Tha'labi from Sumayt ibn Ajlan. Al-Nahhas said: Abu Ubayda holds that the meanings of "hadhirun" and "hadhirun" are one, and this is the view of Sibawayh, who permitted: "huwa hadhirun Zaydan," just as one says "hadhir Zaydan" (be wary of Zayd). He recited:

*Wary of matters that do no harm, and secure*
*From what cannot ward off the decrees.*

Abu Umar al-Jarmi claimed that it is permissible to say "huwa hadhirun Zaydan" by omitting min (from). However, most grammarians distinguish between hadhar and hadhir. Among them are al-Kisa'i, al-Farra', and Muhammad ibn Yazid, who hold that hadhar in its form means being alert and watchful, and so it is intransitive. Hadhir means "prepared," and this explanation was transmitted from the earlier authorities. Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, regarding God's words ﴿And indeed we are a wary multitude﴾, said: "Equipped with weapons and horses, well-prepared." This is the same meaning. His words "equipped (mu'dun)" mean that they have equipment (adah). It has also been said that the meaning is: we have weapons, and they have no weapons, which incites them to fight. As for "hadirun" with an undotted dal, it derives from the expression "a'yun hadratun," meaning full (eyes). That is, we are full of rage against them. From this is the verse of the poet, Imru' al-Qays:

*And an eye full and bright, its lids split from the corners.*

The lexicographers have said: "A man is hadirun" when he is full-fleshed. So it is possible that the meaning is "full of weapons." Al-Mahdawi said: "al-hadir" is strong and powerful.

God's words: ﴿So We expelled them from gardens and springs﴾, meaning from the land of Egypt. From Abdullah ibn Amr who said: "The gardens were on the two banks of the Nile, on both sides from Aswan to Rashid, and between the gardens were fields. The Nile has seven branches (khalij): the Alexandria branch, the Sakha branch, the Damietta branch, the Sardus branch, the Manf branch, the Fayyum branch, and the Manha branch [which is the Sea of Joseph, peace be upon him], all connected, none cut off from another, and the fields lay between all the branches. All of the land of Egypt was irrigated by sixteen cubits, through the dams, bridges and canals they had arranged and measured. For this reason, when the Nile rose to sixteen cubits it was called the Sultan's Nile. Ibn Abi al-Raddad was granted a robe of honour [He was Abdullah ibn al-Salam ibn Abdullah ibn Abi al-Raddad, the muezzin, who came to Egypt from Basra and narrated hadith there. He was appointed to measure the Nile during the governorship of Yazid ibn Abdullah al-Turki, when the Christians had been in charge of measuring it. He was given seven dinars every month, and his measuring remained in his descendants for a long time. Abu al-Raddad died in the year 266 AH. From al-Maqrizi's Khitat, vol. 1, p. 58.], and this state continues to the present. It is called the Sultan's Nile because at that point the kharaj (land tax) becomes due from the people. All of Egypt was irrigated by a finger's width from seventeen cubits. When the Nile rose to seventeen cubits and a finger was called out for it, the eighteen-cubit mark was reached and the kharaj increased by a million dinars. When it exceeded that and a finger was called out for it at nineteen cubits, the kharaj decreased by a million dinars. The reason for this was what was spent on public works, canals, bridges, and attention to their maintenance. As for now, most of it is not irrigated until a finger is called out at nineteen cubits by the Egyptian measure. As for the works of Upper Egypt, some of them are not fully irrigated until the water enters the twenty-second cubit in Upper Egypt."

I (al-Qurtubi) say: As for the land of Egypt, it is now not fully irrigated except from twenty cubits and fingers, because the land has risen and there is no attention to the maintenance of its dams. This is one of the wonders of the world: the Nile rises when the waters pour over all the land until it floods all of Egypt's land, and the regions remain like islands, not reachable except by boats and measuring instruments.

It is narrated from Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As that he said: "The Nile of Egypt is the lord of rivers. God subjected to it every river between East and West, and God made the rivers submissive to it. When God wills that the Nile of Egypt should flow, He commands every river to feed it, and the rivers supply it with their water. God causes springs to gush forth for it. When it reaches what God, the Mighty and Majestic, wills, God, blessed and exalted, reveals to every water to return to its origin."

Qays ibn al-Hajjaj said: "When Egypt was conquered, its people came to Amr ibn al-As when the month of Ba'una (one of the Coptic months) had arrived, and they said to him: 'O Amir, our Nile has a custom and it will not flow except by it.' He said to them: 'And what is that?' They said: 'When it is the twelfth night of this month, we go to a virgin girl between her parents, we satisfy her parents, we dress her in the finest jewelry and clothing, and then we throw her into this Nile.' Amr said to them: 'This cannot happen in Islam, for Islam obliterates what came before it.' So they remained in Abib and Misra, and neither little nor much of the Nile flowed, and they resolved to depart. When Amr ibn al-As saw this, he wrote to Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with them both, informing him of the matter. Umar ibn al-Khattab wrote back to him: 'You have done right in what you did, for Islam obliterates what came before it, and this should not happen.' He sent him a slip of paper inside his letter, and wrote to Amr: 'I have sent you a slip of paper inside my letter; throw it into the Nile when my letter reaches you.' When Umar's letter reached Amr ibn al-As, he took the slip and opened it, and in it was: 'From the servant of God, Umar, Commander of the Believers, to the Nile of Egypt. To proceed: if you flow by your own power, then do not flow; but if it is God, the One, the Subduer, who makes you flow, then we ask God, the One, the Subduer, to make you flow.' He said: 'So he threw the slip into the Nile the day before the Cross (al-Salib), when the people of Egypt had prepared to leave and depart from it, because their welfare there depended only on the Nile.' When he threw the slip into the Nile, they awoke on the day of the Cross and God had made it rise sixteen cubits in a single night, and God cut off that custom from the people of Egypt from that year onward."

Ka'b al-Ahbar said: "Four rivers from Paradise God placed in the world: Sayhan, Jayhan, the Nile, and the Euphrates. Sayhan is the river of water in Paradise, Jayhan is the river of milk in Paradise, the Nile is the river of honey in Paradise, and the Euphrates is the river of wine in Paradise." Ibn Lahi'a said: "The Tigris is the river of milk in Paradise."

I (al-Qurtubi) say: What is in the Sahih on this subject is the hadith of Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "Sayhan, Jayhan, the Nile and the Euphrates are each of them rivers of Paradise." This is the wording of Muslim. In the hadith of the Night Journey, from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik, from Malik ibn Sa'sa'a, a man of his people, he said: "The Prophet of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, related that he saw four rivers emerging from its root: two apparent and two hidden. I said: 'O Gabriel, what are these rivers?' He said: 'As for the two hidden ones, they are two rivers in Paradise; as for the two apparent ones, they are the Nile and the Euphrates.'" This is the wording of Muslim. Al-Bukhari said, through the chain of Shurayk from Anas: "Then he was in the lowest heaven, with two rivers flowing (yattaridan) [yattaridan: i.e., flowing, and they are of the form yaftaʿilan from al-tard]. He said: 'What are these two rivers, O Gabriel?' He said: 'These are the Nile and the Euphrates, their source.' Then he proceeded in the heaven and came upon another river, upon which was a palace of pearl and chrysolite. He struck it with his hand and it was pure musk, very fragrant. He said: 'What is this, O Gabriel?' He said: 'This is al-Kawthar, which your Lord has hidden for you.'" And he mentioned the hadith.

The majority hold that the word "springs" (ʿuyūn) refers to springs of water. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "What is meant is springs of gold." And in the Smoke (surah 44): ﴿How many gardens and springs and fields they left behind﴾. It has been said.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 26, verses 52–68 (part 2 of 2):

Indeed they used to cultivate what lay between the two mountains, from the beginning of Egypt to its end. In the verse of Surah al-Dukhan, "and treasures" (kunuz) is the plural of kanz, and this has already been discussed in Surah al-Tawbah [[See vol. 8, p. 123, first or second edition.]]. Here it means storehouses (al-khaza'in). It has also been said that it means buried treasures (al-dafa'in). Al-Dahhak said it means rivers, but this is open to question, because springs (al-'uyun) already include them.

(And a noble station). Ibn 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: the noble station means the pulpits (al-manabir). There were a thousand pulpits, one for each of a thousand tyrants, who would honour Pharaoh and his kingdom from them. It has also been said that it means the assemblies of the chiefs and rulers, related by Ibn 'Isa, and this is close to the first view. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the fine dwellings. Ibn Lahi'a said: I heard that the noble station is al-Fayyum. It has also been said that Yusuf, peace be upon him, had written on one of his assemblies: "There is no god but Allah; Ibrahim is the friend of Allah," and so Allah called it noble because of this. It has also been said that it means the places where horses were tethered, since the leaders alone kept horses tethered there as a sign of their readiness and adornment, so that its station became the most honoured dwelling because of this. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi. The most apparent view is that it means the fine dwellings in which they were honoured.

In the language, al-maqam (المقام) can mean a place and can also be a verbal noun. Al-Nahhas said: al-maqam in the language means the place, from your saying qama yaqumu. Likewise al-maqamat, whose singular is maqama, as the poet said [[It is Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma. Yantabuha means that what is fine is said in them and done in them.]]:

"Among them are noble assemblies whose faces are fair,
and gatherings in which speech and deed are exchanged."

Al-maqam is also the verbal noun from qama yaqumu. Al-muqam (with a dammah) means a place from aqama, and it is also the verbal noun from aqama yuqimu.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Thus, and We made the Children of Israel inherit them﴾. He means that all that Allah mentioned, the gardens, the springs, the treasures and the noble station, Allah made the Children of Israel inherit. Al-Hasan and others said: the Children of Israel returned to Egypt after the destruction of Pharaoh and his people. It has also been said that by inheritance here is meant what they borrowed of the ornaments of Pharaoh's family by the command of Allah, exalted is He. I say: both matters came to pass for them, and praise belongs to Allah.

(So they pursued them at sunrise). That is, Pharaoh and his people followed the Children of Israel. Al-Suddi said: when the sun rose with its rays. Qatada said: when the earth lit up with light. Al-Zajjaj said: it is said sharaqat al-shams when it rose, and ashraqat when it shone. There is disagreement about the delay of Pharaoh and his people behind Musa and the Children of Israel, on two views. The first: they were busy burying their firstborn during that night, because the plague struck them that night; so his saying "at sunrise" (mushriqin) is a circumstantial clause describing Pharaoh's people. The second: a cloud overshadowed them, and there was darkness, and they said: we are still in the night; and it did not clear from them until morning came. Abu 'Ubayda said: the meaning of "they pursued them at sunrise" is toward the direction of the east. Al-Hasan and 'Amr ibn Maymun read: "fa-attaba'uhum mushriqin" with the shaddah and an alif of connection, meaning toward the east, derived from their saying sharraqa and gharraba when one travels toward the east and the west. The meaning of the speech is: We had determined that the Children of Israel should inherit it, and so the people of Pharaoh pursued the Children of Israel at sunrise and perished, and the Children of Israel inherited their lands.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When the two groups saw each other﴾, that is, the two groups confronted one another in such a way that each party saw the other. It is a form of tafa'ul from ru'ya (seeing).

(The companions of Musa said: "We are surely overtaken"). That is, the enemy drew near to us and we have no power to face him. The reading of the majority is "lamudrakun" with light stress, from adraka. From this is His saying: ﴿until, when drowning overtook him﴾. 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, al-A'raj and al-Zuhri read "lamuddarakun" with stress on the dal [[And with the ra' kasrah, as in al-Bahr, Ruh al-Ma'ani and al-Kashshaf, on the pattern of mufta'alun, which is intransitive, meaning destruction and annihilation, from adraka al-shay' when it follows in succession until it is finished.]], from idda-raka. Al-Farra' said: hafara and ihtaqara have one meaning, and likewise "mudrakun" and "muddarakun" have one meaning. Al-Nahhas said: the skilled grammarians do not say this; rather they say: mudrakun means "overtaken," and muddarakun means "striving to overtake them," just as it is said kasabtu meaning I obtained and won, and iktasabtu meaning I strove and sought. This is the meaning of the words of Sibawayh.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said: "By no means! Indeed my Lord is with me; He will guide me."﴾ When Pharaoh overtook Musa's host with his army and drew near to them, and the Children of Israel saw the strong enemy and the sea before them, their suspicions grew, and they said to Musa, in a manner of reproach and rudeness: "We are surely overtaken." So he rejected their statement, rebuked them, and reminded them of Allah's promise to him of guidance and victory. ("By no means!") meaning: they will not overtake you. ("Indeed my Lord is with me") meaning: with victory over the enemy. ("He will guide me") meaning: He will show me the way to salvation. When the trial grew severe upon the Children of Israel, and they saw the armies, against which they had no power, Allah, exalted and mighty is He, commanded Musa to strike the sea with his staff. This was because He, mighty and majestic, willed that the sign should be connected to Musa and tied to an act he performs; otherwise striking the staff does not split the sea, nor does it in itself help with that, except through what was joined to it of the power and invention of Allah, exalted is He. The story of this sea has already passed in Surah al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, p. 389 and following, second or third edition.]]. When it split, there were twelve paths in it according to the number of the tribes of the Children of Israel, and the water stood between them like a great mountain (tawd 'azim), that is, a great mountain. Al-Tawd is a mountain, and from it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"While a man is among the living, a mountain,
the people cast him from close range, and he leaned over."

Al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur said:

"They alighted at Anqira, over them flows
the water of the Euphrates that comes from the mountains (atwad)."

Atwad is the plural of tawd, that is, mountain. Thus there became for Musa and his companions a dry path in the sea. When the companions of Musa had come out, and the last of Pharaoh's companions had entered, as has been mentioned in Surah Yunus [[See vol. 8, p. 378, first or second edition.]], it closed over them, and Pharaoh drowned. Then some of Musa's companions said: Pharaoh has not drowned, so he was cast onto the sea shore until they looked at him. Ibn al-Qasim related from Malik, who said: two merchants went out with Musa, peace be upon him, to the sea. When they came to it, they said to him: By what did Allah command you? He said: I was commanded to strike the sea with this staff of mine, and it will split. They said to him: Do what Allah has commanded you, for He will not fail you. Then they threw themselves into the sea, affirming him. The sea remained so until Pharaoh and those with him entered, and then it returned to how it had been. This meaning has already passed in Surah al-Baqarah.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We brought the others near there﴾, that is, We brought them near to the sea, meaning Pharaoh and his people. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and others. The poet said:

"Every day that passes, or night that has gone by,
in which souls draw nearer to their appointed terms."

Abu 'Ubayda said: "azlafna" means "We gathered," and from this the night of Muzdalifah is called the night of gathering (layla jam'). Abu 'Abd Allah ibn al-Harith, Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ibn 'Abbas read "wa-azlafna" with the qaf, meaning "We destroyed them," from the saying azlaqat al-naqah and azlaqat al-faras, so she is muzlik when she causes her offspring to slip (azlaqa waladaha).

(And We saved Musa and all those with him. Then We drowned the others.) That is, Pharaoh and his people.

(Indeed in that is a sign.) That is, a token of the power of Allah, exalted is He.

(And most of them were not believers.) Because none of Pharaoh's people believed except the believer from the family of Pharaoh, whose name was Hizqil, and the daughter of Pharaoh, Asiya, wife of Pharaoh, and Maryam daughter of Dhi Musa, the old woman who guided them to the grave of Yusuf the Truthful, peace be upon him. This is because when Musa, peace be upon him, went out with the Children of Israel from Egypt, the moon grew dark over them, and he said to his people: What is this? Their scholars said: when Yusuf, peace be upon him, was approaching death, he took a covenant from us in the name of Allah that we would not leave Egypt until we had carried his bones with us. Musa said: Which of you knows his grave? They said: No one knows it except an old woman of the Children of Israel. So he sent for her and said: Show me the grave of Yusuf. She said: By Allah, I will not do so until you give me my right. He said: And what is your right? She said: My right is that I be with you in Paradise. This was grievous to him, so it was said to him: Give her what she asks. So she showed them where it was, and they dug it up and took out his bones. When they lifted them, the way was like the light of day. In another narration: Allah revealed to him that he should give it to her, and he did so. She brought them to a pool, and said to them: Drain this water. They drained it and took out the bones of Yusuf, peace be upon him, and the way became clear to them like the light of day. This has already passed in Surah Yusuf [[See vol. 9, p. 270, second edition.]].

Abu Burda related from Abu Musa that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ stayed with a Bedouin and honoured him. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "What is your need?" He said: a she-camel that I may ride, and female goats whose milk I may milk. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Why did you fail to be like the old woman of the Children of Israel?" His companions said: What was the old woman of the Children of Israel? So he related to them the story of that old woman who made Musa judge that she should be with him in Paradise.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 26, verses 52–68 (part 1 of 2):**

God's words: ﴿And We revealed to Moses: "Travel by night with My servants, for you will be pursued."﴾ Since it is among God's ways with His servants to save the believing, faithful men among His allies, who acknowledge the messengers and prophets He sent, and to destroy the disbelieving enemies who denied them, He commanded Moses to leave with the Children of Israel by night. He called them "His servants" because they had believed in Moses. The meaning of "for you will be pursued" is that Pharaoh and his people would follow you in order to turn you back. Implicit in this statement is the information that God would deliver them from Pharaoh. So Moses, peace be upon him, set out with the Children of Israel at dawn. He left the road to Syria on his left and headed toward the sea. A man from the Children of Israel would say to him, regarding leaving the road, "Why?" and he would reply, "I have been commanded thus." When Pharaoh rose in the morning and learned of Moses' night departure with the Children of Israel, he set out in their pursuit and sent to the cities of Egypt so that the armies would join him. It is reported that he caught up with them with a hundred thousand dark-coloured (adham) horses, besides the other colours. It is also reported that the Children of Israel numbered six hundred and seventy thousand. God knows best whether this is authentic. What is necessary from the verse, and what can be asserted with certainty, is that Moses, peace be upon him, left with a large host of the Children of Israel, and that Pharaoh pursued them with many times that number.

Ibn Abbas said: "There were with Pharaoh a thousand tyrants, each of whom wore a crown and each of whom was a commander of cavalry."

The shirdhimah (شِرْذِمَةٌ) is a small, despised group. Its plural is shara<u>dh</u>im (شَرَاذِم). Al-Jawhari said: "The shirdhimah is a group of people and a piece of something. A garment that is shara<u>dh</u>im means pieces (qita')." Al-Tha'labi recited the verse of the rajaz poet:

*The winter has come, and my garments are worn out,*
*Tattered; the naww<u>a</u>q laughs at them.*

The naww<u>a</u>q (النَّوَّاق) is a man who tames affairs and sets them right. This is what al-Jawhari said in the Sihah. [It is said that naww<u>a</u>q is the name of his son. It is also narrated as al-tawwaq (التَّوَّاق) with a ta'.]

The lam in God's words ﴿Indeed, these are a small group﴾ (لَشِرْذِمَةٌ) is the lam of emphasis (lam al-tawkid). It frequently enters the predicate of inna, except that the Kufans do not permit "inna Zayd la-sawfa yaqumu" (indeed Zayd will surely stand). The evidence that it is permissible is God's words ﴿So you will surely know﴾ (فَلَسَوْفَ تَعْلَمُونَ), where this same lam of emphasis has entered upon sawfa. This is what al-Nahhas said.

﴿And indeed they are enraging us﴾ (وَإِنَّهُمْ لَنا لَغائِظُونَ), meaning: they are enemies to us because they oppose our religion and take away our wealth, which they had borrowed, as mentioned earlier. Their virgin daughters (al-abkar) died that night. This has been fully discussed in al-A'raf and Ta-Ha. It is said: ghaza-ni kadha wa-aghaza-ni (this enraged me and made me enraged). Al-ghayz is anger, and from it come al-taghayyuz and al-ightiyaz. The meaning is that they enraged us by leaving without permission.

﴿And indeed we are a wary multitude (jami'un hadhirun)﴾ (وَإِنَّا لَجَمِيعٌ حاذِرُونَ), meaning: a gathered host taking precautions with our weapons. It is read as "hadhirun" (حَذِرُونَ), whose meaning is the same as "hadhirun" (حاذِرُونَ), i.e., fearful. Al-Jawhari said: it is read "hadhirun", "hadhirun" and "hadhirun" with a damma on the dhal (ḥadhirūna), reported by al-Akhfash. The meaning of "hadhirun" is "prepared (mutaahhibun)", and the meaning of "hadhirun" is "fearful (khaifun)." Al-Nahhas said: "hadhirun" is the reading of the people of Madina and Abu Amr. The reading of the people of Kufa is "hadhirun" (حَاذِرُونَ), and it is well known from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas. "Hadirun" with an undotted dal (حَادِرُونَ) is the reading of Abu Ubayd, and al-Mahdawi transmitted it from Ibn Abi Ammar, as did al-Mawardi and al-Tha'labi from Sumayt ibn Ajlan. Al-Nahhas said: Abu Ubayda holds that the meanings of "hadhirun" and "hadhirun" are one, and this is the view of Sibawayh, who permitted: "huwa hadhirun Zaydan," just as one says "hadhir Zaydan" (be wary of Zayd). He recited:

*Wary of matters that do no harm, and secure*
*From what cannot ward off the decrees.*

Abu Umar al-Jarmi claimed that it is permissible to say "huwa hadhirun Zaydan" by omitting min (from). However, most grammarians distinguish between hadhar and hadhir. Among them are al-Kisa'i, al-Farra', and Muhammad ibn Yazid, who hold that hadhar in its form means being alert and watchful, and so it is intransitive. Hadhir means "prepared," and this explanation was transmitted from the earlier authorities. Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, regarding God's words ﴿And indeed we are a wary multitude﴾, said: "Equipped with weapons and horses, well-prepared." This is the same meaning. His words "equipped (mu'dun)" mean that they have equipment (adah). It has also been said that the meaning is: we have weapons, and they have no weapons, which incites them to fight. As for "hadirun" with an undotted dal, it derives from the expression "a'yun hadratun," meaning full (eyes). That is, we are full of rage against them. From this is the verse of the poet, Imru' al-Qays:

*And an eye full and bright, its lids split from the corners.*

The lexicographers have said: "A man is hadirun" when he is full-fleshed. So it is possible that the meaning is "full of weapons." Al-Mahdawi said: "al-hadir" is strong and powerful.

God's words: ﴿So We expelled them from gardens and springs﴾, meaning from the land of Egypt. From Abdullah ibn Amr who said: "The gardens were on the two banks of the Nile, on both sides from Aswan to Rashid, and between the gardens were fields. The Nile has seven branches (khalij): the Alexandria branch, the Sakha branch, the Damietta branch, the Sardus branch, the Manf branch, the Fayyum branch, and the Manha branch [which is the Sea of Joseph, peace be upon him], all connected, none cut off from another, and the fields lay between all the branches. All of the land of Egypt was irrigated by sixteen cubits, through the dams, bridges and canals they had arranged and measured. For this reason, when the Nile rose to sixteen cubits it was called the Sultan's Nile. Ibn Abi al-Raddad was granted a robe of honour [He was Abdullah ibn al-Salam ibn Abdullah ibn Abi al-Raddad, the muezzin, who came to Egypt from Basra and narrated hadith there. He was appointed to measure the Nile during the governorship of Yazid ibn Abdullah al-Turki, when the Christians had been in charge of measuring it. He was given seven dinars every month, and his measuring remained in his descendants for a long time. Abu al-Raddad died in the year 266 AH. From al-Maqrizi's Khitat, vol. 1, p. 58.], and this state continues to the present. It is called the Sultan's Nile because at that point the kharaj (land tax) becomes due from the people. All of Egypt was irrigated by a finger's width from seventeen cubits. When the Nile rose to seventeen cubits and a finger was called out for it, the eighteen-cubit mark was reached and the kharaj increased by a million dinars. When it exceeded that and a finger was called out for it at nineteen cubits, the kharaj decreased by a million dinars. The reason for this was what was spent on public works, canals, bridges, and attention to their maintenance. As for now, most of it is not irrigated until a finger is called out at nineteen cubits by the Egyptian measure. As for the works of Upper Egypt, some of them are not fully irrigated until the water enters the twenty-second cubit in Upper Egypt."

I (al-Qurtubi) say: As for the land of Egypt, it is now not fully irrigated except from twenty cubits and fingers, because the land has risen and there is no attention to the maintenance of its dams. This is one of the wonders of the world: the Nile rises when the waters pour over all the land until it floods all of Egypt's land, and the regions remain like islands, not reachable except by boats and measuring instruments.

It is narrated from Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As that he said: "The Nile of Egypt is the lord of rivers. God subjected to it every river between East and West, and God made the rivers submissive to it. When God wills that the Nile of Egypt should flow, He commands every river to feed it, and the rivers supply it with their water. God causes springs to gush forth for it. When it reaches what God, the Mighty and Majestic, wills, God, blessed and exalted, reveals to every water to return to its origin."

Qays ibn al-Hajjaj said: "When Egypt was conquered, its people came to Amr ibn al-As when the month of Ba'una (one of the Coptic months) had arrived, and they said to him: 'O Amir, our Nile has a custom and it will not flow except by it.' He said to them: 'And what is that?' They said: 'When it is the twelfth night of this month, we go to a virgin girl between her parents, we satisfy her parents, we dress her in the finest jewelry and clothing, and then we throw her into this Nile.' Amr said to them: 'This cannot happen in Islam, for Islam obliterates what came before it.' So they remained in Abib and Misra, and neither little nor much of the Nile flowed, and they resolved to depart. When Amr ibn al-As saw this, he wrote to Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with them both, informing him of the matter. Umar ibn al-Khattab wrote back to him: 'You have done right in what you did, for Islam obliterates what came before it, and this should not happen.' He sent him a slip of paper inside his letter, and wrote to Amr: 'I have sent you a slip of paper inside my letter; throw it into the Nile when my letter reaches you.' When Umar's letter reached Amr ibn al-As, he took the slip and opened it, and in it was: 'From the servant of God, Umar, Commander of the Believers, to the Nile of Egypt. To proceed: if you flow by your own power, then do not flow; but if it is God, the One, the Subduer, who makes you flow, then we ask God, the One, the Subduer, to make you flow.' He said: 'So he threw the slip into the Nile the day before the Cross (al-Salib), when the people of Egypt had prepared to leave and depart from it, because their welfare there depended only on the Nile.' When he threw the slip into the Nile, they awoke on the day of the Cross and God had made it rise sixteen cubits in a single night, and God cut off that custom from the people of Egypt from that year onward."

Ka'b al-Ahbar said: "Four rivers from Paradise God placed in the world: Sayhan, Jayhan, the Nile, and the Euphrates. Sayhan is the river of water in Paradise, Jayhan is the river of milk in Paradise, the Nile is the river of honey in Paradise, and the Euphrates is the river of wine in Paradise." Ibn Lahi'a said: "The Tigris is the river of milk in Paradise."

I (al-Qurtubi) say: What is in the Sahih on this subject is the hadith of Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "Sayhan, Jayhan, the Nile and the Euphrates are each of them rivers of Paradise." This is the wording of Muslim. In the hadith of the Night Journey, from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik, from Malik ibn Sa'sa'a, a man of his people, he said: "The Prophet of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, related that he saw four rivers emerging from its root: two apparent and two hidden. I said: 'O Gabriel, what are these rivers?' He said: 'As for the two hidden ones, they are two rivers in Paradise; as for the two apparent ones, they are the Nile and the Euphrates.'" This is the wording of Muslim. Al-Bukhari said, through the chain of Shurayk from Anas: "Then he was in the lowest heaven, with two rivers flowing (yattaridan) [yattaridan: i.e., flowing, and they are of the form yaftaʿilan from al-tard]. He said: 'What are these two rivers, O Gabriel?' He said: 'These are the Nile and the Euphrates, their source.' Then he proceeded in the heaven and came upon another river, upon which was a palace of pearl and chrysolite. He struck it with his hand and it was pure musk, very fragrant. He said: 'What is this, O Gabriel?' He said: 'This is al-Kawthar, which your Lord has hidden for you.'" And he mentioned the hadith.

The majority hold that the word "springs" (ʿuyūn) refers to springs of water. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "What is meant is springs of gold." And in the Smoke (surah 44): ﴿How many gardens and springs and fields they left behind﴾. It has been said.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 26, verses 52–68 (part 2 of 2):

Indeed they used to cultivate what lay between the two mountains, from the beginning of Egypt to its end. In the verse of Surah al-Dukhan, "and treasures" (kunuz) is the plural of kanz, and this has already been discussed in Surah al-Tawbah [[See vol. 8, p. 123, first or second edition.]]. Here it means storehouses (al-khaza'in). It has also been said that it means buried treasures (al-dafa'in). Al-Dahhak said it means rivers, but this is open to question, because springs (al-'uyun) already include them.

(And a noble station). Ibn 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: the noble station means the pulpits (al-manabir). There were a thousand pulpits, one for each of a thousand tyrants, who would honour Pharaoh and his kingdom from them. It has also been said that it means the assemblies of the chiefs and rulers, related by Ibn 'Isa, and this is close to the first view. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the fine dwellings. Ibn Lahi'a said: I heard that the noble station is al-Fayyum. It has also been said that Yusuf, peace be upon him, had written on one of his assemblies: "There is no god but Allah; Ibrahim is the friend of Allah," and so Allah called it noble because of this. It has also been said that it means the places where horses were tethered, since the leaders alone kept horses tethered there as a sign of their readiness and adornment, so that its station became the most honoured dwelling because of this. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi. The most apparent view is that it means the fine dwellings in which they were honoured.

In the language, al-maqam (المقام) can mean a place and can also be a verbal noun. Al-Nahhas said: al-maqam in the language means the place, from your saying qama yaqumu. Likewise al-maqamat, whose singular is maqama, as the poet said [[It is Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma. Yantabuha means that what is fine is said in them and done in them.]]:

"Among them are noble assemblies whose faces are fair,
and gatherings in which speech and deed are exchanged."

Al-maqam is also the verbal noun from qama yaqumu. Al-muqam (with a dammah) means a place from aqama, and it is also the verbal noun from aqama yuqimu.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Thus, and We made the Children of Israel inherit them﴾. He means that all that Allah mentioned, the gardens, the springs, the treasures and the noble station, Allah made the Children of Israel inherit. Al-Hasan and others said: the Children of Israel returned to Egypt after the destruction of Pharaoh and his people. It has also been said that by inheritance here is meant what they borrowed of the ornaments of Pharaoh's family by the command of Allah, exalted is He. I say: both matters came to pass for them, and praise belongs to Allah.

(So they pursued them at sunrise). That is, Pharaoh and his people followed the Children of Israel. Al-Suddi said: when the sun rose with its rays. Qatada said: when the earth lit up with light. Al-Zajjaj said: it is said sharaqat al-shams when it rose, and ashraqat when it shone. There is disagreement about the delay of Pharaoh and his people behind Musa and the Children of Israel, on two views. The first: they were busy burying their firstborn during that night, because the plague struck them that night; so his saying "at sunrise" (mushriqin) is a circumstantial clause describing Pharaoh's people. The second: a cloud overshadowed them, and there was darkness, and they said: we are still in the night; and it did not clear from them until morning came. Abu 'Ubayda said: the meaning of "they pursued them at sunrise" is toward the direction of the east. Al-Hasan and 'Amr ibn Maymun read: "fa-attaba'uhum mushriqin" with the shaddah and an alif of connection, meaning toward the east, derived from their saying sharraqa and gharraba when one travels toward the east and the west. The meaning of the speech is: We had determined that the Children of Israel should inherit it, and so the people of Pharaoh pursued the Children of Israel at sunrise and perished, and the Children of Israel inherited their lands.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When the two groups saw each other﴾, that is, the two groups confronted one another in such a way that each party saw the other. It is a form of tafa'ul from ru'ya (seeing).

(The companions of Musa said: "We are surely overtaken"). That is, the enemy drew near to us and we have no power to face him. The reading of the majority is "lamudrakun" with light stress, from adraka. From this is His saying: ﴿until, when drowning overtook him﴾. 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, al-A'raj and al-Zuhri read "lamuddarakun" with stress on the dal [[And with the ra' kasrah, as in al-Bahr, Ruh al-Ma'ani and al-Kashshaf, on the pattern of mufta'alun, which is intransitive, meaning destruction and annihilation, from adraka al-shay' when it follows in succession until it is finished.]], from idda-raka. Al-Farra' said: hafara and ihtaqara have one meaning, and likewise "mudrakun" and "muddarakun" have one meaning. Al-Nahhas said: the skilled grammarians do not say this; rather they say: mudrakun means "overtaken," and muddarakun means "striving to overtake them," just as it is said kasabtu meaning I obtained and won, and iktasabtu meaning I strove and sought. This is the meaning of the words of Sibawayh.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said: "By no means! Indeed my Lord is with me; He will guide me."﴾ When Pharaoh overtook Musa's host with his army and drew near to them, and the Children of Israel saw the strong enemy and the sea before them, their suspicions grew, and they said to Musa, in a manner of reproach and rudeness: "We are surely overtaken." So he rejected their statement, rebuked them, and reminded them of Allah's promise to him of guidance and victory. ("By no means!") meaning: they will not overtake you. ("Indeed my Lord is with me") meaning: with victory over the enemy. ("He will guide me") meaning: He will show me the way to salvation. When the trial grew severe upon the Children of Israel, and they saw the armies, against which they had no power, Allah, exalted and mighty is He, commanded Musa to strike the sea with his staff. This was because He, mighty and majestic, willed that the sign should be connected to Musa and tied to an act he performs; otherwise striking the staff does not split the sea, nor does it in itself help with that, except through what was joined to it of the power and invention of Allah, exalted is He. The story of this sea has already passed in Surah al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, p. 389 and following, second or third edition.]]. When it split, there were twelve paths in it according to the number of the tribes of the Children of Israel, and the water stood between them like a great mountain (tawd 'azim), that is, a great mountain. Al-Tawd is a mountain, and from it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"While a man is among the living, a mountain,
the people cast him from close range, and he leaned over."

Al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur said:

"They alighted at Anqira, over them flows
the water of the Euphrates that comes from the mountains (atwad)."

Atwad is the plural of tawd, that is, mountain. Thus there became for Musa and his companions a dry path in the sea. When the companions of Musa had come out, and the last of Pharaoh's companions had entered, as has been mentioned in Surah Yunus [[See vol. 8, p. 378, first or second edition.]], it closed over them, and Pharaoh drowned. Then some of Musa's companions said: Pharaoh has not drowned, so he was cast onto the sea shore until they looked at him. Ibn al-Qasim related from Malik, who said: two merchants went out with Musa, peace be upon him, to the sea. When they came to it, they said to him: By what did Allah command you? He said: I was commanded to strike the sea with this staff of mine, and it will split. They said to him: Do what Allah has commanded you, for He will not fail you. Then they threw themselves into the sea, affirming him. The sea remained so until Pharaoh and those with him entered, and then it returned to how it had been. This meaning has already passed in Surah al-Baqarah.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We brought the others near there﴾, that is, We brought them near to the sea, meaning Pharaoh and his people. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and others. The poet said:

"Every day that passes, or night that has gone by,
in which souls draw nearer to their appointed terms."

Abu 'Ubayda said: "azlafna" means "We gathered," and from this the night of Muzdalifah is called the night of gathering (layla jam'). Abu 'Abd Allah ibn al-Harith, Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ibn 'Abbas read "wa-azlafna" with the qaf, meaning "We destroyed them," from the saying azlaqat al-naqah and azlaqat al-faras, so she is muzlik when she causes her offspring to slip (azlaqa waladaha).

(And We saved Musa and all those with him. Then We drowned the others.) That is, Pharaoh and his people.

(Indeed in that is a sign.) That is, a token of the power of Allah, exalted is He.

(And most of them were not believers.) Because none of Pharaoh's people believed except the believer from the family of Pharaoh, whose name was Hizqil, and the daughter of Pharaoh, Asiya, wife of Pharaoh, and Maryam daughter of Dhi Musa, the old woman who guided them to the grave of Yusuf the Truthful, peace be upon him. This is because when Musa, peace be upon him, went out with the Children of Israel from Egypt, the moon grew dark over them, and he said to his people: What is this? Their scholars said: when Yusuf, peace be upon him, was approaching death, he took a covenant from us in the name of Allah that we would not leave Egypt until we had carried his bones with us. Musa said: Which of you knows his grave? They said: No one knows it except an old woman of the Children of Israel. So he sent for her and said: Show me the grave of Yusuf. She said: By Allah, I will not do so until you give me my right. He said: And what is your right? She said: My right is that I be with you in Paradise. This was grievous to him, so it was said to him: Give her what she asks. So she showed them where it was, and they dug it up and took out his bones. When they lifted them, the way was like the light of day. In another narration: Allah revealed to him that he should give it to her, and he did so. She brought them to a pool, and said to them: Drain this water. They drained it and took out the bones of Yusuf, peace be upon him, and the way became clear to them like the light of day. This has already passed in Surah Yusuf [[See vol. 9, p. 270, second edition.]].

Abu Burda related from Abu Musa that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ stayed with a Bedouin and honoured him. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "What is your need?" He said: a she-camel that I may ride, and female goats whose milk I may milk. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Why did you fail to be like the old woman of the Children of Israel?" His companions said: What was the old woman of the Children of Israel? So he related to them the story of that old woman who made Musa judge that she should be with him in Paradise.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 26, verses 52–68 (part 1 of 2):**

God's words: ﴿And We revealed to Moses: "Travel by night with My servants, for you will be pursued."﴾ Since it is among God's ways with His servants to save the believing, faithful men among His allies, who acknowledge the messengers and prophets He sent, and to destroy the disbelieving enemies who denied them, He commanded Moses to leave with the Children of Israel by night. He called them "His servants" because they had believed in Moses. The meaning of "for you will be pursued" is that Pharaoh and his people would follow you in order to turn you back. Implicit in this statement is the information that God would deliver them from Pharaoh. So Moses, peace be upon him, set out with the Children of Israel at dawn. He left the road to Syria on his left and headed toward the sea. A man from the Children of Israel would say to him, regarding leaving the road, "Why?" and he would reply, "I have been commanded thus." When Pharaoh rose in the morning and learned of Moses' night departure with the Children of Israel, he set out in their pursuit and sent to the cities of Egypt so that the armies would join him. It is reported that he caught up with them with a hundred thousand dark-coloured (adham) horses, besides the other colours. It is also reported that the Children of Israel numbered six hundred and seventy thousand. God knows best whether this is authentic. What is necessary from the verse, and what can be asserted with certainty, is that Moses, peace be upon him, left with a large host of the Children of Israel, and that Pharaoh pursued them with many times that number.

Ibn Abbas said: "There were with Pharaoh a thousand tyrants, each of whom wore a crown and each of whom was a commander of cavalry."

The shirdhimah (شِرْذِمَةٌ) is a small, despised group. Its plural is shara<u>dh</u>im (شَرَاذِم). Al-Jawhari said: "The shirdhimah is a group of people and a piece of something. A garment that is shara<u>dh</u>im means pieces (qita')." Al-Tha'labi recited the verse of the rajaz poet:

*The winter has come, and my garments are worn out,*
*Tattered; the naww<u>a</u>q laughs at them.*

The naww<u>a</u>q (النَّوَّاق) is a man who tames affairs and sets them right. This is what al-Jawhari said in the Sihah. [It is said that naww<u>a</u>q is the name of his son. It is also narrated as al-tawwaq (التَّوَّاق) with a ta'.]

The lam in God's words ﴿Indeed, these are a small group﴾ (لَشِرْذِمَةٌ) is the lam of emphasis (lam al-tawkid). It frequently enters the predicate of inna, except that the Kufans do not permit "inna Zayd la-sawfa yaqumu" (indeed Zayd will surely stand). The evidence that it is permissible is God's words ﴿So you will surely know﴾ (فَلَسَوْفَ تَعْلَمُونَ), where this same lam of emphasis has entered upon sawfa. This is what al-Nahhas said.

﴿And indeed they are enraging us﴾ (وَإِنَّهُمْ لَنا لَغائِظُونَ), meaning: they are enemies to us because they oppose our religion and take away our wealth, which they had borrowed, as mentioned earlier. Their virgin daughters (al-abkar) died that night. This has been fully discussed in al-A'raf and Ta-Ha. It is said: ghaza-ni kadha wa-aghaza-ni (this enraged me and made me enraged). Al-ghayz is anger, and from it come al-taghayyuz and al-ightiyaz. The meaning is that they enraged us by leaving without permission.

﴿And indeed we are a wary multitude (jami'un hadhirun)﴾ (وَإِنَّا لَجَمِيعٌ حاذِرُونَ), meaning: a gathered host taking precautions with our weapons. It is read as "hadhirun" (حَذِرُونَ), whose meaning is the same as "hadhirun" (حاذِرُونَ), i.e., fearful. Al-Jawhari said: it is read "hadhirun", "hadhirun" and "hadhirun" with a damma on the dhal (ḥadhirūna), reported by al-Akhfash. The meaning of "hadhirun" is "prepared (mutaahhibun)", and the meaning of "hadhirun" is "fearful (khaifun)." Al-Nahhas said: "hadhirun" is the reading of the people of Madina and Abu Amr. The reading of the people of Kufa is "hadhirun" (حَاذِرُونَ), and it is well known from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas. "Hadirun" with an undotted dal (حَادِرُونَ) is the reading of Abu Ubayd, and al-Mahdawi transmitted it from Ibn Abi Ammar, as did al-Mawardi and al-Tha'labi from Sumayt ibn Ajlan. Al-Nahhas said: Abu Ubayda holds that the meanings of "hadhirun" and "hadhirun" are one, and this is the view of Sibawayh, who permitted: "huwa hadhirun Zaydan," just as one says "hadhir Zaydan" (be wary of Zayd). He recited:

*Wary of matters that do no harm, and secure*
*From what cannot ward off the decrees.*

Abu Umar al-Jarmi claimed that it is permissible to say "huwa hadhirun Zaydan" by omitting min (from). However, most grammarians distinguish between hadhar and hadhir. Among them are al-Kisa'i, al-Farra', and Muhammad ibn Yazid, who hold that hadhar in its form means being alert and watchful, and so it is intransitive. Hadhir means "prepared," and this explanation was transmitted from the earlier authorities. Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, regarding God's words ﴿And indeed we are a wary multitude﴾, said: "Equipped with weapons and horses, well-prepared." This is the same meaning. His words "equipped (mu'dun)" mean that they have equipment (adah). It has also been said that the meaning is: we have weapons, and they have no weapons, which incites them to fight. As for "hadirun" with an undotted dal, it derives from the expression "a'yun hadratun," meaning full (eyes). That is, we are full of rage against them. From this is the verse of the poet, Imru' al-Qays:

*And an eye full and bright, its lids split from the corners.*

The lexicographers have said: "A man is hadirun" when he is full-fleshed. So it is possible that the meaning is "full of weapons." Al-Mahdawi said: "al-hadir" is strong and powerful.

God's words: ﴿So We expelled them from gardens and springs﴾, meaning from the land of Egypt. From Abdullah ibn Amr who said: "The gardens were on the two banks of the Nile, on both sides from Aswan to Rashid, and between the gardens were fields. The Nile has seven branches (khalij): the Alexandria branch, the Sakha branch, the Damietta branch, the Sardus branch, the Manf branch, the Fayyum branch, and the Manha branch [which is the Sea of Joseph, peace be upon him], all connected, none cut off from another, and the fields lay between all the branches. All of the land of Egypt was irrigated by sixteen cubits, through the dams, bridges and canals they had arranged and measured. For this reason, when the Nile rose to sixteen cubits it was called the Sultan's Nile. Ibn Abi al-Raddad was granted a robe of honour [He was Abdullah ibn al-Salam ibn Abdullah ibn Abi al-Raddad, the muezzin, who came to Egypt from Basra and narrated hadith there. He was appointed to measure the Nile during the governorship of Yazid ibn Abdullah al-Turki, when the Christians had been in charge of measuring it. He was given seven dinars every month, and his measuring remained in his descendants for a long time. Abu al-Raddad died in the year 266 AH. From al-Maqrizi's Khitat, vol. 1, p. 58.], and this state continues to the present. It is called the Sultan's Nile because at that point the kharaj (land tax) becomes due from the people. All of Egypt was irrigated by a finger's width from seventeen cubits. When the Nile rose to seventeen cubits and a finger was called out for it, the eighteen-cubit mark was reached and the kharaj increased by a million dinars. When it exceeded that and a finger was called out for it at nineteen cubits, the kharaj decreased by a million dinars. The reason for this was what was spent on public works, canals, bridges, and attention to their maintenance. As for now, most of it is not irrigated until a finger is called out at nineteen cubits by the Egyptian measure. As for the works of Upper Egypt, some of them are not fully irrigated until the water enters the twenty-second cubit in Upper Egypt."

I (al-Qurtubi) say: As for the land of Egypt, it is now not fully irrigated except from twenty cubits and fingers, because the land has risen and there is no attention to the maintenance of its dams. This is one of the wonders of the world: the Nile rises when the waters pour over all the land until it floods all of Egypt's land, and the regions remain like islands, not reachable except by boats and measuring instruments.

It is narrated from Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As that he said: "The Nile of Egypt is the lord of rivers. God subjected to it every river between East and West, and God made the rivers submissive to it. When God wills that the Nile of Egypt should flow, He commands every river to feed it, and the rivers supply it with their water. God causes springs to gush forth for it. When it reaches what God, the Mighty and Majestic, wills, God, blessed and exalted, reveals to every water to return to its origin."

Qays ibn al-Hajjaj said: "When Egypt was conquered, its people came to Amr ibn al-As when the month of Ba'una (one of the Coptic months) had arrived, and they said to him: 'O Amir, our Nile has a custom and it will not flow except by it.' He said to them: 'And what is that?' They said: 'When it is the twelfth night of this month, we go to a virgin girl between her parents, we satisfy her parents, we dress her in the finest jewelry and clothing, and then we throw her into this Nile.' Amr said to them: 'This cannot happen in Islam, for Islam obliterates what came before it.' So they remained in Abib and Misra, and neither little nor much of the Nile flowed, and they resolved to depart. When Amr ibn al-As saw this, he wrote to Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with them both, informing him of the matter. Umar ibn al-Khattab wrote back to him: 'You have done right in what you did, for Islam obliterates what came before it, and this should not happen.' He sent him a slip of paper inside his letter, and wrote to Amr: 'I have sent you a slip of paper inside my letter; throw it into the Nile when my letter reaches you.' When Umar's letter reached Amr ibn al-As, he took the slip and opened it, and in it was: 'From the servant of God, Umar, Commander of the Believers, to the Nile of Egypt. To proceed: if you flow by your own power, then do not flow; but if it is God, the One, the Subduer, who makes you flow, then we ask God, the One, the Subduer, to make you flow.'
