Then he proceeded in the heaven and came upon another river, upon which was a palace of pearl and chrysolite. He struck it with his hand and it was pure musk, very fragrant. He said: 'What is this, O Gabriel?' He said: 'This is al-Kawthar, which your Lord has hidden for you.'" And he mentioned the hadith.

The majority hold that the word "springs" (ʿuyūn) refers to springs of water. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "What is meant is springs of gold." And in the Smoke (surah 44): ﴿How many gardens and springs and fields they left behind﴾. It has been said.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 26, verses 52–68 (part 2 of 2):

Indeed they used to cultivate what lay between the two mountains, from the beginning of Egypt to its end. In the verse of Surah al-Dukhan, "and treasures" (kunuz) is the plural of kanz, and this has already been discussed in Surah al-Tawbah [[See vol. 8, p. 123, first or second edition.]]. Here it means storehouses (al-khaza'in). It has also been said that it means buried treasures (al-dafa'in). Al-Dahhak said it means rivers, but this is open to question, because springs (al-'uyun) already include them.

(And a noble station). Ibn 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: the noble station means the pulpits (al-manabir). There were a thousand pulpits, one for each of a thousand tyrants, who would honour Pharaoh and his kingdom from them. It has also been said that it means the assemblies of the chiefs and rulers, related by Ibn 'Isa, and this is close to the first view. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the fine dwellings. Ibn Lahi'a said: I heard that the noble station is al-Fayyum. It has also been said that Yusuf, peace be upon him, had written on one of his assemblies: "There is no god but Allah; Ibrahim is the friend of Allah," and so Allah called it noble because of this. It has also been said that it means the places where horses were tethered, since the leaders alone kept horses tethered there as a sign of their readiness and adornment, so that its station became the most honoured dwelling because of this. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi. The most apparent view is that it means the fine dwellings in which they were honoured.

In the language, al-maqam (المقام) can mean a place and can also be a verbal noun. Al-Nahhas said: al-maqam in the language means the place, from your saying qama yaqumu. Likewise al-maqamat, whose singular is maqama, as the poet said [[It is Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma. Yantabuha means that what is fine is said in them and done in them.]]:

"Among them are noble assemblies whose faces are fair,
and gatherings in which speech and deed are exchanged."

Al-maqam is also the verbal noun from qama yaqumu. Al-muqam (with a dammah) means a place from aqama, and it is also the verbal noun from aqama yuqimu.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Thus, and We made the Children of Israel inherit them﴾. He means that all that Allah mentioned, the gardens, the springs, the treasures and the noble station, Allah made the Children of Israel inherit. Al-Hasan and others said: the Children of Israel returned to Egypt after the destruction of Pharaoh and his people. It has also been said that by inheritance here is meant what they borrowed of the ornaments of Pharaoh's family by the command of Allah, exalted is He. I say: both matters came to pass for them, and praise belongs to Allah.

(So they pursued them at sunrise). That is, Pharaoh and his people followed the Children of Israel. Al-Suddi said: when the sun rose with its rays. Qatada said: when the earth lit up with light. Al-Zajjaj said: it is said sharaqat al-shams when it rose, and ashraqat when it shone. There is disagreement about the delay of Pharaoh and his people behind Musa and the Children of Israel, on two views. The first: they were busy burying their firstborn during that night, because the plague struck them that night; so his saying "at sunrise" (mushriqin) is a circumstantial clause describing Pharaoh's people. The second: a cloud overshadowed them, and there was darkness, and they said: we are still in the night; and it did not clear from them until morning came. Abu 'Ubayda said: the meaning of "they pursued them at sunrise" is toward the direction of the east. Al-Hasan and 'Amr ibn Maymun read: "fa-attaba'uhum mushriqin" with the shaddah and an alif of connection, meaning toward the east, derived from their saying sharraqa and gharraba when one travels toward the east and the west. The meaning of the speech is: We had determined that the Children of Israel should inherit it, and so the people of Pharaoh pursued the Children of Israel at sunrise and perished, and the Children of Israel inherited their lands.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When the two groups saw each other﴾, that is, the two groups confronted one another in such a way that each party saw the other. It is a form of tafa'ul from ru'ya (seeing).

(The companions of Musa said: "We are surely overtaken"). That is, the enemy drew near to us and we have no power to face him. The reading of the majority is "lamudrakun" with light stress, from adraka. From this is His saying: ﴿until, when drowning overtook him﴾. 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, al-A'raj and al-Zuhri read "lamuddarakun" with stress on the dal [[And with the ra' kasrah, as in al-Bahr, Ruh al-Ma'ani and al-Kashshaf, on the pattern of mufta'alun, which is intransitive, meaning destruction and annihilation, from adraka al-shay' when it follows in succession until it is finished.]], from idda-raka. Al-Farra' said: hafara and ihtaqara have one meaning, and likewise "mudrakun" and "muddarakun" have one meaning. Al-Nahhas said: the skilled grammarians do not say this; rather they say: mudrakun means "overtaken," and muddarakun means "striving to overtake them," just as it is said kasabtu meaning I obtained and won, and iktasabtu meaning I strove and sought. This is the meaning of the words of Sibawayh.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said: "By no means! Indeed my Lord is with me; He will guide me."﴾ When Pharaoh overtook Musa's host with his army and drew near to them, and the Children of Israel saw the strong enemy and the sea before them, their suspicions grew, and they said to Musa, in a manner of reproach and rudeness: "We are surely overtaken." So he rejected their statement, rebuked them, and reminded them of Allah's promise to him of guidance and victory. ("By no means!") meaning: they will not overtake you. ("Indeed my Lord is with me") meaning: with victory over the enemy. ("He will guide me") meaning: He will show me the way to salvation. When the trial grew severe upon the Children of Israel, and they saw the armies, against which they had no power, Allah, exalted and mighty is He, commanded Musa to strike the sea with his staff. This was because He, mighty and majestic, willed that the sign should be connected to Musa and tied to an act he performs; otherwise striking the staff does not split the sea, nor does it in itself help with that, except through what was joined to it of the power and invention of Allah, exalted is He. The story of this sea has already passed in Surah al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, p. 389 and following, second or third edition.]]. When it split, there were twelve paths in it according to the number of the tribes of the Children of Israel, and the water stood between them like a great mountain (tawd 'azim), that is, a great mountain. Al-Tawd is a mountain, and from it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"While a man is among the living, a mountain,
the people cast him from close range, and he leaned over."

Al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur said:

"They alighted at Anqira, over them flows
the water of the Euphrates that comes from the mountains (atwad)."

Atwad is the plural of tawd, that is, mountain. Thus there became for Musa and his companions a dry path in the sea. When the companions of Musa had come out, and the last of Pharaoh's companions had entered, as has been mentioned in Surah Yunus [[See vol. 8, p. 378, first or second edition.]], it closed over them, and Pharaoh drowned. Then some of Musa's companions said: Pharaoh has not drowned, so he was cast onto the sea shore until they looked at him. Ibn al-Qasim related from Malik, who said: two merchants went out with Musa, peace be upon him, to the sea. When they came to it, they said to him: By what did Allah command you? He said: I was commanded to strike the sea with this staff of mine, and it will split. They said to him: Do what Allah has commanded you, for He will not fail you. Then they threw themselves into the sea, affirming him. The sea remained so until Pharaoh and those with him entered, and then it returned to how it had been. This meaning has already passed in Surah al-Baqarah.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We brought the others near there﴾, that is, We brought them near to the sea, meaning Pharaoh and his people. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and others. The poet said:

"Every day that passes, or night that has gone by,
in which souls draw nearer to their appointed terms."

Abu 'Ubayda said: "azlafna" means "We gathered," and from this the night of Muzdalifah is called the night of gathering (layla jam'). Abu 'Abd Allah ibn al-Harith, Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ibn 'Abbas read "wa-azlafna" with the qaf, meaning "We destroyed them," from the saying azlaqat al-naqah and azlaqat al-faras, so she is muzlik when she causes her offspring to slip (azlaqa waladaha).

(And We saved Musa and all those with him. Then We drowned the others.) That is, Pharaoh and his people.

(Indeed in that is a sign.) That is, a token of the power of Allah, exalted is He.

(And most of them were not believers.) Because none of Pharaoh's people believed except the believer from the family of Pharaoh, whose name was Hizqil, and the daughter of Pharaoh, Asiya, wife of Pharaoh, and Maryam daughter of Dhi Musa, the old woman who guided them to the grave of Yusuf the Truthful, peace be upon him. This is because when Musa, peace be upon him, went out with the Children of Israel from Egypt, the moon grew dark over them, and he said to his people: What is this? Their scholars said: when Yusuf, peace be upon him, was approaching death, he took a covenant from us in the name of Allah that we would not leave Egypt until we had carried his bones with us. Musa said: Which of you knows his grave? They said: No one knows it except an old woman of the Children of Israel. So he sent for her and said: Show me the grave of Yusuf. She said: By Allah, I will not do so until you give me my right. He said: And what is your right? She said: My right is that I be with you in Paradise. This was grievous to him, so it was said to him: Give her what she asks. So she showed them where it was, and they dug it up and took out his bones. When they lifted them, the way was like the light of day. In another narration: Allah revealed to him that he should give it to her, and he did so. She brought them to a pool, and said to them: Drain this water. They drained it and took out the bones of Yusuf, peace be upon him, and the way became clear to them like the light of day. This has already passed in Surah Yusuf [[See vol. 9, p. 270, second edition.]].

Abu Burda related from Abu Musa that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ stayed with a Bedouin and honoured him. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "What is your need?" He said: a she-camel that I may ride, and female goats whose milk I may milk. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Why did you fail to be like the old woman of the Children of Israel?" His companions said: What was the old woman of the Children of Israel? So he related to them the story of that old woman who made Musa judge that she should be with him in Paradise.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 26, verses 52–68 (part 1 of 2):**

God's words: ﴿And We revealed to Moses: "Travel by night with My servants, for you will be pursued."﴾ Since it is among God's ways with His servants to save the believing, faithful men among His allies, who acknowledge the messengers and prophets He sent, and to destroy the disbelieving enemies who denied them, He commanded Moses to leave with the Children of Israel by night. He called them "His servants" because they had believed in Moses. The meaning of "for you will be pursued" is that Pharaoh and his people would follow you in order to turn you back. Implicit in this statement is the information that God would deliver them from Pharaoh. So Moses, peace be upon him, set out with the Children of Israel at dawn. He left the road to Syria on his left and headed toward the sea. A man from the Children of Israel would say to him, regarding leaving the road, "Why?" and he would reply, "I have been commanded thus." When Pharaoh rose in the morning and learned of Moses' night departure with the Children of Israel, he set out in their pursuit and sent to the cities of Egypt so that the armies would join him. It is reported that he caught up with them with a hundred thousand dark-coloured (adham) horses, besides the other colours. It is also reported that the Children of Israel numbered six hundred and seventy thousand. God knows best whether this is authentic. What is necessary from the verse, and what can be asserted with certainty, is that Moses, peace be upon him, left with a large host of the Children of Israel, and that Pharaoh pursued them with many times that number.

Ibn Abbas said: "There were with Pharaoh a thousand tyrants, each of whom wore a crown and each of whom was a commander of cavalry."

The shirdhimah (شِرْذِمَةٌ) is a small, despised group. Its plural is shara<u>dh</u>im (شَرَاذِم). Al-Jawhari said: "The shirdhimah is a group of people and a piece of something. A garment that is shara<u>dh</u>im means pieces (qita')." Al-Tha'labi recited the verse of the rajaz poet:

*The winter has come, and my garments are worn out,*
*Tattered; the naww<u>a</u>q laughs at them.*

The naww<u>a</u>q (النَّوَّاق) is a man who tames affairs and sets them right. This is what al-Jawhari said in the Sihah. [It is said that naww<u>a</u>q is the name of his son. It is also narrated as al-tawwaq (التَّوَّاق) with a ta'.]

The lam in God's words ﴿Indeed, these are a small group﴾ (لَشِرْذِمَةٌ) is the lam of emphasis (lam al-tawkid). It frequently enters the predicate of inna, except that the Kufans do not permit "inna Zayd la-sawfa yaqumu" (indeed Zayd will surely stand). The evidence that it is permissible is God's words ﴿So you will surely know﴾ (فَلَسَوْفَ تَعْلَمُونَ), where this same lam of emphasis has entered upon sawfa. This is what al-Nahhas said.

﴿And indeed they are enraging us﴾ (وَإِنَّهُمْ لَنا لَغائِظُونَ), meaning: they are enemies to us because they oppose our religion and take away our wealth, which they had borrowed, as mentioned earlier. Their virgin daughters (al-abkar) died that night. This has been fully discussed in al-A'raf and Ta-Ha. It is said: ghaza-ni kadha wa-aghaza-ni (this enraged me and made me enraged). Al-ghayz is anger, and from it come al-taghayyuz and al-ightiyaz. The meaning is that they enraged us by leaving without permission.

﴿And indeed we are a wary multitude (jami'un hadhirun)﴾ (وَإِنَّا لَجَمِيعٌ حاذِرُونَ), meaning: a gathered host taking precautions with our weapons. It is read as "hadhirun" (حَذِرُونَ), whose meaning is the same as "hadhirun" (حاذِرُونَ), i.e., fearful. Al-Jawhari said: it is read "hadhirun", "hadhirun" and "hadhirun" with a damma on the dhal (ḥadhirūna), reported by al-Akhfash. The meaning of "hadhirun" is "prepared (mutaahhibun)", and the meaning of "hadhirun" is "fearful (khaifun)." Al-Nahhas said: "hadhirun" is the reading of the people of Madina and Abu Amr. The reading of the people of Kufa is "hadhirun" (حَاذِرُونَ), and it is well known from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas. "Hadirun" with an undotted dal (حَادِرُونَ) is the reading of Abu Ubayd, and al-Mahdawi transmitted it from Ibn Abi Ammar, as did al-Mawardi and al-Tha'labi from Sumayt ibn Ajlan. Al-Nahhas said: Abu Ubayda holds that the meanings of "hadhirun" and "hadhirun" are one, and this is the view of Sibawayh, who permitted: "huwa hadhirun Zaydan," just as one says "hadhir Zaydan" (be wary of Zayd). He recited:

*Wary of matters that do no harm, and secure*
*From what cannot ward off the decrees.*

Abu Umar al-Jarmi claimed that it is permissible to say "huwa hadhirun Zaydan" by omitting min (from). However, most grammarians distinguish between hadhar and hadhir. Among them are al-Kisa'i, al-Farra', and Muhammad ibn Yazid, who hold that hadhar in its form means being alert and watchful, and so it is intransitive. Hadhir means "prepared," and this explanation was transmitted from the earlier authorities. Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, regarding God's words ﴿And indeed we are a wary multitude﴾, said: "Equipped with weapons and horses, well-prepared." This is the same meaning. His words "equipped (mu'dun)" mean that they have equipment (adah). It has also been said that the meaning is: we have weapons, and they have no weapons, which incites them to fight. As for "hadirun" with an undotted dal, it derives from the expression "a'yun hadratun," meaning full (eyes). That is, we are full of rage against them. From this is the verse of the poet, Imru' al-Qays:

*And an eye full and bright, its lids split from the corners.*

The lexicographers have said: "A man is hadirun" when he is full-fleshed. So it is possible that the meaning is "full of weapons." Al-Mahdawi said: "al-hadir" is strong and powerful.

God's words: ﴿So We expelled them from gardens and springs﴾, meaning from the land of Egypt. From Abdullah ibn Amr who said: "The gardens were on the two banks of the Nile, on both sides from Aswan to Rashid, and between the gardens were fields. The Nile has seven branches (khalij): the Alexandria branch, the Sakha branch, the Damietta branch, the Sardus branch, the Manf branch, the Fayyum branch, and the Manha branch [which is the Sea of Joseph, peace be upon him], all connected, none cut off from another, and the fields lay between all the branches. All of the land of Egypt was irrigated by sixteen cubits, through the dams, bridges and canals they had arranged and measured. For this reason, when the Nile rose to sixteen cubits it was called the Sultan's Nile. Ibn Abi al-Raddad was granted a robe of honour [He was Abdullah ibn al-Salam ibn Abdullah ibn Abi al-Raddad, the muezzin, who came to Egypt from Basra and narrated hadith there. He was appointed to measure the Nile during the governorship of Yazid ibn Abdullah al-Turki, when the Christians had been in charge of measuring it. He was given seven dinars every month, and his measuring remained in his descendants for a long time. Abu al-Raddad died in the year 266 AH. From al-Maqrizi's Khitat, vol. 1, p. 58.], and this state continues to the present. It is called the Sultan's Nile because at that point the kharaj (land tax) becomes due from the people. All of Egypt was irrigated by a finger's width from seventeen cubits. When the Nile rose to seventeen cubits and a finger was called out for it, the eighteen-cubit mark was reached and the kharaj increased by a million dinars. When it exceeded that and a finger was called out for it at nineteen cubits, the kharaj decreased by a million dinars. The reason for this was what was spent on public works, canals, bridges, and attention to their maintenance. As for now, most of it is not irrigated until a finger is called out at nineteen cubits by the Egyptian measure. As for the works of Upper Egypt, some of them are not fully irrigated until the water enters the twenty-second cubit in Upper Egypt."

I (al-Qurtubi) say: As for the land of Egypt, it is now not fully irrigated except from twenty cubits and fingers, because the land has risen and there is no attention to the maintenance of its dams. This is one of the wonders of the world: the Nile rises when the waters pour over all the land until it floods all of Egypt's land, and the regions remain like islands, not reachable except by boats and measuring instruments.

It is narrated from Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As that he said: "The Nile of Egypt is the lord of rivers. God subjected to it every river between East and West, and God made the rivers submissive to it. When God wills that the Nile of Egypt should flow, He commands every river to feed it, and the rivers supply it with their water. God causes springs to gush forth for it. When it reaches what God, the Mighty and Majestic, wills, God, blessed and exalted, reveals to every water to return to its origin."

Qays ibn al-Hajjaj said: "When Egypt was conquered, its people came to Amr ibn al-As when the month of Ba'una (one of the Coptic months) had arrived, and they said to him: 'O Amir, our Nile has a custom and it will not flow except by it.' He said to them: 'And what is that?' They said: 'When it is the twelfth night of this month, we go to a virgin girl between her parents, we satisfy her parents, we dress her in the finest jewelry and clothing, and then we throw her into this Nile.' Amr said to them: 'This cannot happen in Islam, for Islam obliterates what came before it.' So they remained in Abib and Misra, and neither little nor much of the Nile flowed, and they resolved to depart. When Amr ibn al-As saw this, he wrote to Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with them both, informing him of the matter. Umar ibn al-Khattab wrote back to him: 'You have done right in what you did, for Islam obliterates what came before it, and this should not happen.' He sent him a slip of paper inside his letter, and wrote to Amr: 'I have sent you a slip of paper inside my letter; throw it into the Nile when my letter reaches you.' When Umar's letter reached Amr ibn al-As, he took the slip and opened it, and in it was: 'From the servant of God, Umar, Commander of the Believers, to the Nile of Egypt. To proceed: if you flow by your own power, then do not flow; but if it is God, the One, the Subduer, who makes you flow, then we ask God, the One, the Subduer, to make you flow.' He said: 'So he threw the slip into the Nile the day before the Cross (al-Salib), when the people of Egypt had prepared to leave and depart from it, because their welfare there depended only on the Nile.' When he threw the slip into the Nile, they awoke on the day of the Cross and God had made it rise sixteen cubits in a single night, and God cut off that custom from the people of Egypt from that year onward."

Ka'b al-Ahbar said: "Four rivers from Paradise God placed in the world: Sayhan, Jayhan, the Nile, and the Euphrates. Sayhan is the river of water in Paradise, Jayhan is the river of milk in Paradise, the Nile is the river of honey in Paradise, and the Euphrates is the river of wine in Paradise." Ibn Lahi'a said: "The Tigris is the river of milk in Paradise."

I (al-Qurtubi) say: What is in the Sahih on this subject is the hadith of Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "Sayhan, Jayhan, the Nile and the Euphrates are each of them rivers of Paradise." This is the wording of Muslim. In the hadith of the Night Journey, from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik, from Malik ibn Sa'sa'a, a man of his people, he said: "The Prophet of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, related that he saw four rivers emerging from its root: two apparent and two hidden. I said: 'O Gabriel, what are these rivers?' He said: 'As for the two hidden ones, they are two rivers in Paradise; as for the two apparent ones, they are the Nile and the Euphrates.'" This is the wording of Muslim. Al-Bukhari said, through the chain of Shurayk from Anas: "Then he was in the lowest heaven, with two rivers flowing (yattaridan) [yattaridan: i.e., flowing, and they are of the form yaftaʿilan from al-tard]. He said: 'What are these two rivers, O Gabriel?' He said: 'These are the Nile and the Euphrates, their source.' Then he proceeded in the heaven and came upon another river, upon which was a palace of pearl and chrysolite. He struck it with his hand and it was pure musk, very fragrant. He said: 'What is this, O Gabriel?' He said: 'This is al-Kawthar, which your Lord has hidden for you.'" And he mentioned the hadith.

The majority hold that the word "springs" (ʿuyūn) refers to springs of water. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "What is meant is springs of gold." And in the Smoke (surah 44): ﴿How many gardens and springs and fields they left behind﴾. It has been said.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 26, verses 52–68 (part 2 of 2):

Indeed they used to cultivate what lay between the two mountains, from the beginning of Egypt to its end. In the verse of Surah al-Dukhan, "and treasures" (kunuz) is the plural of kanz, and this has already been discussed in Surah al-Tawbah [[See vol. 8, p. 123, first or second edition.]]. Here it means storehouses (al-khaza'in). It has also been said that it means buried treasures (al-dafa'in). Al-Dahhak said it means rivers, but this is open to question, because springs (al-'uyun) already include them.

(And a noble station). Ibn 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: the noble station means the pulpits (al-manabir). There were a thousand pulpits, one for each of a thousand tyrants, who would honour Pharaoh and his kingdom from them. It has also been said that it means the assemblies of the chiefs and rulers, related by Ibn 'Isa, and this is close to the first view. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the fine dwellings. Ibn Lahi'a said: I heard that the noble station is al-Fayyum. It has also been said that Yusuf, peace be upon him, had written on one of his assemblies: "There is no god but Allah; Ibrahim is the friend of Allah," and so Allah called it noble because of this. It has also been said that it means the places where horses were tethered, since the leaders alone kept horses tethered there as a sign of their readiness and adornment, so that its station became the most honoured dwelling because of this. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi. The most apparent view is that it means the fine dwellings in which they were honoured.

In the language, al-maqam (المقام) can mean a place and can also be a verbal noun. Al-Nahhas said: al-maqam in the language means the place, from your saying qama yaqumu. Likewise al-maqamat, whose singular is maqama, as the poet said [[It is Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma. Yantabuha means that what is fine is said in them and done in them.]]:

"Among them are noble assemblies whose faces are fair,
and gatherings in which speech and deed are exchanged."

Al-maqam is also the verbal noun from qama yaqumu. Al-muqam (with a dammah) means a place from aqama, and it is also the verbal noun from aqama yuqimu.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Thus, and We made the Children of Israel inherit them﴾. He means that all that Allah mentioned, the gardens, the springs, the treasures and the noble station, Allah made the Children of Israel inherit. Al-Hasan and others said: the Children of Israel returned to Egypt after the destruction of Pharaoh and his people. It has also been said that by inheritance here is meant what they borrowed of the ornaments of Pharaoh's family by the command of Allah, exalted is He. I say: both matters came to pass for them, and praise belongs to Allah.

(So they pursued them at sunrise). That is, Pharaoh and his people followed the Children of Israel. Al-Suddi said: when the sun rose with its rays. Qatada said: when the earth lit up with light. Al-Zajjaj said: it is said sharaqat al-shams when it rose, and ashraqat when it shone. There is disagreement about the delay of Pharaoh and his people behind Musa and the Children of Israel, on two views. The first: they were busy burying their firstborn during that night, because the plague struck them that night; so his saying "at sunrise" (mushriqin) is a circumstantial clause describing Pharaoh's people. The second: a cloud overshadowed them, and there was darkness, and they said: we are still in the night; and it did not clear from them until morning came. Abu 'Ubayda said: the meaning of "they pursued them at sunrise" is toward the direction of the east. Al-Hasan and 'Amr ibn Maymun read: "fa-attaba'uhum mushriqin" with the shaddah and an alif of connection, meaning toward the east, derived from their saying sharraqa and gharraba when one travels toward the east and the west. The meaning of the speech is: We had determined that the Children of Israel should inherit it, and so the people of Pharaoh pursued the Children of Israel at sunrise and perished, and the Children of Israel inherited their lands.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When the two groups saw each other﴾, that is, the two groups confronted one another in such a way that each party saw the other. It is a form of tafa'ul from ru'ya (seeing).

(The companions of Musa said: "We are surely overtaken"). That is, the enemy drew near to us and we have no power to face him. The reading of the majority is "lamudrakun" with light stress, from adraka. From this is His saying: ﴿until, when drowning overtook him﴾. 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, al-A'raj and al-Zuhri read "lamuddarakun" with stress on the dal [[And with the ra' kasrah, as in al-Bahr, Ruh al-Ma'ani and al-Kashshaf, on the pattern of mufta'alun, which is intransitive, meaning destruction and annihilation, from adraka al-shay' when it follows in succession until it is finished.]], from idda-raka. Al-Farra' said: hafara and ihtaqara have one meaning, and likewise "mudrakun" and "muddarakun" have one meaning. Al-Nahhas said: the skilled grammarians do not say this; rather they say: mudrakun means "overtaken," and muddarakun means "striving to overtake them," just as it is said kasabtu meaning I obtained and won, and iktasabtu meaning I strove and sought. This is the meaning of the words of Sibawayh.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said: "By no means! Indeed my Lord is with me; He will guide me."﴾ When Pharaoh overtook Musa's host with his army and drew near to them, and the Children of Israel saw the strong enemy and the sea before them, their suspicions grew, and they said to Musa, in a manner of reproach and rudeness: "We are surely overtaken." So he rejected their statement, rebuked them, and reminded them of Allah's promise to him of guidance and victory. ("By no means!") meaning: they will not overtake you. ("Indeed my Lord is with me") meaning: with victory over the enemy. ("He will guide me") meaning: He will show me the way to salvation. When the trial grew severe upon the Children of Israel, and they saw the armies, against which they had no power, Allah, exalted and mighty is He, commanded Musa to strike the sea with his staff. This was because He, mighty and majestic, willed that the sign should be connected to Musa and tied to an act he performs; otherwise striking the staff does not split the sea, nor does it in itself help with that, except through what was joined to it of the power and invention of Allah, exalted is He. The story of this sea has already passed in Surah al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, p. 389 and following, second or third edition.]]. When it split, there were twelve paths in it according to the number of the tribes of the Children of Israel, and the water stood between them like a great mountain (tawd 'azim), that is, a great mountain. Al-Tawd is a mountain, and from it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"While a man is among the living, a mountain,
the people cast him from close range, and he leaned over."

Al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur said:

"They alighted at Anqira, over them flows
the water of the Euphrates that comes from the mountains (atwad)."

Atwad is the plural of tawd, that is, mountain. Thus there became for Musa and his companions a dry path in the sea. When the companions of Musa had come out, and the last of Pharaoh's companions had entered, as has been mentioned in Surah Yunus [[See vol. 8, p. 378, first or second edition.]], it closed over them, and Pharaoh drowned. Then some of Musa's companions said: Pharaoh has not drowned, so he was cast onto the sea shore until they looked at him. Ibn al-Qasim related from Malik, who said: two merchants went out with Musa, peace be upon him, to the sea. When they came to it, they said to him: By what did Allah command you? He said: I was commanded to strike the sea with this staff of mine, and it will split. They said to him: Do what Allah has commanded you, for He will not fail you. Then they threw themselves into the sea, affirming him. The sea remained so until Pharaoh and those with him entered, and then it returned to how it had been. This meaning has already passed in Surah al-Baqarah.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We brought the others near there﴾, that is, We brought them near to the sea, meaning Pharaoh and his people. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and others. The poet said:

"Every day that passes, or night that has gone by,
in which souls draw nearer to their appointed terms."

Abu 'Ubayda said: "azlafna" means "We gathered," and from this the night of Muzdalifah is called the night of gathering (layla jam'). Abu 'Abd Allah ibn al-Harith, Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ibn 'Abbas read "wa-azlafna" with the qaf, meaning "We destroyed them," from the saying azlaqat al-naqah and azlaqat al-faras, so she is muzlik when she causes her offspring to slip (azlaqa waladaha).

(And We saved Musa and all those with him. Then We drowned the others.) That is, Pharaoh and his people.

(Indeed in that is a sign.) That is, a token of the power of Allah, exalted is He.

(And most of them were not believers.) Because none of Pharaoh's people believed except the believer from the family of Pharaoh, whose name was Hizqil, and the daughter of Pharaoh, Asiya, wife of Pharaoh, and Maryam daughter of Dhi Musa, the old woman who guided them to the grave of Yusuf the Truthful, peace be upon him. This is because when Musa, peace be upon him, went out with the Children of Israel from Egypt, the moon grew dark over them, and he said to his people: What is this? Their scholars said: when Yusuf, peace be upon him, was approaching death, he took a covenant from us in the name of Allah that we would not leave Egypt until we had carried his bones with us. Musa said: Which of you knows his grave? They said: No one knows it except an old woman of the Children of Israel. So he sent for her and said: Show me the grave of Yusuf. She said: By Allah, I will not do so until you give me my right. He said: And what is your right? She said: My right is that I be with you in Paradise. This was grievous to him, so it was said to him: Give her what she asks. So she showed them where it was, and they dug it up and took out his bones. When they lifted them, the way was like the light of day. In another narration: Allah revealed to him that he should give it to her, and he did so. She brought them to a pool, and said to them: Drain this water. They drained it and took out the bones of Yusuf, peace be upon him, and the way became clear to them like the light of day. This has already passed in Surah Yusuf [[See vol. 9, p. 270, second edition.]].

Abu Burda related from Abu Musa that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ stayed with a Bedouin and honoured him. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "What is your need?" He said: a she-camel that I may ride, and female goats whose milk I may milk. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Why did you fail to be like the old woman of the Children of Israel?" His companions said: What was the old woman of the Children of Israel? So he related to them the story of that old woman who made Musa judge that she should be with him in Paradise.

﴿وَاتْلُ عَلَيْهِمْ نَبَأَ إِبْرَاهِيمَ﴾ (And recite to them the story of Abraham). He admonishes the polytheists for their extreme ignorance, since they turned away from the belief and religion of Abraham, although he is their father. Naba' means news (khabar). That is, O Muhammad, relate to them his news, his account, and his criticism of his people for what they worship. He said this to impose the proof upon them.

Most of the reciters read the second hamzah with easing (takhfif, softening). This is the best reading, because they have agreed on easing the second of two hamzahs in one word, as in Adam. If you wish, you may pronounce both fully (tahqiq), saying "naba'a Ibrahim". If you wish, you may ease both, saying "naba Ibrahim". If you wish, you may ease only the first. There is also a fifth reading, but it is weak in Arabic: that the hamzah be assimilated into the hamzah (idgham, assimilation, merging one letter into another), as it is said "ra'as" for the one who sells heads (ru'us). It is weak because you would be joining two hamzahs as if they were in one word. It is acceptable in fa''al (the pattern) because such a form only occurs with assimilation.

﴿إِذْ قَالَ لِأَبِيهِ وَقَوْمِهِ مَا تَعْبُدُونَ﴾ (When he said to his father and his people, "What is it that you worship?"). That is, what thing do you worship?

﴿قَالُوا نَعْبُدُ أَصْنَامًا﴾ (They said, "We worship idols"). Their idols were of gold, silver, copper, iron and wood.

﴿فَنَظَلُّ لَهَا عَاكِفِينَ﴾ (So we remain devoted to them). That is, we persist in worshipping them. The intended meaning is not a specific time; rather, it is a report about their continuous state. It was also said: they worshipped them by day but not by night, and at night they worshipped the stars. It is said "zalla yaf'alu kadha" when one does it by day, and "bata yaf'alu kadha" when one does it by night.

﴿قَالَ هَلْ يَسْمَعُونَكُمْ﴾ (He said, "Do they hear you?"). Al-Akhfash said: there is an ellipsis here, and the meaning is: "Do they hear from you?" or "Do they hear your supplication?" The poet says [the verse is by Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma, from a qasida in praise of Harim ibn Sinan. Ahkamat: she made bridles (hukamat) of rawhide for it. The hukamat are the plural of hukma, which is what lies on the nose of the animal. Dawabiruha: the hind parts of its hooves. Mankub: the stones struck its hind hooves and made them bleed]:

"The rider of horses, whose hind hooves are wounded, / Whose bridles of rawhide and abaq (cloth) have been well fastened."

He said: al-abaq is linen, and it is elided. The meaning is "and bridles of abaq were fastened." In al-Sihah (of al-Jawhari): al-abaq, with a vowel on the first letter, is qinnab (hemp). It is reported from Qatadah that he read "hal yasma'unakum" with a damma on the ya', meaning "hal yusmi'unakum asw'atahum" (do they make you hear their voices) ﴿إِذْ تَدْعُونَ﴾ (when you call upon them) ﴿أَوْ يَنْفَعُونَكُمْ أَوْ يَضُرُّونَ﴾ (or do they benefit you or harm you?). That is, can these idols benefit you and provide for you, or can they bring you good or harm if you disobey them? This is a question to establish the proof. If they neither benefit you nor harm you, then what is the point of your worshipping them?

﴿قَالُوا بَلْ وَجَدْنَا آبَاءَنَا كَذَلِكَ يَفْعَلُونَ﴾ (They said, "Rather, we found our fathers doing so"). Thus they resorted to blind imitation (taqlid) without any proof or evidence. The discussion of this has already passed.

﴿قَالَ أَفَرَأَيْتُمْ مَا كُنْتُمْ تَعْبُدُونَ﴾ (He said, "Have you considered what you have been worshipping") of these idols ﴿أَنْتُمْ وَآبَاؤُكُمُ الْأَقْدَمُونَ﴾ (you and your forefathers, the earliest ones?) ﴿فَإِنَّهُمْ عَدُوٌّ لِي﴾ (Indeed they are an enemy to me). "Aduww" is singular but stands for a group, and similarly one says of a woman, "hiya 'aduwwu Allah" and "'aduwwatu Allah," both reported by al-Farra'. 'Ali ibn Sulayman said: whoever says "'aduwwat Allah" with the feminine ending means it is in the sense of "mu'adiyah" (one who opposes), while whoever says "'aduww" for the feminine and plural treats it as a nisba (relative form). The inanimate objects are described with enmity in the sense that they will be enemies to me if I worship them on the Day of Resurrection, as He says: ﴿كَلَّا سَيَكْفُرُونَ بِعِبَادَتِهِمْ وَيَكُونُونَ عَلَيْهِمْ ضِدًّا﴾ (No! They will deny their worship of them and will be opponents to them). Al-Farra' said: it is of the inverted type (maqlub), its figurative sense being: "Indeed I am an enemy to them, because whoever you oppose opposes you."

Then He said: ﴿إِلَّا رَبَّ الْعَالَمِينَ﴾ (except the Lord of the worlds). Al-Kalbi said: that is, except the one who worships the Lord of the worlds, the worshipper of the Lord of the worlds, so the modified noun has been elided. Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj said: the grammarians said that this is an exception that is not from the first part (istithna' munqati', disconnected exception). Abu Ishaq allowed that it could be from the first part, on the basis that they used to worship God, Mighty and Majestic, and worship idols alongside Him; so He informed them that he disassociates himself from what they worship except God. Al-Farra' interpreted it as referring to the idols alone, and the meaning in his view is: "Indeed, if they were worshipped, they would be an enemy to me on the Day of Resurrection," as we have mentioned. Al-Jurjani said: its estimated structure is: "Have you considered what you and your forefathers, the earliest ones, have been worshipping, except the Lord of the worlds? Indeed they are an enemy to me." Here "illa" is in the sense of "dun" (other than) and "siwa" (besides), as in His saying: ﴿لَا يَذُوقُونَ فِيهَا الْمَوْتَ إِلَّا الْمَوْتَةَ الْأُولَى﴾ (they will not taste death therein except the first death), meaning other than the first death.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 26, verses 78–82:**

His saying, Exalted is He: (Who created me, and it is He who guides me) means: He guides me to the religion (al-din).

(And who feeds me and gives me drink) means: He provides for me (yarzuqni). The inclusion of "huwa" (He) in "wa-huwa" serves as an emphasis that no one else feeds or gives drink, just as you say, "Zayd is the one who did such-and-such," meaning no one else did it.

(And when I am ill, it is He who cures me) He said "I am ill" out of regard for courtesy (adab), since illness and cure both come from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, entirely. A parallel to this is the statement of Moses' servant: "And none made me forget it except Satan."

(And who causes me to die, then give me life) He means the resurrection (al-ba'th). They used to attribute death to causes, so He clarified that Allah is the one who causes death and gives life.

All of these verse endings (ru'us al-ay, the closing words of the verses) are without the letter ya': "yahdini," "yashfini," since omitting it at the ends of verses is good, so that they all match in rhyme. However, Ibn Abi Ishaq, despite his eminence and standing in Arabic grammar, read all of these with the ya': because the ya' is the original form and the nun was added for a reason. 

If it is said: this describes the act of creation in general, so how did Abraham make it an argument for his own guidance, when no one else was guided by it? It is said: he mentioned it as proof of the obligation of obedience, because whoever bestows favour is owed obedience and should not be disobeyed, so that others would be bound to the obedience to which he had bound himself. This is a sound argument.

I say: Some of the people of allusive interpretation (ahl al-isharat) took liberties in subtle meanings, departing from the apparent sense we have mentioned toward what primary reason rejects, namely that Abraham is not the intended referent. They said: "And who feeds me and gives me drink" means He feeds me the pleasure of faith and gives me the sweetness of acceptance. As for His saying "And when I am ill, it is He who cures me," they have two interpretations: first, when I become ill through disobedience to Him, He cures me by His mercy; second, when I become ill by contending with creation, He cures me by witnessing the Truth. Ja'far ibn Muhammad al-Sadiq said: when I am ill with sins, He cures me by repentance.

They interpreted His saying "And who causes me to die, then give me life" in three ways: He causes me to die through sins and gives me life through acts of obedience. Second: He causes me to die through fear and gives me life through hope. Third: He causes me to die through greed and gives me life through contentment. A fourth opinion: He causes me to die through justice and gives me life through grace. A fifth: He causes me to die through separation and gives me life through reunion. A sixth: He causes me to die through ignorance and gives me life through reason. And there are others, none of which is intended by the verse. These subtle interpretations and hidden meanings belong only to one who is skilled and knows the Truth. As for one who is blind to the Truth and does not know it, how can hidden meanings be hinted at for him, while the apparent meanings are set aside? This is impossible. And Allah knows best.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the One from whom I hope He will forgive me my error on the Day of Judgment﴾. ("Atma'u," I hope, meaning "arju.") It is said: it carries the meaning of certainty with regard to Abraham, and the meaning of hope with regard to the believers other than him. Al-Hasan and Ibn Abi Ishaq read "khata'aya" (plural) and said: it is not a single error. Al-Nahhas said: "khati'ah" in the sense of "khata'aya" is well known in the speech of the Arabs. They have agreed on the singular in His saying, Mighty and Majestic, "So they acknowledged their sin" (fa'taraf'u bi-dhanbihim), meaning "their sins." Likewise, "wa-aqimu al-salah" means "al-salawat" (the prayers). Likewise, "khati'ati," if it refers to "khata'aya." And Allah knows best.

Mujahid said: by "his error" he means His saying: "Rather, this one, the largest of them, did it" (Q. 21:63), and his saying "Indeed, I am sick" (Q. 37:89), and his saying that Sarah was his sister. Al-Hasan added his saying to the star: "This is my Lord" (Q. 6:76). The explanation of this has already passed in full detail. Al-Zajjaj said: the prophets are human beings, so error may occur from them. Yes, major sins (al-kaba'ir) are not permitted for them, because they are protected (ma'sumun) from them.

(On the Day of Judgment) the Day of Recompense, when servants are repaid for their deeds. This statement from Abraham was a manifestation of servanthood, even though he knew he had been forgiven.

In Sahih Muslim, from A'ishah: I said, "O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Ibn Ju'dan used to uphold the ties of kinship and feed the poor in the Jahiliyyah; would that benefit him?" He said: "It will not benefit him, for he never said on a single day: 'My Lord, forgive me my error on the Day of Judgment.'"

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 26, verses 83–89:**

His Exalted words: ﴿My Lord, grant me wisdom and join me with the righteous.﴾ "Hukman" (wisdom): knowledge of You, of Your limits and of Your rulings. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Muqatil said: understanding and knowledge, and this returns to the first meaning. Al-Kalbi said: prophethood, a messenger to the creation. "And join me with the righteous" means: with the prophets before me in rank. Ibn 'Abbas said: with the people of Paradise, and this is a confirmation of his words, "Grant me wisdom."

His Exalted words: ﴿And appoint for me a tongue of truthfulness among the later generations.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: it is that the nations gather upon him (i.e., agree on his excellence). Mujahid said: it is good praise. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is praise and enduring high standing, by the consensus of the exegetes (mufassirun), and thus Allah answered his supplication: every community holds fast to him and magnifies him, and they follow the primordial monotheistic faith (hanifiyyah) which Muhammad ﷺ brought. Makki said: it was also said that its meaning is his request that among his offspring at the end of time there would be one who upholds the truth, and so the supplication was answered in Muhammad ﷺ. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this meaning is good, except that the wording of the verse does not yield it except by forcing the word. Al-Qushayri said: he meant a good invocation until the Hour, for the increase of reward is sought for everyone. I say: Allah has indeed done this, for no one sends blessings upon the Prophet ﷺ except that he also sends blessings upon Ibrahim, especially in the prayers and on the pulpits, which are the best of states and the highest of ranks. And "salah" (blessing) is supplication for mercy. By "tongue" is meant speech, and its original sense is the organ of speech. Al-Qutabi said: the place of "tongue" here is the place of "speech" by metaphor, and the Arabs have used it as a figure of speech for the word. Al-A'sha said:

"Indeed there came to me a tongue (report) by which I am not pleased,
from on high; there is no wonder in it nor mockery."

Al-Jawhari said: it is narrated as "min 'ulw," with the vowel on the waw pronounced with damma, fatha or kasra, meaning: a report came to me from above, and the feminine is for the word. He had received news of the killing of his brother al-Muntashir. Ashhab narrated from Malik, who said: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: "And appoint for me a tongue of truthfulness among the later generations." There is no harm in a man loving to be praised for righteousness and to be seen in the deeds of the righteous, provided he intends by it the Face of Allah, Exalted. Allah, Exalted, has said: "And I cast upon you love from Me," and He said: "Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, the Most Merciful will appoint for them affection," meaning love in the hearts of His servants and good praise. Thus by His words, "And appoint for me a tongue of truthfulness among the later generations," He drew attention to the recommendation of acquiring that which brings a good remembrance. Al-Layth ibn Sulaym said: for it is the second life. It has been said:

"Some people have died while among the people they are living."

Ibn al-'Arabi said: the verifying scholars among the shaykhs of asceticism (zuhd) said that this is evidence of encouragement to righteous deeds which earn a good name. The Prophet ﷺ said: "When the son of Adam dies, his deeds are cut off except for three" [the hadith], and in another narration it is likewise regarding planting and sowing, and likewise for one who dies while stationed on the frontier (murabit), his deed is recorded for him until the Day of Resurrection. We have explained this at the end of "Al 'Imran" [[See vol. 4, p. 323, first or second edition.]], and praise be to Allah.

His Exalted words: ﴿And make me among the inheritors of the Garden of Bliss.﴾ This is a supplication for Paradise and for those who inherit it, and it refutes the saying of some: "I do not ask for Paradise or Fire."

His Exalted words: (And forgive my father, for he was among the astray.) His father had promised him, outwardly, that he would believe, so he sought forgiveness for him on this account; then when it became clear that he would not fulfil what he had said, he disavowed him. This meaning has already been mentioned. "Indeed he was among the astray" means: among the polytheists. And "kana" (was) is redundant (zaидah).

(And do not disgrace me on the Day they are resurrected) meaning: do not expose me before the witnesses, or do not punish me on the Day of Resurrection. In al-Bukhari, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet ﷺ, he said: "Indeed Ibrahim will see his father on the Day of Resurrection, and upon him will be dust and gloom," and "al-ghabarah" is the same as "al-qatarah." And from him (Abu Hurayrah), from the Prophet ﷺ, he said: "Ibrahim will meet his father and say: O Lord, You promised me that You would not disgrace me on the Day they are resurrected. Then Allah, Exalted, will say: Indeed I have forbidden Paradise to the disbelievers." Al-Bukhari alone narrated both, may Allah have mercy on him.

His Exalted words: ﴿The Day when neither wealth nor children will benefit,﴾ "Yawma" (the Day) is a substitute for the first "yawma," meaning: the Day when wealth and children will benefit no one. By His words "wa la banun" (nor children) is meant helpers, for if the son does not benefit, who else will benefit? It was also said: He mentioned the sons because the father of Ibrahim had been mentioned, meaning: Ibrahim did not benefit him. "Except one who comes to Allah with a sound heart" is an exception from the disbelievers, meaning: his wealth and his sons will not benefit him. It was also said: it is an exception from a different category, meaning: but "one who comes to Allah with a sound heart" will benefit, because of the soundness of his heart. The heart was singled out for mention because when it is sound the limbs are sound, and when it is corrupt all the limbs are corrupt. This was mentioned earlier at the beginning of "al-Baqarah" [[See vol. 1, p. 187 and following, first or second edition.]]. There is disagreement about the sound heart. It was said: it is free from doubt and polytheism; as for sins, no one is free from them. This was said by Qatadah, Ibn Zayd and most of the exegetes. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: the sound, healthy heart is the heart of the believer, for the heart of the disbeliever and the hypocrite is diseased, Allah, Exalted, said: "In their hearts is a disease." Abu 'Uthman al-Sayyari said: it is the heart empty of innovation (bid'ah) and at rest with the Sunnah. Al-Hasan said: sound from the affliction of wealth and children. Al-Junayd said: "al-salim" in the language means the one stung (by a scorpion), so its meaning is a heart like one stung from fear of Allah. Al-Dahhak said: "al-salim" means the pure, sincere.

I say: this statement gathers the scattered sayings by its generality, and it is good: that is, pure from blameworthy qualities, and characterized by praiseworthy qualities. And Allah knows best. It has been narrated from 'Urwah that he said: "O my sons, do not be ones who curse much, for Ibrahim never cursed anything at all." Allah, Exalted, said: "When he came to his Lord with a sound heart." Muhammad ibn Sirin said: the sound heart is that one knows that Allah is true, that the Hour is coming, and that Allah will resurrect those in the graves. In Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet ﷺ, he said: "There will enter Paradise peoples whose hearts are like the hearts of birds." He means, and Allah knows best, that their hearts are like them in being free from sin and sound from every defect, having no experience of worldly affairs. As Anas ibn Malik narrated, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Most of the people of Paradise are the simple (al-bulh)," and this is a sound hadith, meaning: the simple regarding the disobedience of Allah. Al-Azhari said: "al-ableh" here is one who is disposed to good and heedless of evil, not knowing it. Al-Qutabi said: "al-bulh" are those in whom the soundness of their breasts and good opinion of people have prevailed.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is praise and enduring high standing, by the consensus of the exegetes (mufassirun), and thus Allah answered his supplication: every community holds fast to him and magnifies him, and they follow the primordial monotheistic faith (hanifiyyah) which Muhammad ﷺ brought. Makki said: it was also said that its meaning is his request that among his offspring at the end of time there would be one who upholds the truth, and so the supplication was answered in Muhammad ﷺ. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this meaning is good, except that the wording of the verse does not yield it except by forcing the word. Al-Qushayri said: he meant a good invocation until the Hour, for the increase of reward is sought for everyone. I say: Allah has indeed done this, for no one sends blessings upon the Prophet ﷺ except that he also sends blessings upon Ibrahim, especially in the prayers and on the pulpits, which are the best of states and the highest of ranks. And "salah" (blessing) is supplication for mercy. By "tongue" is meant speech, and its original sense is the organ of speech. Al-Qutabi said: the place of "tongue" here is the place of "speech" by metaphor, and the Arabs have used it as a figure of speech for the word. Al-A'sha said:

"Indeed there came to me a tongue (report) by which I am not pleased,
from on high; there is no wonder in it nor mockery."

Al-Jawhari said: it is narrated as "min 'ulw," with the vowel on the waw pronounced with damma, fatha or kasra, meaning: a report came to me from above, and the feminine is for the word. He had received news of the killing of his brother al-Muntashir. Ashhab narrated from Malik, who said: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: "And appoint for me a tongue of truthfulness among the later generations." There is no harm in a man loving to be praised for righteousness and to be seen in the deeds of the righteous, provided he intends by it the Face of Allah, Exalted. Allah, Exalted, has said: "And I cast upon you love from Me," and He said: "Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, the Most Merciful will appoint for them affection," meaning love in the hearts of His servants and good praise. Al-Layth ibn Sulaym said: for it is the second life. It has been said:

"Some people have died while among the people they are living."

Ibn al-'Arabi said: the verifying scholars among the shaykhs of asceticism (zuhd) said that this is evidence of encouragement to righteous deeds which earn a good name. The Prophet ﷺ said: "When the son of Adam dies, his deeds are cut off except for three" [the hadith], and in another narration it is likewise regarding planting and sowing, and likewise for one who dies while stationed on the frontier (murabit), his deed is recorded for him until the Day of Resurrection. We have explained this at the end of "Al 'Imran" [[See vol. 4, p. 323, first or second edition.]], and praise be to Allah.

His Exalted words: ﴿And make me among the inheritors of the Garden of Bliss.﴾ This is a supplication for Paradise and for those who inherit it, and it refutes the saying of some: "I do not ask for Paradise or Fire."

His Exalted words: (And forgive my father, for he was among the astray.) His father had promised him, outwardly, that he would believe, so he sought forgiveness for him on this account; then when it became clear that he would not fulfil what he had said, he disavowed him. This meaning has already been mentioned. "Indeed he was among the astray" means: among the polytheists. And "kana" (was) is redundant (zaидah).

(And do not disgrace me on the Day they are resurrected) meaning: do not expose me before the witnesses, or do not punish me on the Day of Resurrection. In al-Bukhari, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet ﷺ, he said: "Indeed Ibrahim will see his father on the Day of Resurrection, and upon him will be dust and gloom," and "al-ghabarah" is the same as "al-qatarah." And from him (Abu Hurayrah), from the Prophet ﷺ, he said: "Ibrahim will meet his father and say: O Lord, You promised me that You would not disgrace me on the Day they are resurrected. His Exalted words: ﴿The Day when neither wealth nor children will benefit,﴾ "Yawma" (the Day) is a substitute for the first "yawma," meaning: the Day when wealth and children will benefit no one. By His words "wa la banun" (nor children) is meant helpers, for if the son does not benefit, who else will benefit? It was also said: He mentioned the sons because the father of Ibrahim had been mentioned, meaning: Ibrahim did not benefit him. It was also said: it is an exception from a different category, meaning: but "one who comes to Allah with a sound heart" will benefit, because of the soundness of his heart. Al-Qutabi said: "al-bulh" are those in whom the soundness of their breasts and good opinion of people have prevailed.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 26, verses 90–104:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Paradise will be brought near for the God-fearing﴾, meaning it will be brought close and made near so that they may enter it. Al-Zajjaj said: their entry into it has come near.

(And Hell will be made manifest) meaning it will be displayed (al-Jahim), that is, Jahannam.

(For the misguided) meaning the disbelievers who strayed from guidance. That is, Hell will appear to its people before they enter it, so that they feel dread and sorrow, just as the people of Paradise feel joy because they know they will enter Paradise.

(And it will be said to them: "Where are those you used to worship besides Allah?" [i.e., the idols and rivals]) (Can they help you [against the punishment of Allah], or can they help themselves?) This is all reproach.

(So they will be hurled into it, they and the misguided) "Kubkibu" means they will be turned upside down on their heads. It was also said: they will be thrown down, with some of them falling upon others. It was also said: they will be gathered together. It is derived from *al-kabkaba*, which means a group, as al-Harawi reported. Al-Nahhas said it is derived from *kawkab al-shay'*, meaning its main part or mass. A group of horses is called *kawkab* and *kabkaba*. Ibn 'Abbas said: they will be gathered and then cast into the Fire. Mujahid said: they will be pushed down headlong. Muqatil said: they will be flung. The meaning is one. You say, "I *dahwartu* the thing" when you gather it and then throw it into a pit. It is said, "He *yudahwiru* the morsels" when he rolls them up into a ball. It is also said in supplication, "May Allah overturn (*kabba*) the enemy of the Muslims," and one does not say *akabbahu*; rather, *kabbakahu* means he overturned him and turned him over. From this is the verse ﴿So they will be hurled into it﴾. The original form is *kubbibu*, and the middle *ba'* was replaced by a *kaf* because of the disliked accumulation of the letter *ba'*. Al-Suddi said: the pronoun in "fa-kubkibu" refers to the polytheists of the Arabs. (And the misguided) refers to the gods.

(And the hosts of Iblis) those from his offspring. It was also said: everyone who called him to the worship of idols and followed him. Qatadah, al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: "the misguided" are the devils. It was also said: the idols will be cast into the Fire, and they are made of iron and copper, so that others may be punished by them.

(They will say, while they dispute therein) meaning the humans, the devils, the misguided, and the worshipped ones will dispute at that time.

(By Allah) they swear by Allah: (we were indeed in clear error) meaning in loss, perdition, and confusion, far from the truth, when we took rivals with Allah and worshipped them as one worships Allah. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿when we equated you with the Lord of the worlds﴾, that is, in worship; and you cannot now help us or help yourselves.

(And none led us astray except the criminals) meaning the devils who adorned for us the worship of idols. It was also said: our forefathers whom we imitated. Abu al-'Aliyah and 'Ikrimah said: "the criminals" are Iblis and the son of Adam who killed (his brother), for they were the first to establish disbelief, murder, and all kinds of sin.

(So we have no intercessors) meaning intercessors who would intercede for us from among the angels, the prophets, and the believers.

(Nor a sincere friend) meaning a compassionate friend. 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) used to say: "Keep to your brothers, for they are the provision of this world and the provision of the Hereafter. Do you not hear the words of the people of the Fire: ﴿So we have no intercessors, nor a sincere friend﴾?" Al-Zamakhshari said: the word "intercessor" is in the plural because intercessors are many, while "friend" is in the singular because true friends are few. Do you not see that when a man is afflicted with the oppression of a tyrant, a large group of the people of his town go out to intercede for him, out of mercy and for the sake of Allah, even if most of them do not know him beforehand? As for the *sadiq* (true friend), he is the one who is truthful in his affection for you, who cares about what concerns you; he is rarer than white crows (*bid al-uquq*). It is reported from one of the wise men that he was asked about the true friend and said: "A name with no meaning." It is also permissible that by *sadiq* one means the plural. The *hamim* is the close and intimate one, and from this comes *hammat al-rajul*, meaning his relatives. The origin of this is from *al-hamim*, which is hot water, and from it come *al-hammam* (bath) and *al-humma* (fever). So a man's *hamma* are those whom what burns him burns, as it is said: "They are his *huzzan*," meaning what grieves him grieves them. It is also said: "*Hamma al-shay'*" and "*ahamma*" when it draws near. From this comes *al-humma*, because it brings one close to the end of life. 'Ali ibn 'Isa said: the close one is called *hamim* only because he becomes hot (*yuhma*) out of anger for his companion, so he took it as derived from *al-hamiyya* (zeal). Qatadah said: on the Day of Resurrection, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will remove the affection of the true friend and the tenderness of the intimate. It is permissible to read ﴿nor a sincere friend﴾ with *raf'* (nominative), in agreement with the place of "min shafi'in," since "min shafi'in" is in a nominative position. The plural of *sadiq* is *asdiqa'*, *suduqa'* and *sidaq*. One does not say *suduq*, to distinguish the adjective from other forms. The Kufans reported that its plural is also said to be *sudqan*. Al-Nahhas said: this is far-fetched, because this is the plural of a non-adjectival noun, like *raghif* and *rughfan*. They also have *sadiq* and *aSadiq*. The pattern *afa'il* is only the plural of *af'al* when it is not an adjective, like *ashja'* and *ashaji'*. It is said: *sadiq* is used for the singular, the plural, and the feminine. The poet said [it is Jarir]:

"They planted love in us, then shot our hearts
With the eyes of enemies, and they are (still) friends."

It is said: "So-and-so is my *sadiqi*," meaning my closest friend; and it is diminutive only as an expression of praise, like the saying of Hubab ibn al-Mundhir:

"I am its *juthayl* (stump) that is rubbed,
And its *udhayq* (little palm) that is propped up."

Al-Jawhari mentioned this. [Note: *juthayl* refers to the trunk of a tree, or a stick set upright against which camels rub themselves to be cured; i.e., experience has tested me, and I have knowledge and opinion by which people are healed, as camels with mange are healed by this stick. The *tarjib* here means propping up a palm tree from one side to keep it from falling; i.e., I have a clan that supports me and protects me. *Udhayq* is the diminutive of *idhq* (with a fatha), which is the palm with its fruit.] Al-Nahhas said: the plural of *hamim* is *ahimma'* and *ahimma*, and they disliked the pattern *af'ila'* because of the doubling of letters.

(So if only we had a return) "Anna" is in a nominative position. The meaning is: if we had a return to the world, we would believe, so that we would have intercessors. They wished for this when wishing would no longer benefit them.

They only said this when the angels and the believers were interceding. Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "A man will say in Paradise, 'What became of so-and-so, and his friend who is in Hell?' Then he will continue to intercede for him until Allah grants him intercession concerning him. When he is saved, the polytheists will say: ﴿So we have no intercessors, nor a sincere friend﴾." Al-Hasan said: no assembly gathers in remembrance of Allah in which there is a servant of the people of Paradise without Allah granting them intercession through him. Indeed the people of faith intercede for one another, and they are intercessors before Allah and are interceded for. Ka'b said: two men were friends in the world. One of them passes by his companion while he is being dragged to the Fire, and his brother says to him: "By Allah, I have only one good deed left with which I may be saved. Take it, my brother, so that you may be saved by it from what I see. As for me and you, we will remain among the people of the Heights (al-A'raf)." He said: Allah then commands both of them, and they both enter Paradise.

(Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers. And indeed your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful) This has been mentioned before, and praise be to Allah.
