Do you not see that when a man is afflicted with the oppression of a tyrant, a large group of the people of his town go out to intercede for him, out of mercy and for the sake of Allah, even if most of them do not know him beforehand? As for the *sadiq* (true friend), he is the one who is truthful in his affection for you, who cares about what concerns you; he is rarer than white crows (*bid al-uquq*). It is reported from one of the wise men that he was asked about the true friend and said: "A name with no meaning." It is also permissible that by *sadiq* one means the plural. The *hamim* is the close and intimate one, and from this comes *hammat al-rajul*, meaning his relatives. The origin of this is from *al-hamim*, which is hot water, and from it come *al-hammam* (bath) and *al-humma* (fever). So a man's *hamma* are those whom what burns him burns, as it is said: "They are his *huzzan*," meaning what grieves him grieves them. It is also said: "*Hamma al-shay'*" and "*ahamma*" when it draws near. From this comes *al-humma*, because it brings one close to the end of life. 'Ali ibn 'Isa said: the close one is called *hamim* only because he becomes hot (*yuhma*) out of anger for his companion, so he took it as derived from *al-hamiyya* (zeal). Qatadah said: on the Day of Resurrection, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will remove the affection of the true friend and the tenderness of the intimate. It is permissible to read ﴿nor a sincere friend﴾ with *raf'* (nominative), in agreement with the place of "min shafi'in," since "min shafi'in" is in a nominative position. The plural of *sadiq* is *asdiqa'*, *suduqa'* and *sidaq*. One does not say *suduq*, to distinguish the adjective from other forms. The Kufans reported that its plural is also said to be *sudqan*. Al-Nahhas said: this is far-fetched, because this is the plural of a non-adjectival noun, like *raghif* and *rughfan*. They also have *sadiq* and *aSadiq*. The pattern *afa'il* is only the plural of *af'al* when it is not an adjective, like *ashja'* and *ashaji'*. It is said: *sadiq* is used for the singular, the plural, and the feminine. The poet said [it is Jarir]:

"They planted love in us, then shot our hearts
With the eyes of enemies, and they are (still) friends."

It is said: "So-and-so is my *sadiqi*," meaning my closest friend; and it is diminutive only as an expression of praise, like the saying of Hubab ibn al-Mundhir:

"I am its *juthayl* (stump) that is rubbed,
And its *udhayq* (little palm) that is propped up."

Al-Jawhari mentioned this. [Note: *juthayl* refers to the trunk of a tree, or a stick set upright against which camels rub themselves to be cured; i.e., experience has tested me, and I have knowledge and opinion by which people are healed, as camels with mange are healed by this stick. The *tarjib* here means propping up a palm tree from one side to keep it from falling; i.e., I have a clan that supports me and protects me. *Udhayq* is the diminutive of *idhq* (with a fatha), which is the palm with its fruit.] Al-Nahhas said: the plural of *hamim* is *ahimma'* and *ahimma*, and they disliked the pattern *af'ila'* because of the doubling of letters.

(So if only we had a return) "Anna" is in a nominative position. The meaning is: if we had a return to the world, we would believe, so that we would have intercessors. They wished for this when wishing would no longer benefit them.

They only said this when the angels and the believers were interceding. Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "A man will say in Paradise, 'What became of so-and-so, and his friend who is in Hell?' Then he will continue to intercede for him until Allah grants him intercession concerning him. When he is saved, the polytheists will say: ﴿So we have no intercessors, nor a sincere friend﴾." Al-Hasan said: no assembly gathers in remembrance of Allah in which there is a servant of the people of Paradise without Allah granting them intercession through him. Indeed the people of faith intercede for one another, and they are intercessors before Allah and are interceded for. Ka'b said: two men were friends in the world. One of them passes by his companion while he is being dragged to the Fire, and his brother says to him: "By Allah, I have only one good deed left with which I may be saved. Take it, my brother, so that you may be saved by it from what I see. As for me and you, we will remain among the people of the Heights (al-A'raf)." He said: Allah then commands both of them, and they both enter Paradise.

(Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers. And indeed your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful) This has been mentioned before, and praise be to Allah.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 26, verses 105–122:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The people of Noah denied the messengers.﴾ He said "denied" (kadhdhabat), though "the people" (al-qawm) is masculine, because the meaning is "the group of the people of Noah denied." He said "the messengers" (al-mursalin) because whoever denies one messenger has denied all the messengers, since every messenger commands belief in all the messengers. It was also said that they denied Noah in his prophethood and in what he told them about the coming of messengers after him. It was also said that the plural refers to the category, while the intended person is Noah, peace be upon him. This has already been discussed in "al-Furqan" [[See p. 13 of this part.]].

(When their brother Noah said to them) ﴿Their brother Noah said to them﴾, meaning, the son of their father, and this is a brotherhood of lineage, not a brotherhood of religion. It was also said that it is a brotherhood of kinship in kind. God Exalted says: ﴿And We did not send any messenger except in the language of his people﴾, and this has been discussed in "al-A'raf" [[See vol. 7, p. 235, first or second edition.]]. It was also said that it is from the Arab saying "O brother of Banu Tamim," meaning "O one of them." Al-Zamakhshari said: From this is the verse of the Hamasa (an anthology of early Arabic poetry):

They do not ask their brother when he calls them
in calamities, about what he has said as proof.

(Do you not fear God?) ﴿Will you not be wary (of God)?﴾, meaning, will you not fear God regarding the worship of idols?

(Indeed I am to you a trustworthy messenger) ﴿I am to you a faithful messenger﴾, meaning truthful in what I convey to you from God Exalted. It was also said: "trustworthy" among you, for they had known his trustworthiness and truthfulness beforehand, as Muhammad ﷺ was known among Quraysh.

(So fear God) ﴿So be wary of God﴾, meaning, take shelter in obedience to God Exalted from His punishment.

(And obey me) in what I command you of faith.

(And I do not ask you for any reward for it) meaning, I have no desire for your wealth.

(My reward is only from the Lord of the worlds) meaning, my recompense is only from the Lord of the worlds.

(So fear God and obey me) is repeated for emphasis.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They said, "Shall we believe you, when the most despised follow you?"﴾ In this there are two issues. The first: His saying, ﴿Shall we believe you?﴾, meaning, shall we accept your words as true? "When the most despised follow you": the waw here is for the circumstantial clause (hal), and it implies the particle qad (already), meaning "while the most despised have already followed you." "Al-arhalun" (the most despised) is the plural of "al-arhal"; the broken plural is "al-arazil," the feminine is "al-ruhla," and the plural is "al-rudhl." Al-Nahhas said: No one among the grammarians whom we know permits dropping the definite article (alif and lam) from any of this. Ibn Mas'ud, al-Dahhak, Ya'qub al-Hadrami and others read: "wa-atba'uka al-arhalun" (and your followers are the most despised). Al-Nahhas said: This is a good reading, and this waw is mostly followed by nouns and verbs with qad. "Atba'" is the plural of "tabi'" and "tabi'," and it can be used for the singular and the plural. The poet said:

He has a follower, whom people know,
over whoever approaches him, a summer and a spring.

The nominative of "atba'uka" may be a subject (mubtada'), and "al-arhalun" the predicate, the sense being: "Shall we believe you, when your followers are only the most despised?" It may also be coordinated with the pronoun in "Shall we believe you," the sense being: "Shall we, and your followers the most despised, believe you, so that we would be counted among them?" This coordination is made acceptable by the intervening word "laka" (for you). The discussion of "al-arazil" has already been given in full in Surat Hud [[See vol. 9, p. 23 onward, first or second edition.]], and we add here further clarification.

The second issue: It was said that those who believed in him were his sons, his women, his daughters-in-law, and his grandsons. It is disputed whether there were others with them or not. Whichever of the two views is correct, all of them were righteous. Noah had said: ﴿Save me and those who are with me of the believers﴾, and those who were with him were those who followed him. No disgrace or blame from the words of the disbelievers reaches them; rather, the "most despised" are those who denied them. Al-Suhayli said: Many of the common people have been misled by a saying narrated in the interpretation of this verse: that they were weavers and cuppers. Had they been weavers, as they claimed, their faith in the Prophet of God and their following of him would still have been honorable, just as Bilal and Salman were honored by their precedence in Islam, for they were among the foremost companions of the Prophet ﷺ and among his nobles. So the descendants of Noah were neither weavers nor cuppers, and the disbelievers' remark about weavers and cuppers, even if they had believed in them, does not bring today any blame or deficiency upon our weaving, because this is a report of the words of the disbelievers, unless the disbelievers are taken as proof and their statement as a foundation. This is great ignorance, and God Exalted has informed us that crafts do not harm religion.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He said, "And what is my knowledge of what they used to do?"﴾ "Kana" (was) is redundant here, and the meaning is: "And what is my knowledge of what they do," that is, I was not charged with knowing their deeds; I was only charged with calling them to faith, and with judging by faith, not by trades and crafts. It seems they said: "Only these weak people follow you, out of desire for power and wealth." So he said: "I have not reached the inner reality of their affairs; I am only responsible for their outward state." It was also said: the meaning is, "I did not know that God guides them and leads you astray, that He gives them guidance and makes you go astray, that He grants them success and forsakes you."

(Their reckoning is only with my Lord) ﴿Their reckoning is only upon my Lord﴾, meaning, regarding their deeds and their faith, (if you only perceived) ﴿if you were aware﴾. The answer to "law" (if) is omitted, meaning: if you had perceived that their reckoning is with their Lord, you would not have blamed them for their crafts. The common reading is "tash'urun" with the letter ta', as addressed to the disbelievers, and this is the apparent reading. Ibn Abi Ablah and Muhammad ibn al-Sumayqa' read "law yash'urun" with the letter ya', as if it were a report about the disbelievers, leaving out the direct address to them, similar to His saying: ﴿until, when you were in the ship and it sailed with them﴾. It is reported that a man asked Sufyan about a woman who committed adultery and killed her child, and she was a Muslim: would she be assured of the Fire? He said: ﴿Their reckoning is only upon my Lord, if you only perceived.﴾

(And I am not one to drive away the believers) meaning, because of the lowliness of their conditions and their occupations. It seems they asked him to drive away the weak, as Quraysh had asked of him.

(I am only a clear warner) ﴿I am only a plain warner﴾, meaning: God did not send me to favor the wealthy over the poor. I am only a messenger who conveys what I was sent with, and whoever obeys me is the one fortunate with God, even if he is poor.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They said, "If you do not desist, O Noah"﴾, meaning: from reviling our gods and disparaging our religion, (you will surely be among those stoned) ﴿you will surely be among the stoned﴾, meaning, with stones. Qatada said this. Ibn Abbas and Muqatil said: among those killed. Al-Thumali said: Every "marjumin" (stoned) in the Quran means killing, except in Maryam: ﴿If you do not desist, I will surely stone you﴾, meaning, I will surely revile you. It was also said: "among the stoned" means among the reviled, as said by al-Sadi. From this is the saying of Abu Dawud [[This is as it stands in all copies of the original. Here there appears to be a lacuna, perhaps a line of poetry which the author cited as evidence that rajm means reviling, just as he cited the line of al-Ja'di as evidence for this at the interpretation of His saying: "Were it not for your clan, we would have stoned you." See vol. 9, p. 91.]].

(He said, "My Lord, my people have denied me. So judge between me and them with a judgment, and save me and those of the believers who are with me.") He said this when he had despaired of their faith. "Al-fath" is judgment, and this has already been mentioned.

(So We saved him and those with him in the laden ship) ﴿We saved him and those with him in the laden ship﴾, meaning the ark, which has already been mentioned. "Al-mashhun" means filled, and "al-shahn" is the filling of the ship with people, animals and others. "Al-fulk" is not made feminine here because "al-fulk" here is singular, not plural.

(Then We drowned the rest afterward) ﴿Then We drowned the remaining ones afterward﴾, meaning after We saved Noah and those who believed.

(Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers. And indeed your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful.) ﴿Indeed in that is a sign, yet most of them were not believers. And indeed your Lord — He is the Mighty, the Merciful.﴾

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They said, "If you do not desist, O Noah"﴾, meaning: from reviling our gods and disparaging our religion, (you will surely be among those stoned) ﴿you will surely be among the stoned﴾, meaning, with stones. Qatada said this. Ibn Abbas and Muqatil said: among those killed. Al-Thumali said: Every "marjumin" (stoned) in the Quran means killing, except in Maryam: ﴿If you do not desist, I will surely stone you﴾, meaning, I will surely revile you. It was also said: "among the stoned" means among the reviled, as said by al-Sadi. From this is the saying of Abu Dawud [[This is as it stands in all copies of the original. Here there appears to be a lacuna, perhaps a line of poetry which the author cited as evidence that rajm means reviling, just as he cited the line of al-Ja'di as evidence for this at the interpretation of His saying: "Were it not for your clan, we would have stoned you." (He said, "My Lord, my people have denied me. So judge between me and them with a judgment, and save me and those of the believers who are with me.") He said this when he had despaired of their faith. "Al-fath" is judgment, and this has already been mentioned.

(So We saved him and those with him in the laden ship) ﴿We saved him and those with him in the laden ship﴾, meaning the ark, which has already been mentioned. "Al-mashhun" means filled, and "al-shahn" is the filling of the ship with people, animals and others. "Al-fulk" is not made feminine here because "al-fulk" here is singular, not plural.

(Then We drowned the rest afterward) ﴿Then We drowned the remaining ones afterward﴾, meaning after We saved Noah and those who believed.

(Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers. And indeed your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful.) ﴿Indeed in that is a sign, yet most of them were not believers. And indeed your Lord — He is the Mighty, the Merciful.﴾

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 26, verses 123–140:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The people of ʿAd denied the messengers.﴾ The feminine form is because the word means the tribe and the group. Their denying the messengers is as has already been explained.

(When their brother Hud said to them: "Will you not be mindful of God? I am a trustworthy messenger to you. So be mindful of God and obey me. I ask you for no wage for it; my wage is only from the Lord of the worlds.") The meaning is clear, and it has already been explained.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Do you build a landmark on every high place, playing?﴾ Al-rīʿ (high ground) is what rises from the earth, according to the saying of Ibn ʿAbbas and others, and its plural is rīʿa. And "kam rīʿu arḍika" means "how high is your land," that is, how high it rises. Qatada said: al-rīʿ is the road. This is also the view of al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Kalbī, Muqatil and al-Suddi. Ibn ʿAbbas also said it. From this is the verse of al-Musayyab ibn ʿAlas:

"In the mirage, it lowers it and raises it, a rīʿ that shines as if it were a white cloth."

He compared the road to a white garment. Al-Naḥḥas said: It is well known in the language that rīʿ is said of what rises from the earth, and also of the road. A poet said [it is Dhu al-Rumma describing a falcon; in his Diwan, printed in Europe, "wāqiʿ" appears instead of "mushriq"]:

"The flight-feathers of the secondaries are beating, shining above a rīʿa, the dew of its night glistening in its feathers."

ʿUmara said: al-rīʿ is a single mountain, rīʿa, and its plural is riyāʿ. Mujahid said: it is the wide path between two mountains. And from him: a small mountain pass. And from him: a lookout. ʿIkrima and Muqatil said: they used to be guided by the stars when they traveled, so they built tall figures on the road so that they could be guided by them. This is shown by his saying "āya," meaning a sign. From Mujahid: al-rīʿ is the building of pigeon-houses, and the proof of this is "taʿbathūn," meaning "you play." That is: you build on every high place a sign, a landmark, with which you play, in the sense of pigeon-houses and their towers. It was also said: "taʿbathūn" means you mock those who pass along the road, that is, you build on every high spot in order to look down on the travelers and mock them. Al-Kalbī said: it is the play of tax-collectors with the wealth of those who pass by them, mentioned by al-Mawardi. Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: al-rabʿ is the hermitage, and al-rīʿ is the pigeon tower that stands in the desert. And al-rīʿ is a high hill. For al-rīʿ there are two forms: with the rāʾ kasra and with the rāʾ fatha, and its plural is aryāʿ, mentioned by al-Thaʿlabi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And you take for yourselves maṣāniʿ (fortresses).﴾ That is, dwellings, as said by al-Kalbī. It was also said: fortified castles, as said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid. From this is the verse of the poet:

"We left their dwellings empty of them, and we demolished the maṣāniʿ and the towers."

It was also said: lofty palaces, which Mujahid also said. From him: pigeon towers, and al-Suddi said this. I say: this is far from Mujahid, because it has already been reported from him regarding al-rīʿ that it is the building of pigeon-houses, so this would be a repetition in the speech. Qatada said: they are reservoirs for water beneath the earth. Likewise al-Zajjaj said: they are water cisterns; its singular is muṣnaʿa and maṣnaʿ. From this is the verse of Labid:

"We wore out, but the rising stars do not wear out, and the mountains remain after us, and the maṣāniʿ."

Al-Jawhari said: al-muṣnaʿa is like a basin in which rainwater gathers, and likewise al-muṣnuʿa with a damma on the nūn. And al-maṣāniʿ are fortresses. Abu ʿUbayda said: every building is called muṣnuʿa. This is related by al-Mahdawi. ʿAbd al-Razzaq said: in our language, the Yemeni, al-maṣāniʿ are the old palaces.

(Perhaps you will live forever.) That is, so that you might live forever. It was also said: laʿalla is an interrogative in the sense of rebuke, that is, "will you live forever?" like your saying "laʿallaka tashtumunī," meaning "will you insult me?" This meaning is narrated from Ibn Zayd. Al-Farrāʾ said: "so that you live forever," meaning you do not reflect on death. Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatada said: as if you were going to remain forever in them. In some readings it is "kaʾannakum takhludūn" [passive, lightened and emphasized], mentioned by al-Naḥḥas. Qatada reported that in some readings it was "kaʾannakum khālidūn."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when you strike, you strike as tyrants.﴾ Al-baṭsh is domination and seizing with violence. One says "baṭasha bihi yabṭushu wa yabṭishu baṭshan," and "bāṭashahu mubāṭashatan." Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid said: al-baṭsh is oppression, killing by the sword and beating with the whip. The meaning of that is: you did this as oppression. Mujahid also said: it is beating with whips, and Malik ibn Anas related it from Nafiʿ from Ibn ʿUmar, as mentioned by Ibn al-ʿArabi. It was also said: it is killing by the sword without right, related by Yahya ibn Sallam. Al-Kalbī and al-Hasan said: it is killing by usurpation without deliberation. All of this returns to the saying of Ibn ʿAbbas. It was also said: it is punishing for intentional and unintentional acts without pardon or mercy. Ibn al-ʿArabi said: what Malik said is supported by the saying of God Exalted about Moses: ﴿So when he wished to strike the one who was an enemy to both of them, he said: "O Moses, do you intend to kill me as you killed a soul yesterday? You only want to be a tyrant in the land."﴾ Moses, peace be upon him, did not draw a sword against him nor pierce him with a spear; he only pushed him, and his death came from that push. Striking is done with the hand, and its least form is the punch and the push, followed by the whip and the stick, and then iron, and all of these are blameworthy except with right. The verse was revealed as a report about the nations that came before, and as an admonition from God, Mighty and Majestic, to us, to keep away from that act for which He blamed them and disapproved of it in them. I say: these blameworthy characteristics have become common among many of this community, especially in the land of Egypt since the Bahriyya (the Bahri Mamluks) ruled it, so they strike people with the whip and the stick without right. The Prophet (ﷺ) informed that this would happen, as in Sahih Muslim from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "There are two kinds of the people of the Fire I have not seen: a people who have whips like the tails of cows with which they strike people, and women who are clothed yet naked, leaning and enticing, their heads like the humps of Bactrian camels leaning. They will not enter Paradise nor smell its fragrance, though its fragrance can be found from such-and-such distance." Abu Dawud also brought from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, who said: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "When you engage in ʿīna (a sale in which you sell a commodity to a man for a known price until a known term, then buy it back from him for less than the price at which you sold it) and take the tails of cows, and are content with farming, and abandon jihad, God will impose upon you a humiliation which He will not lift until you return to your religion."

"Jabbārīn" means killers. The jabbār is the one who kills without right. Likewise is the verse: ﴿If you wish only to be a tyrant in the land﴾, said by al-Harawi. It was also said: al-jabbār is the domineering, the insolent one. From this is His saying: ﴿And you are not over them a jabbār,﴾ that is, one who dominates. The poet said:

"We took from the jabbār by the sword his kingdom, in the evening, and the points of spears were glittering."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So be mindful of God and obey me﴾ has already been explained.

(And be mindful of the One who has supplied you with what you know.) That is, with the good things. Then he explained them by saying: "He has supplied you with cattle and sons, and gardens and springs." That is, He subjected these to you and bestowed them upon you, so He is the One who must be worshipped and thanked, and not disbelieved in.

(Indeed I fear for you the punishment of a great day) if you disbelieve in Him and persist in that.

(They said: "It is all the same to us whether you admonish or are not among the admonishers.") All of that is the same to us: we do not listen to you, and we pay no attention to what you say. Al-ʿAbbas related from Abu ʿAmr and Bishr from al-Kisaʾi: "awaʿaẓta" with the ẓāʾ assimilated into the tāʾ, but this is far, because the ẓāʾ is an emphatic letter, and assimilation occurs only into what is very close to it, being similar to it and of the same articulation point.

(This is only the custom of the ancients.) That is, their religion, according to Ibn ʿAbbas and others. Al-Farrāʾ said: the habit of the ancients. Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr and al-Kisaʾi read "khalq al-awwalīn" [creation of the ancients]; the rest read "khuluq." Al-Harawi said: His saying, Mighty and Majestic: "This is only the khuluq of the ancients" means their fabrications and their lies. Whoever reads "khuluq al-awwalīn," its meaning is their customs. The Arabs say: "So-and-so related to us with stories of the khulq," that is, with fables and fabricated tales. Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: al-khuluq is religion, al-khuluq is nature, and al-khuluq is manliness. Al-Naḥḥas said: "khuluq al-awwalīn" according to al-Farrāʾ means the habit of the ancients. Muhammad ibn al-Walid related to us from Muhammad ibn Yazid, who said: "khuluq al-awwalīn" is their way and what their affairs proceeded upon. Abu Jaʿfar said: the two views are close. From this is the hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The most complete of believers in faith is the best of them in character," that is, the best of them in way, habit, and what affairs proceed upon in obedience to God Mighty and Majestic. It is not permissible that one who has good character be a wicked sinner, nor that he be more complete in faith than one with bad character who is not a sinner. Abu Jaʿfar said: it was related to us from Muhammad ibn Yazid that the meaning of "khuluq al-awwalīn" is their denial and their fabrication, but he leaned toward the first reading, because in it there is praise of their fathers, and most of what the Qur'an says about them is their praise of their fathers and their saying: ﴿We found our fathers upon a community.﴾ From Abu Qilaba: he read "khalq" with a damma on the khāʾ and sukūn on the lām, as a lightening of "khuluq." Ibn Jubayr related it from the companions of Nafiʿ, from Nafiʿ. It has been said that the meaning of "khuluq al-awwalīn" is the religion of the ancients, and from this is His saying: ﴿So they will change the creation of God,﴾ that is, the religion of God. "Khuluq al-awwalīn" is the custom of the ancients: a life, then death, and no resurrection. It was also said: what you denounce us for regarding the building and the striking is only the custom of those before us, so we follow them. (And we will not be punished) for what we do. It was also said: the meaning is the creation of the bodies of the ancients, that is, we were created only like the ancients who were created before us and died, and no punishment of what you warn us about has befallen them.

(So they denied him, and We destroyed them.) That is, by a violent, raging wind, as will come in al-Haqqa.

(Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers.) Some said: three hundred thousand and more believed with him, and the rest of them perished.

(And indeed your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful.)

(And be mindful of the One who has supplied you with what you know.) That is, with the good things. Then he explained them by saying: "He has supplied you with cattle and sons, and gardens and springs." That is, He subjected these to you and bestowed them upon you, so He is the One who must be worshipped and thanked, and not disbelieved in.

(Indeed I fear for you the punishment of a great day) if you disbelieve in Him and persist in that.

(They said: "It is all the same to us whether you admonish or are not among the admonishers.") All of that is the same to us: we do not listen to you, and we pay no attention to what you say. Al-ʿAbbas related from Abu ʿAmr and Bishr from al-Kisaʾi: "awaʿaẓta" with the ẓāʾ assimilated into the tāʾ, but this is far, because the ẓāʾ is an emphatic letter, and assimilation occurs only into what is very close to it, being similar to it and of the same articulation point.

(This is only the custom of the ancients.) That is, their religion, according to Ibn ʿAbbas and others. Al-Farrāʾ said: the habit of the ancients. Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr and al-Kisaʾi read "khalq al-awwalīn" [creation of the ancients]; the rest read "khuluq." Al-Harawi said: His saying, Mighty and Majestic: "This is only the khuluq of the ancients" means their fabrications and their lies. Whoever reads "khuluq al-awwalīn," its meaning is their customs. The Arabs say: "So-and-so related to us with stories of the khulq," that is, with fables and fabricated tales. Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: al-khuluq is religion, al-khuluq is nature, and al-khuluq is manliness. Al-Naḥḥas said: "khuluq al-awwalīn" according to al-Farrāʾ means the habit of the ancients. Muhammad ibn al-Walid related to us from Muhammad ibn Yazid, who said: "khuluq al-awwalīn" is their way and what their affairs proceeded upon. Abu Jaʿfar said: the two views are close. From this is the hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The most complete of believers in faith is the best of them in character," that is, the best of them in way, habit, and what affairs proceed upon in obedience to God Mighty and Majestic. It is not permissible that one who has good character be a wicked sinner, nor that he be more complete in faith than one with bad character who is not a sinner. Abu Jaʿfar said: it was related to us from Muhammad ibn Yazid that the meaning of "khuluq al-awwalīn" is their denial and their fabrication, but he leaned toward the first reading, because in it there is praise of their fathers, and most of what the Qur'an says about them is their praise of their fathers and their saying: ﴿We found our fathers upon a community.﴾ From Abu Qilaba: he read "khalq" with a damma on the khāʾ and sukūn on the lām, as a lightening of "khuluq." Ibn Jubayr related it from the companions of Nafiʿ, from Nafiʿ. It has been said that the meaning of "khuluq al-awwalīn" is the religion of the ancients, and from this is His saying: ﴿So they will change the creation of God,﴾ that is, the religion of God. "Khuluq al-awwalīn" is the custom of the ancients: a life, then death, and no resurrection. It was also said: what you denounce us for regarding the building and the striking is only the custom of those before us, so we follow them. (And we will not be punished) for what we do. It was also said: the meaning is the creation of the bodies of the ancients, that is, we were created only like the ancients who were created before us and died, and no punishment of what you warn us about has befallen them.

(So they denied him, and We destroyed them.) That is, by a violent, raging wind, as will come in al-Haqqa.

(Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers.) Some said: three hundred thousand and more believed with him, and the rest of them perished.

(And indeed your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful.)

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 26, verses 141–159:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Thamud denied the messengers﴾. This is the account of Salih and his people, who were Thamud. They dwelt in al-Hijr (the rocky tract), as has already been discussed in the commentary on Surah al-Hijr [[See vol. 10, p. 45 onward, first or second edition.]], and it was a land of palm groves, crops and water.

(Will you be left secure in what is here?) That is, secure in this world from death and punishment. Ibn 'Abbas said: "They were long-lived, and their buildings did not outlast their lifespans." This is indicated by His saying: ﴿and He settled you in it﴾. Salih rebuked and reproached them and said: Do you suppose you will remain in this world without death? (In gardens and springs, and crops and palm trees, whose spathes are soft-ripe.) Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask why He said ﴿and palm trees﴾ after ﴿gardens﴾, when gardens already include palm trees first of all, just as the word 'cattle' (al-ni'am) includes camels, so that among the kinds of trees they would mention 'the garden' while meaning only the palm, just as they mention 'cattle' while meaning only camels." Zuhayr said:

*As if my two eyes, at the dark-wine-jar ... of a water-camel that waters a garden of tall palms*

Here "garden" means the palm, and a *sahuq* palm is one that is very tall. I say: there are two possible interpretations. The first is that the palms are singled out by being mentioned separately after being included among all the other trees, to draw attention to their distinction from them through their particular excellence. The second is that by "gardens" he means other trees besides palms, since the word allows for that, and then palms are added to them by conjunction.

The *tal'a* (spathe) is the sheath that emerges from the palm tree like the blade of a sword, and inside it are the strands of the cluster. The *qinw* (bunch) is the name for what comes out of the trunk, together with its stalk (*'urjun*) and its strands (*shamarikh*). As for ﴿*hadim*﴾, Ibn 'Abbas said: it is soft so long as it is within its sheath. *Al-hadim* means fine and delicate, and from it comes the line of Imru' al-Qays:

*Upon her, slender of waist, sweet-scented of anklets ...*

*I bent her head by its two temples, and it inclined*

Al-Jawhari said: "The spathe is called *hadim* as long as it has not emerged from its sheath, because parts of it are folded into one another." *Al-hadim* among women is one with slender flanks. Al-Harawi reported similarly, and said: it is that which is compressed within its container before it appears, and from this is the expression "a man with compressed sides," meaning his sides are drawn in. This is the view of the lexicographers.

Al-Mawardi and others reported twelve opinions on this:
1. It is soft and tender. This was said by 'Ikrima.
2. It is the ripe-tipped one among the moist dates. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Al-Nahhas said: Abu Ishaq narrated from Yazid, who is Ibn Abi Ziyad of Kufa, and Yazid ibn Abi Maryam of Syria, on the words ﴿and palm trees whose spathes are soft-ripe﴾, that some of it had become moist (ripe) and some were still tipped.
3. It is that which has no pit. This was said by al-Hasan.
4. It is that which is brittle and crumbles, so that when touched it crumbles. This was said by Mujahid. Abu al-'Aliya said: it crumbles in the mouth.
5. It is that which has become thin through the rubbing of some of it against others. This was said by al-Dahhak and Muqatil.
6. It is that whose parts are pressed tightly against one another. This was said by Abu Sakhr.
7. It is the spathe when it splits and turns green. This was also said by al-Dahhak.
8. It is the ripe and mature one. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.
9. It is that which is compact before the skin splits open over it. This was reported by Ibn Shajara, who said:

*As if a load being unveiled upon it ... is compacted, with no cracks perceptible in it*

10. It is the soft one. This was said by al-Hasan.
11. It is the tender, delicate thing when it first emerges, namely the layered spathe. This was said by al-Harawi.
12. It is the *barni* [[*Barni*: a kind of date, the finest of them; its singular is *barniyya*.]]. This was said by Ibn al-A'rabi. It is of the form *fa'il* in the sense of *fa'il*, that is, wholesome and pleasant, from the digestion of food.

The word *tal'* (spathe) is derived from *tulu'* (emergence), which means appearance, and from it come the rising of the sun, the moon, and vegetation.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you hew houses out of the mountains, skilfully﴾. *Al-nahat* means to carve and shape. One says *nahatahu yanhituhu* (with kasra) *nahtan* when he shaped it, and *al-nahata* means shaving. *Al-minhat* is that with which something is carved. In al-Saffat He said: ﴿Do you worship what you carve?﴾. They used to carve these from the mountains because their lifespans were long, and their buildings had fallen apart from clay.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Nafi' read ﴿*farihin*﴾ without an alif. The rest read ﴿*farihin*﴾ with an alif. The two forms have one meaning according to Abu 'Ubayda and others, like ﴿*'izaman nakhirah*﴾ and ﴿*nakhirah*﴾. Qutrub also reported this. It is also reported: *farha yafrahu, fahuwa farih*, and *farih yafrah, fahuwa farih* and *farih*, when someone is energetic. It is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*). Some people distinguished between the two, saying: ﴿*farihin*﴾ means "skilled in carving them." This was said by Abu 'Ubayda, and reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Salih and others. 'Abd Allah ibn Shaddad said: ﴿*farihin*﴾ means "arrogant." It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the meaning of ﴿*farihin*﴾ without an alif is "exultant and insolent." This was said by Mujahid, and it is also reported from him as "greedy." al-Dahhak said: "shrewd." Qatada said: "conceited"; this was said by al-Kalbi, and from him also: "comfortable." And also from him: "secure." This is the view of al-Hasan. It was also said: "choosy." This was said by al-Kalbi and al-Suddi. From this is the line of the poet:

*To a noble man who outdoes every matter, I set out to test his nature*

It was said: "marveling." This was said by Khusayf. Ibn Zayd said: "strong." It was also said: ﴿*farihin*﴾ means ﴿*farihin*﴾ "rejoicing." This was said by al-Akhfash. The Arabs interchange *ha'* and *ha'* [[The text here refers to the interchange of the letters *ha'* (ه) and *ha'* (ح).]]; one says *madahtuhu* and *madahtuhu*, so *al-farah* means insolent and exultant. Then *al-farah* in the sense of *al-maraḥ* (exultation) is blameworthy. God Exalted said: ﴿And do not walk upon the earth exultantly﴾, and He said: ﴿Indeed, God does not love the exultant﴾.

﴿So fear God and obey me, and do not obey the command of the extravagant﴾. It was said: the intended ones are those who hamstrung the she-camel. It was also said: they were the nine men of the group who corrupted the land and did not set things right. Al-Suddi and others said: God revealed to Salih: "Your people will hamstring your she-camel." He said this to them, and they said: "We would never do that." Salih said to them: "A boy will be born in this month of yours who will hamstring her, and your destruction will be at his hands." They said: "No male will be born in this month without our killing him." So nine of them had sons born to them in that month, and they slaughtered their children. Then a son was born to the tenth, but he refused to slaughter his son, though he had had no child before that. The tenth man's son was blue-eyed and reddish, and he grew up quickly. When he passed by the nine and they saw him, they said: "If our children were alive they would be like this." The nine became angry at Salih, because he had been the cause of their killing their children. So they swore by God together: "We shall surely raid him and his family by night." They said: "We will go out on a journey, and people will see us departing, and we will be in a cave. When night falls and Salih goes out to his mosque, we will come to him and kill him. Then we will say: 'We did not witness the destruction of his family, and we are truthful,' and they will believe us, knowing that we went out on a journey." Salih did not sleep with them in the town; he would retreat to his mosque, and when morning came he would come to them and admonish them. When they entered the cave, they wanted to come out, but the cave collapsed upon them and killed them. Some people who had been watching saw this, and they shouted in the town: "O servants of God! Has Salih not been content that he ordered the killing of their children, until he killed them?" The people of the town then agreed to kill the she-camel.

Ibn Ishaq said: the nine gathered to curse Salih only after they had hamstrung the she-camel and after he had warned them of the punishment, as will be explained, God willing, in the commentary on Surah al-Naml, in the explanation of His saying: ﴿And there were in the city nine men of a group﴾.

﴿They said: "You are only one of the bewitched"﴾. The word is from *sihr* (sorcery), according to Mujahid and Qatada, as al-Mahdawi stated, meaning: you have been struck by sorcery and your mind has been disabled, for you are a human like us, so why do you claim prophethood over us? It was also said: it means "one of those fed food and drink," as said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Kalbi, Qatada and also Mujahid, as al-Tha'labi reported. On this view it is from *sahr*, which means the lungs, that is, you are a human with lungs, eating and drinking like us, as the poet said:

*So if you ask us what we are, we are sparrows from this bewitched (fed) humankind*

And Imru' al-Qays said:

*We are fed with food and drink ...*

*You see us hastening toward an unseen matter*

"Hastening" means hurrying. "An unseen matter" means death, which has been hidden from us in its time, while we are distracted from it by food and drink.

﴿So bring a sign, if you are among the truthful﴾ in what you say.

﴿He said: "This is a she-camel; she has a share of water, and you have a share of water on an appointed day"﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: They said: "If you are truthful, ask God to bring forth for us from this mountain a red she-camel in her tenth month, who will give birth while we watch, and who will come to this water, drink, and in return give us milk like it." So he prayed to God, and God did that. ﴿He said: "This is a she-camel; she has a share﴾, that is, a portion of the water, meaning: you have a day's share, and she has a day's share. So on her day of drinking she would drink all their water at the beginning of the day, and would give them milk at the end of the day. On their day of drinking, it was for themselves, their livestock and their land, and on her day of coming they were not to drink any of her share, nor was she to drink any of their water on their day.

Al-Farra' said: *al-shirb* means the portion of water. Al-Nahhas said: as for the verbal noun, it is said *shariba shorban* and *shurban* and *shirban*, and the commonest is the *damma* form, because the *kasra* and *fatha* forms are shared with something else, so *al-shirb* means a share of water, and *al-shurb* may be the plural of *shari'* (drinker), as the poet said [[It is al-A'sha, and the complete line is: "*Shimu, fa-kayfa yashimmu al-sharibu al-thamilu*" (Smell [the water], but how can the drinker, when drunk, smell?).]]:

*Then I said to the drinkers at Darna, and they were drunk*

However, Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' and al-Kisa'i preferred *al-shirb* with *fatha* in the first position, arguing with a report from some scholars that the Prophet ﷺ said: "They are days of eating and drinking" [[Darna (with *damma* on the *dal* and *fatha*) is said to be a place in the region of al-Yamama. Source: Lisan al-'Arab.]].

﴿And do not touch her with harm﴾. It is not permissible to show the doubling here, because they are two consonants moving from the same class.

﴿So He seizes you﴾ is the response to the prohibition. The *fa'* may be omitted from it, and the jussive mood, as in the case of the imperative. But there is one exception, which is reported from al-Kisa'i, that he permits it.

﴿So they hamstrung her, and then they became regretful﴾, that is, regretful over hamstringing her when they became certain of the punishment. That is because He gave them respite for three days, and the sign appeared upon them each day, and they regretted it, but their regret did not benefit them at the sight of the punishment. It was also said: their regret did not benefit them because they did not repent; rather, when they became certain of the punishment they sought Salih, peace be upon him, in order to kill him. It was also said: their regret was over leaving the child alive, since they had not killed him along with her. This last view is far-fetched.

﴿Indeed, in that is a sign﴾, to the end of the verse, which has already been discussed. It is said: none of those nations believed in it except two thousand and eight hundred men and women. It was also said: they were four thousand. Ka'b said: the people of Salih were twelve thousand clans, each clan about twelve thousand, besides the women and children, and the people of 'Ad were six times like them.

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 26, verses 141–159:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Thamud denied the messengers﴾. This is the account of Salih and his people, who were Thamud. They dwelt in al-Hijr (the rocky tract), as has already been discussed in the commentary on Surah al-Hijr [[See vol. 10, p. 45 onward, first or second edition.]], and it was a land of palm groves, crops and water.

(Will you be left secure in what is here?) That is, secure in this world from death and punishment. Ibn 'Abbas said: "They were long-lived, and their buildings did not outlast their lifespans." This is indicated by His saying: ﴿and He settled you in it﴾. Salih rebuked and reproached them and said: Do you suppose you will remain in this world without death? (In gardens and springs, and crops and palm trees, whose spathes are soft-ripe.) Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask why He said ﴿and palm trees﴾ after ﴿gardens﴾, when gardens already include palm trees first of all, just as the word 'cattle' (al-ni'am) includes camels, so that among the kinds of trees they would mention 'the garden' while meaning only the palm, just as they mention 'cattle' while meaning only camels." Zuhayr said:

*As if my two eyes, at the dark-wine-jar ... of a water-camel that waters a garden of tall palms*

Here "garden" means the palm, and a *sahuq* palm is one that is very tall. I say: there are two possible interpretations. The first is that the palms are singled out by being mentioned separately after being included among all the other trees, to draw attention to their distinction from them through their particular excellence. The second is that by "gardens" he means other trees besides palms, since the word allows for that, and then palms are added to them by conjunction.

The *tal'a* (spathe) is the sheath that emerges from the palm tree like the blade of a sword, and inside it are the strands of the cluster. The *qinw* (bunch) is the name for what comes out of the trunk, together with its stalk (*'urjun*) and its strands (*shamarikh*). As for ﴿*hadim*﴾, Ibn 'Abbas said: it is soft so long as it is within its sheath. *Al-hadim* means fine and delicate, and from it comes the line of Imru' al-Qays:

*Upon her, slender of waist, sweet-scented of anklets ...*

*I bent her head by its two temples, and it inclined*

Al-Jawhari said: "The spathe is called *hadim* as long as it has not emerged from its sheath, because parts of it are folded into one another." *Al-hadim* among women is one with slender flanks. Al-Harawi reported similarly, and said: it is that which is compressed within its container before it appears, and from this is the expression "a man with compressed sides," meaning his sides are drawn in. This is the view of the lexicographers.

Al-Mawardi and others reported twelve opinions on this:
1. It is soft and tender. This was said by 'Ikrima.
2. It is the ripe-tipped one among the moist dates. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Al-Nahhas said: Abu Ishaq narrated from Yazid, who is Ibn Abi Ziyad of Kufa, and Yazid ibn Abi Maryam of Syria, on the words ﴿and palm trees whose spathes are soft-ripe﴾, that some of it had become moist (ripe) and some were still tipped.
3. It is that which has no pit. This was said by al-Hasan.
4. It is that which is brittle and crumbles, so that when touched it crumbles. This was said by Mujahid. Abu al-'Aliya said: it crumbles in the mouth.
5. It is that which has become thin through the rubbing of some of it against others. This was said by al-Dahhak and Muqatil.
6. It is that whose parts are pressed tightly against one another. This was said by Abu Sakhr.
7. It is the spathe when it splits and turns green. This was also said by al-Dahhak.
8. It is the ripe and mature one. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.
9. It is that which is compact before the skin splits open over it. This was reported by Ibn Shajara, who said:

*As if a load being unveiled upon it ... is compacted, with no cracks perceptible in it*

10. It is the soft one. This was said by al-Hasan.
11. It is the tender, delicate thing when it first emerges, namely the layered spathe. This was said by al-Harawi.
12. It is the *barni* [[*Barni*: a kind of date, the finest of them; its singular is *barniyya*.]]. This was said by Ibn al-A'rabi. It is of the form *fa'il* in the sense of *fa'il*, that is, wholesome and pleasant, from the digestion of food.

The word *tal'* (spathe) is derived from *tulu'* (emergence), which means appearance, and from it come the rising of the sun, the moon, and vegetation.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you hew houses out of the mountains, skilfully﴾. *Al-nahat* means to carve and shape. One says *nahatahu yanhituhu* (with kasra) *nahtan* when he shaped it, and *al-nahata* means shaving. *Al-minhat* is that with which something is carved. In al-Saffat He said: ﴿Do you worship what you carve?﴾. They used to carve these from the mountains because their lifespans were long, and their buildings had fallen apart from clay.

The two forms have one meaning according to Abu 'Ubayda and others, like ﴿*'izaman nakhirah*﴾ and ﴿*nakhirah*﴾. Qutrub also reported this. It is also reported: *farha yafrahu, fahuwa farih*, and *farih yafrah, fahuwa farih* and *farih*, when someone is energetic. It is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*). Some people distinguished between the two, saying: ﴿*farihin*﴾ means "skilled in carving them." This was said by Abu 'Ubayda, and reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Salih and others. 'Abd Allah ibn Shaddad said: ﴿*farihin*﴾ means "arrogant." It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the meaning of ﴿*farihin*﴾ without an alif is "exultant and insolent." This was said by Mujahid, and it is also reported from him as "greedy." al-Dahhak said: "shrewd." Qatada said: "conceited"; this was said by al-Kalbi, and from him also: "comfortable." And also from him: "secure." This is the view of al-Hasan. It was also said: "choosy." This was said by al-Kalbi and al-Suddi. From this is the line of the poet:

*To a noble man who outdoes every matter, I set out to test his nature*

It was said: "marveling." This was said by Khusayf. Ibn Zayd said: "strong." It was also said: ﴿*farihin*﴾ means ﴿*farihin*﴾ "rejoicing." This was said by al-Akhfash. The Arabs interchange *ha'* and *ha'* [[The text here refers to the interchange of the letters *ha'* (ه) and *ha'* (ح).]]; one says *madahtuhu* and *madahtuhu*, so *al-farah* means insolent and exultant. Then *al-farah* in the sense of *al-maraḥ* (exultation) is blameworthy. God Exalted said: ﴿And do not walk upon the earth exultantly﴾, and He said: ﴿Indeed, God does not love the exultant﴾.

﴿So fear God and obey me, and do not obey the command of the extravagant﴾. It was said: the intended ones are those who hamstrung the she-camel. It was also said: they were the nine men of the group who corrupted the land and did not set things right. Al-Suddi and others said: God revealed to Salih: "Your people will hamstring your she-camel." He said this to them, and they said: "We would never do that." Salih said to them: "A boy will be born in this month of yours who will hamstring her, and your destruction will be at his hands." They said: "No male will be born in this month without our killing him." So nine of them had sons born to them in that month, and they slaughtered their children. Then a son was born to the tenth, but he refused to slaughter his son, though he had had no child before that. The tenth man's son was blue-eyed and reddish, and he grew up quickly. When he passed by the nine and they saw him, they said: "If our children were alive they would be like this." The nine became angry at Salih, because he had been the cause of their killing their children. So they swore by God together: "We shall surely raid him and his family by night." They said: "We will go out on a journey, and people will see us departing, and we will be in a cave. When night falls and Salih goes out to his mosque, we will come to him and kill him. Salih did not sleep with them in the town; he would retreat to his mosque, and when morning came he would come to them and admonish them. When they entered the cave, they wanted to come out, but the cave collapsed upon them and killed them. Some people who had been watching saw this, and they shouted in the town: "O servants of God! *So if you ask us what we are, we are sparrows from this bewitched (fed) humankind*

And Imru' al-Qays said:

*We are fed with food and drink ...*

*You see us hastening toward an unseen matter*

"Hastening" means hurrying. "An unseen matter" means death, which has been hidden from us in its time, while we are distracted from it by food and drink.

**Qur'an 26:176–191**

﴿The companions of the Thicket denied the messengers.﴾ *Al-Ayka* (the Thicket) is dense, abundant trees; its singular is *ayka*. Whoever reads *Ashab al-Ayka* (the companions of the Thicket) takes it to mean a thicket (*ghayda*). Whoever reads *Layka* takes it as the name of a town. It is said that they are like *Bakka* and *Makka*; this is what al-Jawhari (the lexicographer) reported. Al-Nahhas said: Abu Ja'far and Nafi' read "*Kadhdhaba Ashabu Layka al-mursalin*" ("the companions of Layka denied the messengers"), and so did [Nafi'] in *Sad*. The reciters agreed on the genitive case in the instances in *al-Hijr* and in *Qaf*, so what they differed on must be referred back to what they agreed upon, since the meaning is one. As for what Abu 'Ubayd related, that *Layka* is the name of the town in which they lived and *al-Ayka* is the name of the region, it is not established, and no one is known to have said it, so its authority cannot be confirmed. Even if the one who said it were known, it would be open to question, because all the people of knowledge, both among the exegetes and among those versed in the speech of the Arabs, hold the opposite view.

Abdullah ibn Wahb related from Jarir ibn Hazim, from Qatada, who said: Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, was sent to two nations: to his own people, the people of Madyan, and to the companions of the Thicket. He said: *al-Ayka* is a thicket of dense trees. Sa'id related from Qatada, who said: The companions of the Thicket were people of a thicket and trees, and most of their trees were *al-Dawm*, which is the palm-tree of the *muql* (doum palm). Ibn Jubayr related from al-Dahhak, who said: The companions of the Thicket went out, namely when the heat afflicted them, and gathered in the thicket and the trees. So God sent a cloud over them, and they took shelter beneath it, but when they had all gathered beneath it, they were burned. Also, were there nothing in this except what is related from Ibn Abbas, who said: "*al-Ayka*" means trees, it would suffice. We know of no disagreement among the lexicographers that *al-Ayka* is dense trees. As for the argument of some who relied on the reading of those who read *Layka* with a fatha in these two places, claiming that it is so written in the consonantal text (*al-sawad*), this has no proof behind it. The explanation is that its original form is *al-Ayka*; the hamza was softened, so its vowel was transferred to the lam, which then dropped, and it no longer needed the connecting alif, since the lam had already taken a vowel. Therefore, according to this, only the genitive is permissible, just as you say *bi-l-Ahmar* (with al-Ahmar): you pronounce the hamza clearly and then drop it, saying *bi-Lhmar*. If you wish, you may write it in the script as you first wrote it, or if you wish, you may write it with the omission, but only the genitive is permitted. Sibawayh said: Know that a diptote (*ma la yanṣarif*), when the definite article *al-* is attached to it or it is put in an annexed construction (*idafa*), becomes declinable (*yanṣarif*). We know of no one who opposed Sibawayh in this. Al-Khalil said: *al-Ayka* is a thicket that grows the lote-tree (*sidr*), the acacia (*arak*), and similar soft trees.

﴿When Shu'ayb said to them,﴾ "Shu'ayb did not say 'their brother' ... " — rather, he did not say "their brother" in the sense of kinship, because he was not a brother to the companions of the Thicket by lineage. When [the Qur'an] mentioned Madyan, it said: "their brother Shu'ayb," because he was from them. The discussion of his lineage has already passed in *al-A'raf* [[See vol. 7, p. 247 onwards, first or second edition.]]. Ibn Zayd said: God sent Shu'ayb as a messenger to his people, the people of Madyan, and to the people of the desert, who are the companions of the Thicket. Qatada also said this, and we have mentioned it.

﴿Will you not fear God?﴾ (*Alla tattaqun*): fear God. ﴿Indeed I am a trustworthy messenger to you. So fear God and obey me.﴾ The reason the response of these messengers was one and in one form is that they all agreed on commanding piety, obedience, sincerity in worship, and refraining from taking a wage for conveying the message.

﴿Give full measure and do not be of those who cause loss,﴾ meaning those who diminish the measure and the weight.

﴿And weigh with a true balance,﴾ meaning give the right. This has already been discussed in *Subhan* and elsewhere.

﴿And do not deprive people of their due, and do not commit corruption on the earth, causing mischief,﴾ which has already been discussed in *Hud* and elsewhere.

﴿Fear Him who created you and the former generations.﴾ Mujahid said: *al-Jibilla* is the creation. It is said "Fulan was made (*jubila*) for such-and-such," meaning he was created for it. So *al-khuluq* (creation) is *jibilla*, *jubulla*, *jibla*, and *jubla*; al-Nahhas mentioned this in *Ma'ani al-Qur'an*. *Wa-al-jibilla* is conjoined to the *kaf* and *mim* (of *khalaqakum*). Al-Harawi said: *al-jibilla*, *al-jubulla*, *al-jibill*, *al-jubull*, and *al-jabl* are dialectal variants, and it means a large group of people with many numbers, and from this is the Qur'anic statement: ﴿a great multitude (*jibillan kathira*)﴾. Al-Nahhas said in his book *I'rab al-Qur'an* (the grammatical analysis of the Qur'an): It is said *jibilla*, and the plural of both is *jabbal*. The damma and kasra are dropped from the *ba'*, and likewise the doubling is dropped from the lam, so it is said *jubla* and *jubal*; and it is said *jibla* and *jibal*. The *ha'* is dropped from all of this. Al-Hasan, with variation on his authority, read *wa-al-jibilla al-awwalin* with a damma on the *jim* and the *ba'*; it is related from Shayba and al-A'raj. The rest read it with a kasra. He said:

*"Death is the greatest calamity*
*among what passes over the creation (al-jibilla)."*

﴿They said: "You are only one of the bewitched.﴾ Those who eat food and drink, as has already been explained.

﴿And we think you are surely among the liars,﴾ meaning: we do not think you are anything but one of the liars concerning your being a messenger of God, the Exalted.

﴿So cause a piece of the sky to fall upon us,﴾ *kisafan* (with a sukun on the sin is the reading of Nafi') ﴿from the heaven,﴾ meaning a side of the sky and a fragment of it, so that we may look at it, as He said: ﴿And if they should see a piece of the sky falling, they would say, "It is a massed cloud."﴾ It is also said that they meant: send down the punishment upon us. This is an exaggeration in denial. Abu 'Ubayda said: *al-kisf* is the plural of *kisfa*, like *sidr* and *sidra*. Al-Sulami and Hafs read *kisafan*, also the plural of *kisfa*, which is a piece and a side; its pattern is *kisra* and *kisr*. Al-Jawhari said: *al-kisfa* is a piece of a thing; it is said, "Give me a piece (*kisfa*) of your garment," and the plural is *kisaf* and *kisf*. It is also said that *al-kisf* and *al-kisfa* are the same. Al-Akhfash said: whoever reads *kisfan* makes it singular, and whoever reads *kisafan* makes it plural. This has already been discussed in *Surat Subhan* [[See vol. 10, p. 330, first or second edition.]]. Al-Harawi said: whoever reads *kisfan* as singular, its plural is *akhsaf* and *kusuf*, as if he had said: "or cause it to fall upon us as one layer (*tabaqan wahidan*)." It is from *kasafa al-shay'* (he covered the thing), meaning he covered it.

﴿If you are among the truthful.﴾ ﴿He said: "My Lord knows best what you do."﴾ This is a threat, meaning: my duty is only to convey, and the punishment you asked for is not mine; He will requite you.

﴿So they denied him, and the punishment of the Day of the Canopy seized them.﴾ Ibn Abbas said: a severe heat afflicted them, so God, glorified is He, sent a cloud, and they fled to it to shade themselves beneath it. When they were beneath it, they were struck with a cry and perished. It is also said: God raised it over their heads and set it ablaze with heat until they died of inflammation of the eyes. It was among the greatest days of punishment in this world. It is also said: God sent upon them a scorching wind, so they went out to the Thicket to shade themselves there, and God set it on fire over them, and they were burned. Also related from Ibn Abbas and others: God opened for them a gate of the gates of Hell, and sent upon them a thunderous noise and a severe heat, which seized their breaths. They entered their houses, but neither shade nor water availed them, and the heat cooked them. So they fled out into the open desert, and God, mighty and majestic, sent a cloud which shaded them. They found in it coolness, refreshment, and a pleasant breeze, so they called to one another. When they gathered beneath the cloud, God set fire upon them from it, and the earth shook beneath them, and they burned as locusts burn in a frying pan, and became ashes. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿So they became prostrate in their homes, as though they had never dwelt there﴾ and His saying: ﴿So the punishment of the Day of the Canopy seized them. Indeed, it was the punishment of a tremendous day.﴾ It is also said: God withheld the wind from them for seven days and imposed upon them the heat until it seized their breaths. Neither shade nor water availed them, so they would enter the underground tunnels to cool themselves there, but they found them hotter than the outside. So they fled to the open desert, and a cloud overshadowed them, which is the *zulla* (canopy). They found in it coolness and gentle breeze, but it rained fire upon them, and they burned. Yazid al-Juraysi said: God imposed upon them the heat for seven days and their nights; then a mountain was raised for them from afar, and a man came to it, and beneath it were rivers, springs, trees, and cold water. So they all gathered beneath it, and the mountain fell upon them, and this is the *zulla* (canopy). Qatada said: God sent Shu'ayb to two nations: the companions of Madyan and the companions of the Thicket. God destroyed the companions of the Thicket by the canopy, while as for the companions of Madyan, Gabriel shouted at them with a single cry, and they all perished.

﴿Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers.﴾ It is said: nine hundred men from the two groups believed in Shu'ayb.

Whoever reads *Ashab al-Ayka* (the companions of the Thicket) takes it to mean a thicket (*ghayda*). Whoever reads *Layka* takes it as the name of a town. Even if the one who said it were known, it would be open to question, because all the people of knowledge, both among the exegetes and among those versed in the speech of the Arabs, hold the opposite view.

Abdullah ibn Wahb related from Jarir ibn Hazim, from Qatada, who said: Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, was sent to two nations: to his own people, the people of Madyan, and to the companions of the Thicket. He said: *al-Ayka* is a thicket of dense trees. Sa'id related from Qatada, who said: The companions of the Thicket were people of a thicket and trees, and most of their trees were *al-Dawm*, which is the palm-tree of the *muql* (doum palm). We know of no one who opposed Sibawayh in this. Al-Khalil said: *al-Ayka* is a thicket that grows the lote-tree (*sidr*), the acacia (*arak*), and similar soft trees.

Sa'id related from Qatada, who said: The companions of the Thicket were people of a thicket and trees, and most of their trees were *al-Dawm*, which is the palm-tree of the *muql* (doum palm). Ibn Jubayr related from al-Dahhak, who said: The companions of the Thicket went out, namely when the heat afflicted them, and gathered in the thicket and the trees. The explanation is that its original form is *al-Ayka*; the hamza was softened, so its vowel was transferred to the lam, which then dropped, and it no longer needed the connecting alif, since the lam had already taken a vowel. Therefore, according to this, only the genitive is permissible, just as you say *bi-l-Ahmar* (with al-Ahmar): you pronounce the hamza clearly and then drop it, saying *bi-Lhmar*. If you wish, you may write it in the script as you first wrote it, or if you wish, you may write it with the omission, but only the genitive is permitted. Sibawayh said: Know that a diptote (*ma la yanṣarif*), when the definite article *al-* is attached to it or it is put in an annexed construction (*idafa*), becomes declinable (*yanṣarif*). " — rather, he did not say "their brother" in the sense of kinship, because he was not a brother to the companions of the Thicket by lineage. ﴿And weigh with a true balance,﴾ meaning give the right. This has already been discussed in *Subhan* and elsewhere.

﴿And do not deprive people of their due, and do not commit corruption on the earth, causing mischief,﴾ which has already been discussed in *Hud* and elsewhere.

﴿Fear Him who created you and the former generations.﴾ Mujahid said: *al-Jibilla* is the creation. It is said "Fulan was made (*jubila*) for such-and-such," meaning he was created for it. *"Death is the greatest calamity*
*among what passes over the creation (al-jibilla)."*

﴿They said: "You are only one of the bewitched.﴾ Those who eat food and drink, as has already been explained.

﴿And we think you are surely among the liars,﴾ meaning: we do not think you are anything but one of the liars concerning your being a messenger of God, the Exalted.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 26, verse 192–196:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed, it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾. It returns to what was explained earlier at the beginning of the surah, concerning the aversion of the polytheists from the Qur'an.

(﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down upon your heart﴾) "Nazala" (with a light, unstressed form) is recited by Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr. The rest recite "nazzala" (with a doubled, stressed form), with "al-ruh al-amin" in the accusative. This is the choice of Abu Hatim and Abu 'Ubayd, because of His saying: "And indeed, it is a revelation (tanzil)," which is the verbal noun of nazzala. The argument for the one who recites with the light form is that one may say: this is not a problem, because the meaning is: "And indeed the Qur'an is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds, which Gabriel (Jibril) brought down to you," as He, may He be exalted, said: "Say: Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel, indeed he has brought it down upon your heart" (nazzalahu), meaning he recites it to you so that your heart comprehends it. And it has been said: so that it may strengthen your heart.

(﴿So that you may be among the warners, in a clear Arabic tongue﴾) That is, lest they say, "We do not understand what you say."

(﴿And indeed it is in the scriptures of the former peoples﴾) That is, indeed the mention of its descent is in the books of the former peoples, meaning the prophets. It has also been said: that is, indeed the mention of Muhammad (ﷺ) is in the books of the former peoples, as He, may He be exalted, said: "They find it written with them in the Torah and the Gospel." The word "zubur" means books; its singular is "zabur," like "rasul" and "rusul," and this has been discussed earlier.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 26, verse 192–196:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed, it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾. It returns to what was explained earlier at the beginning of the surah, concerning the aversion of the polytheists from the Qur'an.

(﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down upon your heart﴾) "Nazala" (with a light, unstressed form) is recited by Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr. The rest recite "nazzala" (with a doubled, stressed form), with "al-ruh al-amin" in the accusative. This is the choice of Abu Hatim and Abu 'Ubayd, because of His saying: "And indeed, it is a revelation (tanzil)," which is the verbal noun of nazzala. The argument for the one who recites with the light form is that one may say: this is not a problem, because the meaning is: "And indeed the Qur'an is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds, which Gabriel (Jibril) brought down to you," as He, may He be exalted, said: "Say: Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel, indeed he has brought it down upon your heart" (nazzalahu), meaning he recites it to you so that your heart comprehends it. And it has been said: so that it may strengthen your heart.

(﴿So that you may be among the warners, in a clear Arabic tongue﴾) That is, lest they say, "We do not understand what you say."

(﴿And indeed it is in the scriptures of the former peoples﴾) That is, indeed the mention of its descent is in the books of the former peoples, meaning the prophets. It has also been said: that is, indeed the mention of Muhammad (ﷺ) is in the books of the former peoples, as He, may He be exalted, said: "They find it written with them in the Torah and the Gospel." The word "zubur" means books; its singular is "zabur," like "rasul" and "rusul," and this has been discussed earlier.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 26, verse 197–203:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is it not a sign for them that the scholars of the Children of Israel know it?﴾ Mujahid said: It refers to ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam, Salman and others who embraced Islam. Ibn ʿAbbas said: The people of Makkah sent to the Jews, who were in Madinah, asking them about Muhammad (peace be upon him). They said: "This is indeed his time, and we find his description and attributes in the Torah." According to this view, the word "scholars" refers to anyone who had knowledge of their books, whether or not he embraced Islam. The testimony of the People of the Book became a proof against the polytheists because they used to refer to the People of the Book in some matters of religion, since they were presumed to have knowledge.

Ibn ʿAmir recited "أَوَلَمْ تَكُنْ لَهُمْ آيَةٌ" (with the feminine ta' on takun). The rest recited "أَوَلَمْ يَكُنْ لَهُمْ آيَةً" with the accusative, as a predicate, the subject of "yakun" being "أَنْ يَعْلَمَهُ" (that they know it). The sense is: "Or was it not a clear sign for them that the knowledge of the scholars of the Children of Israel who embraced Islam..." On the first reading, the subject of "kana" is "āyatan" and the predicate is "an ya'lamahu ʿulamāʾu Banī Isrāʾīl." ʿĀsim al-Jahdari recited "أَنْ تَعْلَمُهُ عُلَمَاءُ بَنِي إِسْرَائِيلَ" (with ta').

﴿And had We sent it down upon some of the non-Arabs﴾, that is, upon a man who was not Arabic-speaking, ﴿and he had recited it to them﴾ in other than the language of the Arabs, ﴿they would not have believed in it, and they would have said, "We do not understand."﴾ A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿And had We made it a non-Arabic Qur'an...﴾ the verse. It is also said: its meaning is that had We sent it down upon a man who was not of the Arabs, they would not have believed in it out of arrogance and pride. It is said: "a man is a-ʿjam (a-ʿjam) and aʿjamī" when he is not eloquent even if he is an Arab, while "a man is ʿajamī" even if he is eloquent, and he is attributed to his origin. However, al-Farra' permitted saying "rajul ʿajamī" with the meaning of "aʿjamī". Al-Hasan recited "عَلَى بَعْضِ الْأَعْجَمِيِّينَ" with a double yā', treating it as a relative form. As for those who recited "al-aʿjamīn," it is said that it is the plural of "aʿjam," but this is far-fetched, because adjectives whose feminine form is "faʿlāʾ" are not pluralized with the sound masculine plural (waw and nun) nor with the feminine plural (alif and ta'); one does not say "aḥmarūn" nor "ḥamrāwāt." It is also said that its original form was "al-aʿjamīn," as in the reading of al-Jahdari, then the relative yā' was deleted and the plural with yā' and nun was made to indicate it. This was said by Abu al-Fath ʿUthman ibn Jinni, and it is the view of Sibawayh.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Thus We have caused it to enter into the hearts of the criminals﴾, meaning the Qur'an, that is, disbelief in it. (They do not believe in it.) It is also said: We caused denial to enter their hearts, and that is what prevented them from faith; this was said by Yahya ibn Salam. ʿIkrimah said: it is hardness (of heart). The meanings are close, and this has passed in "al-Hijr". [See vol. 10, p. 7, first or second edition.] Al-Farra' permitted the jussive in "lā yu'minūna" because it carries the sense of a condition and consequence. He claimed that it is characteristic of the Arabs that when they place "lā" in the position of "kay lā" in such a context, they sometimes make what follows jussive and sometimes marfu'; so one says "rabaṭtu al-faras lā yanfalitu" with both raising and jussive, because the meaning is "if I do not tie it, it will escape," while the raising carries the meaning of "kayla yanfalita." He cited for the raised form a line from a man of Banu ʿUqayl:

"Until we saw the best of deeds among us / a dwelling in which no evil doer harms" (marfu', since "kay" is omitted).

And for the jussive, the saying of another:

"How often did you two keep her from drinking, so do not come (lā tird), / so leave her and the large buckets, let her cool down" [Ḥallaʾtumāhā: prevented her from reaching the water. Sijāl: plural of sajl, a large bucket full of water. Tabtarid: drinks water to cool her liver. The verse was said by some women to another when they visited a woman who had married a man who had been in love with her.]

Al-Nahhas said: All of this regarding "yu'minūna" is an error according to the Basran grammarians; it is not permissible to make a verb jussive without a jussive particle, and a thing that operates an effect, when removed, cannot operate a stronger effect than its effect while it is present. This is a clear argument.

﴿Until they see the painful punishment, and it comes upon them suddenly﴾, that is, the punishment. Al-Hasan recited "فَتَأْتِيَهُمْ" with ta'; the meaning is: "the Hour will come upon them suddenly," and it was elided because the punishment that occurs in it is indicated, and because of how frequently its mention occurs in the Qur'an. A man said to al-Hasan, when he recited "fa-ta'tiyahum": "O Abu Sa'id, it is the punishment that comes upon them suddenly." He rebuked him and said: "It is rather the Hour that comes upon them suddenly," that is, unexpectedly.

﴿And they do not perceive﴾ its coming.

﴿Then they will say, "Will we be given respite?"﴾, that is, be delayed and granted time. They will seek a return at that moment, but they will not be answered in it. Al-Qushayri said: His saying "fa-ya'tiyahum" is not a conjunction upon "ḥattā yaraw", but rather it is the answer to His saying "lā yu'minūna"; since it is an answer to a negation, it is in the accusative, and likewise His saying "fa-yaqūlū."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 26, verse 204–209:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Do they then seek to hasten Our punishment?﴾ Muqatil said: The polytheists said to the Prophet (ﷺ), "O Muhammad, how long will you threaten us with punishment without bringing it?" So this was revealed: "Do they then seek to hasten Our punishment?"

(﴿Have you considered, if We let them enjoy for years﴾) meaning in this world. What is meant is the people of Makkah, according to al-Dahhak and others.

(﴿Then there comes to them that which they were promised﴾) of punishment and destruction, (﴿what good will their enjoyment avail them?﴾). The first "ma" is an interrogative, meaning affirmation (taqrir), and it is in a position of accusative governed by "aghna" (avail). The second "ma" is in a position of nominative. It is also permissible for the second to be a negation with no grammatical position. It was also said: the first "ma" is a particle of negation, and the second "ma" is in the nominative position governed by "aghna," and the returning pronoun is omitted. The meaning is: the time in which they were given enjoyment did not avail them. From al-Zuhri: that when 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz woke in the morning, he would hold his beard, then recite "Have you considered, if We let them enjoy for years. Then there comes to them that which they were promised. What good will their enjoyment avail them?" and then he would weep and say:

Your day, O deluded one, is heedlessness and negligence,
and your night is sleep, while death is necessarily yours.

Neither are you among the wakeful, alert and resolute,
nor among the sleepers, saved and safe.

You are delighted by what perishes, and rejoice in hopes,
as the dreamer is delighted by pleasures in sleep.

And you strive toward that whose consequence you will dislike,
just as the beasts live in this world.

His saying, Exalted is He: (﴿And We never destroyed a town﴾) "min" is extra (silah); the meaning is: and We never destroyed a town.

(﴿but it had warners﴾) i.e., messengers.

(﴿as a reminder﴾) Al-Kisa'i said: "dhikra" is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state (hal). Al-Nahhas said: This does not hold, and the correct view is that of al-Farra' and Abu Ishaq, that it is in the accusative position as a verbal noun (masdar). Al-Farra' said: that is, they remind with a reminder. This is a sound view, because the meaning of "but it had warners" is "but it had reminders." "Dhikra" does not show its case ending, because it ends in a short (maqsura) alif. It is also permissible to read "dhikran" with tanwin, and it is permissible for "dhikra" to be in the nominative position by supposing an omitted subject. Abu Ishaq said: that is, Our warning is a reminder. Al-Farra' said: that is, that is a reminder, and those are a reminder. Ibn al-Anbari said: Some exegetes said: there is no complete pause (waqf tam) in "al-Shu'ara'" except His saying "but it had warners," but in our view this is a good pause (waqf hasan), then one begins with "dhikra" with the meaning "it is a reminder," i.e., it reminds them with a reminder; and stopping on "dhikra" is better.

(﴿And We were never unjust﴾) in punishing them, since We sent forth the proof against them and gave them excuse.
