**Qur'an 26:210–213**

Allah's statement: ﴿The devils have not brought it down﴾, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿but the Trustworthy Spirit brings it down﴾.

(﴿It is not fitting for them, nor are they able to do it. Indeed, they are kept far from hearing it﴾), meaning they are barred by being pelted with shooting stars, as explained earlier in Surat al-Hijr [see vol. 10, p. 10 and following, first or second edition].

Al-Hasan (al-Basri) and Muhammad ibn al-Sumayqa' recited: "wa ma tanazzalat bihi al-shayatinu" (with the final word in the nominative, al-shayatinu, as a subject of tanazzalat). Al-Mahdawi said: "This is impermissible in Arabic and contrary to the written text (al-khatt)." Al-Nahhas said: "This is an error according to all the grammarians. I heard Ali ibn Sulayman say: I heard Muhammad ibn Yazid say: This is an error according to the scholars. It arose only from a confusion: when al-Hasan saw the ya' and nun at the end of the word, and it was in the position of the nominative, he confused it with the sound masculine plural and so made the error."

There is a hadith: "Beware of the slip of the scholar." Al-Hasan himself read, along with the people, ﴿and when they go back to their devils (shayatinihim)﴾, and if this (the reading of tanazzalat) were with the waw (plural) in the nominative position, the nun would have to be dropped because of the idafah (annexation). Al-Tha'labi said: al-Farra' said: "The Shaykh (i.e. al-Hasan) erred." This was said to al-Nadr ibn Shumayl, and he replied: "If it is permissible to cite the speech of Ru'bah, al-Ajjaj and their like, it is permissible to cite the speech of al-Hasan and his companion, although we know that they did not recite this except after having heard something about it." Al-Mu'arrij said: "If the word shaytan is derived from shata yashitu, then their recitation has a basis." Yunus ibn Habib said: "I heard a Bedouin say: We entered gardens behind which were gardens (bisatun)," and I said: "How similar this is to the recitation of al-Hasan."

Allah's statement: ﴿So do not call upon another god along with Allah, lest you be among those punished﴾. It was said: the meaning is, "Say this to those who disbelieve." It was also said: it is an address to him, peace be upon him, although he would not do this, because he is protected from sin and chooses rightly; but he was addressed with it while the intended audience was someone else. This is indicated by His statement: ﴿And warn your closest kinsmen﴾, meaning that they should not rely on their lineage and kinship and thereby neglect what is obligatory upon them.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 26, verse 214–220:

The Most High said: ﴿And warn your nearest kinsmen﴾. In this there are two issues.

The first: The Most High's words ﴿And warn your nearest kinsmen﴾. He singled out his nearest kinsmen for warning, so that the hopes of the rest of his clan and of outsiders, that he would leave them in their polytheism, might be cut off. His nearest kinsmen were the Quraysh. It was also said: the Banu 'Abd Manaf. And it occurs in Sahih Muslim: "And warn your nearest kinsmen and your kin among those who are sincere." The apparent meaning of this is that it was a Qur'an that was recited and that it was abrogated, since its transmission was not established in the Mushaf and was not transmitted through mass narration (tawatur). If its establishment is granted, a difficulty follows from it: it would have required that he warn only those of his kinsmen who believed, since the believers are the ones described as sincere in the religion of Islam and in love for the Prophet ﷺ, not the polytheists, because they have none of that. Yet the Prophet ﷺ called all of his kinsmen, believing and disbelieving alike, and warned all of them, and those who were with them, and those who would come after them (ﷺ). That is not established either by transmission or by meaning.

Muslim related from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: When this verse was revealed, "And warn your nearest kinsmen," the Messenger of Allah ﷺ summoned the Quraysh, and they gathered. He addressed them generally and specifically, saying: "O Banu Ka'b ibn Lu'ayy, save yourselves from the Fire. O Banu Murrah ibn Ka'b, save yourselves from the Fire. O Banu 'Abd Shams, save yourselves from the Fire. O Banu 'Abd Manaf, save yourselves from the Fire. O Banu Hashim, save yourselves from the Fire. O Banu 'Abd al-Muttalib, save yourselves from the Fire. O Fatimah, save yourself from the Fire, for I possess nothing for you against Allah, except that you have a kinship tie which I will keep moist with its moisture." [[ "sabiluha bi-bilalaha": meaning, your relationship in this world; and I do not avail you anything against Allah.]]

The second: In this hadith and verse there is evidence that nearness of lineage does not benefit when there is distance in deeds, and evidence for the permissibility of a believer maintaining ties with, guiding, and advising a disbeliever, based on his saying: "Indeed you have a kinship tie which I will keep moist with its moisture," and the Most High's saying: "Allah does not forbid you from those who do not fight you over religion..." (the verse), as will be explained there.

The Most High's saying: ﴿And lower your wing to those who follow you among the believers﴾ has been mentioned in Surah al-Hijr and Surah Subhan. It is said: "He lowered his wing" when he became gentle (lana).

(﴿And if they disobey you﴾) i.e., oppose your command.

(﴿Then say: Indeed I am free of what you do﴾) i.e., free of your disobedience to me, because their disobedience to him is disobedience to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, since he (peace be upon him) only commands what pleases Him; and whoever disowns him, Allah has disowned him.

The Most High's saying: ﴿And rely upon the Mighty, the Merciful﴾, i.e., entrust your affair to Him, for He is the Mighty who cannot be overcome, the Merciful who does not forsake His allies. The majority of reciters read "wa-tawakkal" with the waw, and it is so in their codices. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "fa-tawakkal" with the fa, and it is so in the codices of Madinah and Syria.

(﴿Who sees you when you stand﴾), i.e., when you stand for prayer, according to the view of most exegetes: Ibn 'Abbas and others. Mujahid said: it means when you stand wherever you are.

(﴿And your movement among those who prostrate﴾). Mujahid and Qatadah said: among those who pray. Ibn 'Abbas said: i.e., in the loins of the fathers, Adam, Noah and Abraham, until He brought him forth as a prophet. 'Ikrimah said: He sees you standing, bowing and prostrating, and Ibn 'Abbas also said this. It was also said: the meaning is that you see with your heart in your prayer those behind you just as you see with your eye those in front of you. This is narrated from Mujahid, mentioned by al-Mawardi and al-Tha'labi. The Prophet (peace be upon him) used to see those behind him as he saw those before him, and that is established in the Sahih; but as an interpretation of the verse it is remote.

(﴿Indeed He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾). Already mentioned.

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary on Surah 26, verses 221–223:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Shall I inform you upon whom the devils descend? They descend upon every lying sinner﴾. He said "tanazzalu" (they descend) because they are mostly in the air, and because they pass through the wind.

(They cast the hearing, and most of them are liars.) This was discussed earlier in "al-Hijr". So "they cast the hearing" is a description of the devils, and "most of them" refers to the soothsayers (kahana). It was also said: it refers to the devils.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the poets—the erring follow them.﴾ On this there are six issues.

The first: His saying, ﴿And the poets﴾, is the plural of shā'ir (poet), like jāhil (ignorant) and juhalā' (ignorant ones). Ibn 'Abbas said: they are the disbelievers. ﴿The erring follow them﴾: the misguided among the jinn and mankind. It is also said that "al-ghāwūn" (the erring) are those who have departed from the truth. This indicates that the poets too are erring, for if they were not erring, their followers would not be as they are. We have already mentioned in the surah "al-Nur" [[See vol. 12, p. 271, first or second edition.]] that among poetry there is that which is permissible to recite, that which is disliked, and that which is forbidden. Muslim related from the hadith of 'Amr ibn al-Sharid, from his father, who said: I rode behind the Messenger of Allah ﷺ [one day [[The addition is from Sahih Muslim.]]], and he said: "Do you have with you any of the poetry of Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt?" I said: Yes. He said: "Hih." So I recited to him a line. He said: "Hih." Then I recited to him another line. He said: "Hih," until I had recited to him a hundred lines. This is the correct form of this chain and the sound version of its narration. Some of the transmitters of Muslim's book have it as: from 'Amr ibn al-Sharid, from al-Sharid his father, and this is an error, because al-Sharid is the one whom the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had seated behind him. The name of Abu al-Sharid is Suwayd. In this there is evidence for memorizing poetry and attending to it when it contains wisdom and meanings that are praiseworthy in the Sharia and in natural disposition. The Prophet ﷺ only requested much of Umayya's poetry because he was a man of wisdom. Do you not see his saying, peace be upon him: "Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt almost embraced Islam." As for what contains the remembrance of Allah, His praise and glorification, this is recommended, like the saying of the speaker:
"All praise is to Allah, the Exalted, the Bestower... the crumbled bread has become atop the wooden bowls" [[Thus in the originals.]]
or mention of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ or praise of him, like the saying of al-'Abbas:
"From before, you were pure in the shades and in a repository, where the leaves are sewn together.
Then you descended to the lands, not a human are you, nor a lump of flesh nor a clot,
but a drop that rides the ark when it had surged, and Nasr and its people were drowned,
transferred from loin to womb; whenever a generation passes, another generation appears."
[[Tabaq: a generation. He means: when a generation passes, another generation appears.]]
Then the Prophet ﷺ said to him: "May Allah not break your mouth." Or defending him, like the saying of Hassan:
"You satirized Muhammad, so I answered on his behalf, and with Allah is the recompense for that."
These are verses which Muslim mentioned in his Sahih, and they are more complete in the biographies. Or invoking blessings upon him, as Zayd ibn Aslam related: 'Umar went out one night on patrol, and he saw a lamp in a house, and there was an old woman carding wool and saying:
"Upon Muhammad be the blessings of the righteous; blessed upon him are the good and the chosen ones.
You were ever standing in prayer and weeping at the dawns; O, would that I knew, while the fates are varied,
whether the abode will gather me with my beloved"—meaning the Prophet ﷺ.
So 'Umar sat down weeping. Likewise the mention of his Companions and their praise, may Allah be pleased with them. Muhammad ibn Sabiq said well when he said:
"I am pleased with 'Ali as a guide to guidance, just as I am pleased with 'Atiq, the companion of the cave.
And I am pleased with Abu Hafs and his party, and I am not pleased with the killing of the elder in the house.
All the Companions are for me exemplars and banners; so is there shame upon me for this saying?
If You know that I do not love them except for Your sake, then free me from the Fire."
Another said and did well:
"The love of the Prophet, Messenger of Allah, is obligatory, and love of his Companions is a light by proof.
Whoever knows that Allah is his Creator, let him not accuse Abu Bakr with slander,
nor Abu Hafs al-Faruq his companion, nor the caliph 'Uthman ibn 'Affan.
As for 'Ali, his virtues are well known, and a house is not sound except with its pillars."
Ibn al-'Arabi said: As for metaphors within comparisons, they are permitted, even if they extend to the limit and exceed what is customary; by such means the angel charged with dreams strikes the parable. Ka'b ibn Zuhayr recited to the Prophet ﷺ:
"Su'ad has departed, so my heart today is enslaved, lovesick, pursuing her steps, unransomed and fettered.
And Su'ad, at the dawn of parting when they departed, was but a gazelle, with languid glance, kohl-lined.
She polishes the teeth of one with a darkness when she smiles, as if it were a spring mixed with wine, tempered."
In this ode there came metaphors and comparisons of every marvel, and the Prophet ﷺ listened and did not object to his comparison of her saliva to wine. Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him [[He said this in lament for the Prophet ﷺ.]], recited:
"We lost the revelation when you turned away from us, and the word of Allah bade us farewell,
except what you left us as a pledge, which the noble scrolls inherit,
for you bequeathed us an inheritance of truth, upon you be greetings and peace."
So if the Messenger of Allah ﷺ heard it while Abu Bakr recited it, is there a place for imitation and emulation higher than this? Abu 'Umar said: No one among the people of knowledge and the intelligent denies good poetry, and no one from among the great Companions and those of knowledge and worthy of emulation has not composed poetry, or quoted it, or listened to it and approved of it, as long as it contained wisdom or was permissible and had no obscenity, no indecency, and no harm to a Muslim. If that is so, it is the same as prose speech; its hearing and its utterance are not lawful [[sic; the sense is that the content governs]]. Abu Hurayrah related: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say on the pulpit: "The truest word—or the most poetic word—spoken by the Arabs is the saying of Labid:
'Surely everything other than Allah is vain.'"
Muslim reported it and added: "Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt almost embraced Islam." It is related from Ibn Sirin that he recited a poem, and one of his companions said to him: "Someone like you recites poetry, O Abu Bakr?" He said: "Woe to you, O fool! Is poetry anything but speech that differs from ordinary speech only in its rhymes; its good is good and its bad is bad!" He said: And they used to discuss poetry together. He said: I heard Ibn 'Umar recite:
"He loves wine from the wealth of companions, and dislikes that the sweet-smelling should part from him."
'Ubayd Allah ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Utbah ibn Mas'ud, one of the ten jurists of Madinah and then the seven shaykhs, was an accomplished poet and foremost in it. Al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar the judge has a book on his poetry. He had a beautiful wife called 'Athmah, and he reproached her in some matter and divorced her, and he composed many poems about her, among them his saying:
"The love of 'Athmah has seeped into my heart; its apparent and its hidden are slight.
It seeped where neither drink reached, nor sorrow, nor joy reached.
I nearly fly when I recall the covenant with her, if a human could fly."
Ibn Shihab said: I said to him: "You recite poetry in your devotions and your merit!" He said: "Indeed the one afflicted with a cough, when he spits, is healed."

The second: As for blameworthy poetry, whose hearing is not lawful and whose speaker is blameworthy, it is that which speaks falsehood, such as preferring the most cowardly of people over 'Antarah, and the most stingy over Hatim, and slandering the innocent and calling the pious a sinner, and exaggerating in speech about what a man has not done, seeking to console the self and beautify speech, as was related about al-Farazdaq, that Sulayman ibn 'Abd al-Malik heard his saying:
"They spent the night beside me, intoxicated, and I spent the night unlocking the seals of the wine-jar."
He said: "The legal punishment has become obligatory upon you." He said: "O Commander of the Faithful, Allah has averted the punishment from me by His saying: 'And that they say what they do not do.'" And it is related that al-Nu'man ibn 'Adi ibn Nadlah was an agent of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, and he said:
"Who will convey to the beauty that her spouse, in Maysan, is given to drink from glass and jar?
When I wish, the peasants of a village sing to me, and a dancing girl stepping on the tips of her toes on every path."
"So if you are my companion, then pour me the greater; and do not pour me the lesser, the chipped one.
Perhaps the Commander of the Faithful will be displeased by our carousing in the crumbling palace."
This reached 'Umar, and he sent for him to come to him. He said: "By Allah, indeed it displeases me." He said: "O Commander of the Faithful, I did nothing of what I said; it was only an overflow of speech, and Allah, may He be exalted, has said: ﴿And the poets—the erring follow them. Do you not see that they wander in every valley? And that they say what they do not do.﴾" 'Umar said to him: "As for your excuse, it has averted the legal punishment from you, but never work for me any task, since you have said what you have said." Al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar mentioned, saying: Mus'ab ibn 'Uthman related to me that when 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz assumed the caliphate, he had no concern except 'Umar ibn Abi Rabi'ah and al-Ahwas. So he wrote to his agent in Madinah: "I have come to know 'Umar and al-Ahwas for evil and corruption; when this letter of mine reaches you, bind them tightly and bring them to me." When the letter reached him, he brought them to him. He turned to 'Umar and said: "Hih!"
"I have not seen a gaze like the gaze of one who looks at the pilgrims' fires, nor like the sheep of the pilgrimage who have left a man of desire,
and how many a one filling his eyes with something other than it, when he goes toward the white pillar like dolls!"
"By Allah, if you had been concerned with your pilgrimage, you would not have looked at anything but yourself. If people do not escape from you in these days, when will they escape!" Then he ordered his exile. He said: "O Commander of the Faithful! Or something better than that?" He said: "What is it?" He said: "I pledge to Allah that I will never return to the like of this poetry, and I will never mention women in poetry ever, and I renew my repentance." He said: "Will you do it?" He said: "Yes." So he made a covenant with Allah upon his repentance and released him. Then he summoned al-Ahwas, and he said: "Hih!"
"Allah is between me and her who guards her, who flees from me with her, and I pursue."

The text is "Allah is between her guardian and you!" Then he ordered him to be banished. Some men from the Ansar spoke to him about it, but he refused and said, "By Allah, I will not reverse it as long as I have authority, for he is a flagrant sinner." This is the ruling on blameworthy poetry and on its composer. It is not permitted to listen to it or to recite it, whether in a mosque or elsewhere, just as with ugly prose and the like.

Isma'il ibn 'Ayyash narrated from 'Abdullah ibn 'Awn, from Muhammad ibn Sirin, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Good poetry is like good speech, and bad poetry is like bad speech." Isma'il narrated it from 'Abdullah al-Shami, and his narrations from the people of Syria are sound, according to Yahya ibn Ma'in and others. 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As narrated: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Poetry is on the level of speech: its good is like good speech and its bad is like bad speech."

Third: Muslim narrated from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "For one of you to have his insides filled with pus until it consumes him is better than for him to have them filled with poetry." Also in the Sahih, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: "While we were travelling with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), a poet appeared reciting poetry. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Seize the devil'—or 'Hold back the devil'—'for a man's insides filled with pus is better for him than being filled with poetry.'"

Our scholars said: The Prophet's (ﷺ) action with this poet was because of what he knew of his condition. Perhaps this poet was one who was known to have taken poetry as a means of earning a living, exaggerating in praise when given, and in satire and censure when denied, thereby harming people in their wealth and their honour. There is no disagreement that whoever is in such a state, everything he earns through poetry is unlawful, and everything he says of this kind is unlawful for him. Listening to him is not permitted, and rather it is obligatory to denounce him. If that is not possible, and one fears his tongue, it becomes incumbent upon him to placate him as much as he can and to ward him off as far as is possible. It is not permitted for him to give him anything at the outset, because that would be aiding him in disobedience. If he finds no alternative to that, he may give with the intention of protecting his honour, for whatever a person protects his honour with, a charity is recorded for him by it.

His saying, "For one of you to have his insides filled with pus until he..." (qayh): pus, which is matter mixed with blood. It is said of it: "qaha al-jurh yaqihu, wa tqayyaha, wa qayyaha" (the wound oozed pus, and it became festering). As for "yariyahu" (until it consumes him), al-Asma'i said: it is from al-wary, on the pattern of al-ramy, which is when the inside is rotted or consumed. From it one says: "rajul mawriyy" (a man so affected), intensive, and not hamzated. In al-Sihah: "It is narrated that pus fills his insides and consumes him (yariyuhu wariyan) when it eats him." Al-Yazidi recited: "She said to him: 'Wary' whenever he clears his throat."

This hadith is the best of what has been said in its interpretation: it refers to the one whom poetry has overwhelmed, and whose chest is filled with it, with no knowledge other than it and no remembrance of Allah, one who plunges into falsehood with it and takes paths that are not praiseworthy for him, like one who is excessive in noise, idle talk, backbiting and ugly speech. Whoever has poetry as his dominant occupation will be burdened with these blameworthy and base qualities, by the rule of literary habit. This is the meaning that al-Bukhari pointed to in his Sahih when he titled a chapter on this hadith: "Chapter on what is disliked: that poetry should be what dominates a person." It has also been said in its interpretation that what is meant is the poetry in which the Prophet (ﷺ) was satirized, or other than that. This is not sound, because a little satire of the Prophet (ﷺ) and a lot of it are equal in being disbelief and blameworthy, and likewise satirizing any Muslim other than the Prophet (ﷺ) is forbidden, whether little or much; in that case there is no sense in restricting the blame to the abundant.

Fourth: al-Shafi'i said: Poetry is a type of speech: its good is like good speech and its bad is like bad speech. He means that poetry is not disliked in itself, but is disliked for its contents. It had a great standing among the Arabs. The first of them said:

"And the wound of the tongue is like the wound of the hand."

The Prophet (ﷺ) said about the poetry with which Hassan replied to the polytheists: "It is swifter against them than a shower of arrows." Muslim narrated it. Al-Tirmidhi narrated and graded as sound from Ibn 'Abbas that the Prophet (ﷺ) entered Makkah during the 'Umrat al-Qada' while 'Abdullah ibn Rawahah walked before him, saying:

"Clear the way for the sons of the disbelievers from his path.
Today we shall strike you over his revelation,
A blow that removes the skull from its resting place,
And makes the close friend forget his close friend."

'Umar said: "O Ibn Rawahah! In the sanctuary of Allah and before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)!" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Leave him alone, O 'Umar, for he is swifter against them than a spray of arrows."

Fifth: His Exalted saying: ﴿And the poets, the erring follow them﴾. The reciters did not differ, as far as I know, on the raising of "wash-shu'ara'" (and the poets). The accusative is also permissible, by supposing a verb that is explained by "yattabi'uhum" (follow them), and 'Isa ibn 'Umar recited it that way. Abu 'Ubayd said: He was predominantly fond of the accusative, reciting "wa's-sariqu wa's-sariqatu" (the male thief and the female thief), "hammalata al-hatab" (the carrier of firewood), and "surah anzalnaha" (a surah We revealed). Nafi', Shaybah, al-Hasan and al-Sulami recited "yatba'uhum" with a light (unshaddah) ta'. The rest recited "yattabi'uhum."

Al-Dahhak said: Two men insulted each other during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), one of them an Ansari and the other a Muhajir, each with the erring ones of his people, who were the foolish ones, so this was revealed. Ibn 'Abbas also said this. And from him: they are the narrators of poetry. 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah narrated from him that they are the disbelievers, followed by the misguided among jinn and men, and we have mentioned this. Ghudayf [in another copy: Khusayf] narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever initiates satire in Islam, cut out his tongue." And from Ibn 'Abbas: when the Prophet (ﷺ) conquered Makkah, Iblis let out a cry (rann) and gathered his offspring to him, and said: "Despair of ever getting the community of Muhammad back to polytheism after this day of yours. But spread poetry in these two places"—meaning Makkah and Madinah.

Sixth: His Exalted saying: ﴿Have you not seen that they wander in every valley?﴾ It means: they plunge into every idle talk, and they do not follow the ways of truth. For whoever follows the truth and knows that what he says is recorded against him will be careful, and will not be a wanderer going in any direction without caring what he says. It was revealed concerning 'Abdullah ibn al-Zib'ara, Musafi' ibn 'Abd Manaf, and Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt.

﴿And that they say what they do not do﴾: it means most of them lie, that is, they boast through their words of generosity and goodness, but do not do them. It was also said: it was revealed concerning Abu 'Izzah al-Jumahi when he said:

"Let me convey from me to the Prophet Muhammad:
That you are true, and the King is Praiseworthy.
But when Badr and its people are mentioned,
My bones and skin groan with pain."

Then He excepted the poetry of the believers: Hassan ibn Thabit, 'Abdullah ibn Rawahah, Ka'b ibn Malik, Ka'b ibn Zuhayr, and whoever follows their path of true speech. He said: ﴿Except those who believe and do righteous deeds and remember Allah often﴾ in their speech ﴿and who defend themselves after they have been wronged﴾. Defending oneself is only by means of truth and within what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has set as limits. If one exceeds that, he has defended himself by falsehood.

Abu al-Hasan al-Mubarrad said: When "wash-shu'ara'" was revealed, Hassan, Ka'b ibn Malik and Ibn Rawahah came weeping to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Prophet of Allah! Allah the Exalted revealed this verse, and He knows that we are poets?" He said: "Recite what follows it: ﴿except those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾"—the verse—"you are"; "and who defend themselves after they have been wronged"—"you are"—meaning by responding to the polytheists. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Defend yourselves, but say only what is true, and do not mention fathers and mothers."

Hassan then said to Abu Sufyan:

"You satirized Muhammad, so I replied on his behalf,
And with Allah is the recompense for that.
My father, my mother, and my honour
Are a shield for the honour of Muhammad from you.
Do you insult him when you are no match for him?
So your evil and your good are the ransom of the good among you."
"My tongue is a sharp blade with no fault in it,
And my sea is not made turbid by buckets."

Ka'b said: "O Messenger of Allah! Allah has revealed what you know about poetry, so how do you see it?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The believer strives with his self, his sword and his tongue. By Him in whose hand my soul is, what you hurl at them is like a shower of arrows." Ka'b said:

"Sakhinah came hoping to overcome her Lord,
But the overcomer of the overcomers will surely be overcome."

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Allah has praised you, O Ka'b, for this saying of yours."

Al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said concerning His saying: ﴿And the poets, the erring follow them﴾ that it was abrogated (mansukh) by His saying: ﴿except those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾. Al-Mahdawi said: In the Sahih, from Ibn 'Abbas, it is an exception.

﴿And those who have wronged will know what overturning they will be overturned to﴾. In this is a threat to whoever defends himself by wrongdoing [i.e., an addition required by context]. The wrongdoers will know how they will be extricated before Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The wrongdoer awaits punishment, and the wronged awaits victory. Ibn 'Abbas recited: "ayya munfalatin yanfalitun" (what escape they will escape), with fa' and ta', and the meaning is the same. Al-Tha'labi said: The meaning of "ayya munqalabin yanqalibun" (what overturning they will be overturned to) is: what destination they will reach and what return they will return to, for their destination is the Fire, which is the worst destination, and their return is to punishment, which is the worst return. The difference between "munqalab" and "marji'" (return) is that munqalab is a transfer to the opposite of what one is in, while marji' is a return from a state one is in to a state one was previously in. So every return is a munqalab, but not every munqalab is a return. And Allah knows best; this was mentioned by al-Mawardi. "Ayya" is in the accusative governed by "yanqalibun" and is in the sense of a verbal noun (masdar). It cannot be governed by "sa-ya'lamu" (they will know), because, as the grammarians mentioned, interrogative particles and all interrogative words are not governed by what precedes them. Al-Nahhas said: The essence of this is that the interrogative has a meaning and what precedes it has another meaning, so if what precedes it governed it, some meanings would enter into others.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 26, verse 224–227 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the poets—the erring follow them.﴾ On this there are six issues.

The first: His saying, ﴿And the poets﴾, is the plural of shā'ir (poet), like jāhil (ignorant) and juhalā' (ignorant ones). Ibn 'Abbas said: they are the disbelievers. ﴿The erring follow them﴾: the misguided among the jinn and mankind. It is also said that "al-ghāwūn" (the erring) are those who have departed from the truth. This indicates that the poets too are erring, for if they were not erring, their followers would not be as they are. We have already mentioned in the surah "al-Nur" [[See vol. 12, p. 271, first or second edition.]] that among poetry there is that which is permissible to recite, that which is disliked, and that which is forbidden. Muslim related from the hadith of 'Amr ibn al-Sharid, from his father, who said: I rode behind the Messenger of Allah ﷺ [one day [[The addition is from Sahih Muslim.]]], and he said: "Do you have with you any of the poetry of Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt?" I said: Yes. He said: "Hih." So I recited to him a line. He said: "Hih." Then I recited to him another line. He said: "Hih," until I had recited to him a hundred lines. This is the correct form of this chain and the sound version of its narration. Some of the transmitters of Muslim's book have it as: from 'Amr ibn al-Sharid, from al-Sharid his father, and this is an error, because al-Sharid is the one whom the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had seated behind him. The name of Abu al-Sharid is Suwayd. In this there is evidence for memorizing poetry and attending to it when it contains wisdom and meanings that are praiseworthy in the Sharia and in natural disposition. The Prophet ﷺ only requested much of Umayya's poetry because he was a man of wisdom. Do you not see his saying, peace be upon him: "Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt almost embraced Islam." "All praise is to Allah, the Exalted, the Bestower... the crumbled bread has become atop the wooden bowls" [[Thus in the originals.]]

Then you descended to the lands, not a human are you, nor a lump of flesh nor a clot,
but a drop that rides the ark when it had surged, and Nasr and its people were drowned,
transferred from loin to womb; whenever a generation passes, another generation appears."
[[Tabaq: a generation. He means: when a generation passes, another generation appears.]]
Then the Prophet ﷺ said to him: "May Allah not break your mouth." Or defending him, like the saying of Hassan:
"You satirized Muhammad, so I answered on his behalf, and with Allah is the recompense for that."
These are verses which Muslim mentioned in his Sahih, and they are more complete in the biographies. Or invoking blessings upon him, as Zayd ibn Aslam related: 'Umar went out one night on patrol, and he saw a lamp in a house, and there was an old woman carding wool and saying:
